lessons.title: What Data Science Is
lessons.content:
Imagine your mother runs a small grocery shop in Mirpur. Every evening she writes in a khata how much rice, oil, eggs and biscuits she sold. After a year the khata is thick, but it just sits on a shelf. Now imagine you open it and ask one simple question: on which days do eggs run out before closing time? You count, you compare, you notice that eggs vanish every Friday and every day before a holiday. You tell your mother, she buys two extra trays on Thursdays, and she stops losing customers. Congratulations, you just did data science. You had a question, you had data, you cleaned and counted, you found a pattern, and you changed a decision.

What it is: Data science is the practice of using data to answer questions and make better decisions. The key word is decisions. Data on its own is just a pile of facts. A data scientist turns that pile into understanding, and turns understanding into action. It uses ideas from statistics, computer science and the field you are working in, whether that field is cricket, health, banking or farming. In this course we will walk the whole journey: asking the question, collecting data, cleaning it, exploring it, drawing charts, using statistics to avoid fooling ourselves, building features and models, explaining the result, and doing all of it ethically.

Why it is needed: Today almost everything leaves a data trail. Every bKash transfer, every Daraz order, every Pathao ride, every hospital visit and every phone call creates a record. Companies and governments are sitting on mountains of records, but records do not make decisions. Someone has to ask the right questions, check whether the data can answer them, and explain the answer in words a manager or a minister understands. Before data science became a named job, these decisions were often made by gut feeling, by the loudest person in the meeting, or by copying what was done last year. Data science does not replace judgment; it gives judgment better evidence.

A tiny bit of history: The phrase data science was used in the 1960s and 1970s, and the statistician John Tukey argued in 1962 that analysing data deserves to be a science of its own, not just a corner of mathematics. In 2001 William Cleveland proposed data science as an expanded field of statistics. Around 2008 companies like LinkedIn and Facebook started using the job title data scientist, and in 2012 a Harvard Business Review article called it the sexiest job of the 21st century. The name is new, but the activity, learning from data, is as old as the first farmer who wrote down rainfall.

Drew Conway's Venn diagram: In 2010 Drew Conway drew three overlapping circles to explain the skills. The first circle is hacking skills: being comfortable with code, files, databases and messy formats. The second is math and statistics knowledge: knowing what an average hides, what a confidence interval means, why a sample can mislead. The third is substantive expertise, which means knowing the field: a cricket analyst must know what a yorker is, a health analyst must know how dengue spreads. Data science sits where all three overlap. Hacking plus statistics without domain knowledge gives clever answers to the wrong questions. Statistics plus domain without hacking means you cannot handle real data at scale. Hacking plus domain without statistics is what Conway called the danger zone: you can produce results that look convincing but are wrong.

Data science and its cousins: Students often mix up related fields, so let us separate them. Statistics is the science of learning from data under uncertainty; it gives data science its reasoning tools, like sampling, estimation and testing, which you studied in deep-cse-2-6. Machine learning is about algorithms that learn patterns from data to make predictions; it is one powerful tool inside data science, covered in deep-cse-6-1. Data mining focuses on discovering patterns, like groups of customers or items bought together, in large databases; you will study it in deep-cse-7-6. Data engineering builds the pipes and storage that move data reliably from apps into warehouses; that is deep-cse-7-11. Business intelligence, or BI, builds reports and dashboards that show what happened. Data science borrows from all of them and is responsible for the full path from question to decision.

The four kinds of analytics: A handy way to see what data science does is a ladder of four questions. Descriptive analytics asks what happened: total sales last month were 4.2 lakh taka. Diagnostic analytics asks why it happened: sales dropped because a competitor opened next door, or because of a week of heavy rain. Predictive analytics asks what will happen: next month we expect about 4.6 lakh taka because Eid is coming. Prescriptive analytics asks what should we do: stock 30 percent more semai and sugar in the two weeks before Eid. Each step up the ladder is harder and more valuable. Many companies never get past descriptive; good data science climbs as high as the data honestly allows.

The roles in a data team: In a real company the work is split. A data analyst mostly answers descriptive and diagnostic questions with SQL, spreadsheets and dashboards. A data scientist designs experiments, builds predictive models and does deeper statistical analysis. A data engineer builds and runs the pipelines that collect, clean and store data. A machine learning engineer takes a working model and turns it into a reliable service that answers thousands of requests a second. In a small startup in Dhaka one person might do all four jobs; in a large bank they are separate teams. Titles also vary a lot between companies, so read the job description, not just the title.

What a day really looks like: Movies show data scientists staring at beautiful glowing models. Real life is different. A common estimate from surveys is that a large share of time, often quoted as more than half, goes into finding, understanding and cleaning data. Then comes exploring, checking, talking with the people who own the problem, and writing up results. Modeling is often a small slice. This is not a sad fact; it is the job. A simple model on clean, well-understood data beats a fancy model on garbage almost every time. People say garbage in, garbage out, and it is true.

The shape of the work: A data science project is a loop, not a straight line. You start with a question, look at data, discover the data cannot answer it as asked, sharpen the question, collect something new, clean again, explore again. In lesson 02 we will meet CRISP-DM, the most widely used map of this loop. For now remember the core steps: ask, get, clean, explore, model or test, communicate, and then act and measure whether the action worked.

How it works on a small example: Let us run the grocery example with real numbers. Suppose over 10 weeks the shop sold these numbers of egg trays on Fridays: 9, 10, 8, 11, 10, 9, 12, 10, 9, 12. The average is 100 divided by 10, which is 10 trays. On other days the average was about 6 trays. The shop orders 7 trays every day. Descriptively, Fridays sell about 4 more trays than other days. Diagnostically, Friday is the weekend and families cook more. Predictively, next Friday we expect about 10 trays, give or take 1 or 2. Prescriptively, order 11 trays on Thursday evening so Friday rarely runs out. That small chain of reasoning is the whole field in miniature.

Real-life example 1, cricket: Team analysts record every ball: line, length, speed, the shot played and the runs scored. Raw data is messy; a few balls have the wrong bowler name, some speeds are missing. After cleaning, the analyst groups balls by the opposing batter and the type of delivery. She notices one batter scores 4 runs per over against full balls but only 1.5 against short balls outside off stump in the first 10 overs. She draws a simple pitch map, explains it to the bowling coach in two sentences, and the plan for the next match changes. That last step, changing the plan, is what makes it data science and not just number collecting.

Real-life example 2, dengue in Dhaka: Health officials collect daily dengue cases by ward, along with rainfall. A data scientist cleans the data (different hospitals spell ward names differently, some days are missing), plots cases against rainfall, and sees cases tend to rise a couple of weeks after heavy rain, which fits how mosquito larvae grow in standing water. She is careful: this is a pattern, not proof, and many other things also change. Still, it is useful. A simple forecast tells the city corporation which wards may see a jump soon, so cleanup teams and hospital beds can be prepared earlier.

More places you meet data science: When Daraz shows phones you might like, a recommendation model is working. When a bank blocks a strange card payment at 3 AM, a fraud model flagged it. When a telecom operator offers you a cheap data pack just as you were about to switch, a churn model predicted you might leave. When the weather office forecasts a cyclone's path, huge data and models are behind it. When a garments factory tracks defects per line, simple data analysis decides where to send the quality inspector.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: The first mistake is starting with the tool instead of the question: "let's use deep learning" before knowing what decision will change. The second is thinking data science equals machine learning; ML is one tool. The third is trusting data blindly; data is made by people and machines that make mistakes. The fourth is stopping at a chart; if no decision changes, the work did not finish. Exams typically ask you to define data science, draw and explain Conway's Venn diagram, compare data science with statistics, ML, data mining and BI, list the four types of analytics with examples, and describe the roles in a data team.

Course map: Lessons 02 and 03 cover the life cycle and how to ask sharp questions and choose metrics. Lessons 04 to 11 are about data itself: types, collecting, SQL, Python, pandas and cleaning. Lessons 12 to 15 are exploration and visualization. Lessons 16 to 18 are statistics for real decisions: uncertainty, A/B tests and causation. Lessons 19 to 22 are features and modeling as a practitioner. Lessons 23 and 24 are communication and ethics, and lesson 25 brings it all together in a capstone project.

Recap: Data science is learning from data to make better decisions. It needs coding, statistics and domain knowledge together. It climbs from describing what happened to recommending what to do. Most of the effort goes into the data, and the work is only finished when someone acts on it. Keep the grocery shop in mind; every big project in this course is that same story at a larger scale.
key_points: Data science is the whole journey from a real question, through data, to a decision people can act on.
Drew Conway's Venn diagram: hacking skills, math and statistics, and domain knowledge; all three together make data science.
Statistics gives the reasoning, machine learning gives prediction tools, data engineering moves and stores data, BI reports it; data science stitches them together.
Four kinds of analytics: descriptive (what happened), diagnostic (why), predictive (what will happen), prescriptive (what should we do).
Roles differ: analysts explain the past, data scientists predict and test, data engineers build pipelines, ML engineers put models into production.
Most of the work is not modeling but questions, data, cleaning, checking and explaining.
Good data science changes a decision; a pretty chart that changes nothing is not the goal.
lessons.tip: Every time you see a number in the news or an app, ask the data scientist's four questions: what happened, why, what will happen, and what should we do? You will start seeing data science everywhere.
lessons.task: Pick one thing you can count at home for a week, like how many cups of tea the family drinks or how long the load-shedding lasts each day. Write a sharp question about it, record the numbers in a small table, and at the end of the week write one descriptive finding and one decision it suggests.

quiz.q: Which is the best description of data science?
options: Training neural networks on big computers
Storing data safely in a database
Turning a real question and raw data into an answer that drives a decision
quiz.explain: Data science is the whole journey. Models, databases and charts are tools used along the way.

quiz.q: "Sales fell 12 percent in July" is an example of which kind of analytics?
quiz.explain: It only reports what happened. Asking why it fell would be diagnostic.

quiz.q: In Drew Conway's Venn diagram, someone with strong coding and statistics but no domain knowledge risks what?
options: Answering the wrong question or missing obvious real-world facts
Being unable to make any charts
quiz.explain: Without knowing the field you can build clever analyses that miss what actually matters.

quiz.q: Who mainly builds and maintains the pipelines that move data from apps into a warehouse?
quiz.explain: Data engineers build the plumbing. Analysts and scientists use what flows through it.

quiz.q: A model predicts which shops will run out of stock and then suggests how much to reorder. The reorder suggestion is which kind of analytics?
quiz.explain: Recommending an action is prescriptive. Predicting the stock-out alone would be predictive.

lessons.title: The Data Science Life Cycle
lessons.content:
Think about cooking biryani for a family dawat. You do not start by throwing rice into a pot. First you find out how many guests are coming and whether anyone cannot eat beef. Then you check what is in the kitchen. You wash rice, cut meat and marinate. You cook. You taste and adjust the salt. Finally you serve, and next day you hear what people liked so the next dawat is better. A data science project follows a very similar recipe, and over the years people have written that recipe down so teams do not skip steps. This lesson is about that recipe, called the data science life cycle.

What it is: The life cycle is a map of the phases a data project goes through, from the first conversation to the moment a result is used every day. The most widely used map is CRISP-DM, the Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining. It was created in the late 1990s by a group of companies so that data projects in any industry could share a common language. Despite the old name, it fits modern data science very well. It has six phases: business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modeling, evaluation and deployment.

Why a map is needed: Without a map, teams jump straight to the fun part, the model, and discover weeks later that they answered the wrong question or used data that does not exist in real time. A map forces you to ask the boring but vital questions first. It also helps managers see where a project is and why it takes time. Finally, it gives a checklist: if you cannot write the success criteria in phase one, you are not ready for phase four.

Phase 1, business understanding: Here you talk to the people who own the problem. What decision will change? Who makes it, how often, and what does a good result look like in their units, like taka saved or patients reached? What are the constraints: time, budget, privacy, the data you are allowed to use? You also turn the business goal into a data goal. "Lose fewer customers" might become "predict which postpaid customers will cancel in the next 30 days so the retention team can call the top 500". You write success criteria now, before seeing results, so you cannot move the goalposts later.

Phase 2, data understanding: Now you find out what data exists. Which tables, which columns, how far back, how complete? You load samples, count rows, check missing values, look at simple charts and talk to whoever collects the data. This is where unpleasant surprises appear: the stock-out you wanted to predict was never recorded, or customer ids changed format two years ago. Often you must go back to phase 1 and adjust the question. That loop back is normal, not a failure.

Phase 3, data preparation: This is usually the biggest phase in time. You select the rows and columns you need, clean errors, handle missing values, join tables, create new features, and reshape everything into the form the analysis needs, often one row per thing you are predicting. Lessons 08 to 11 and 19 of this course live here. A good habit is to write preparation as code that can be rerun from raw data, not as manual edits in a spreadsheet.

Phase 4, modeling: Here you choose and fit techniques. It might be a simple statistical test, a regression, a decision tree or a clustering. You start with a baseline, the simplest reasonable answer, so you know whether a fancy model actually helps. Different models may need different preparation, so you often bounce between phases 3 and 4. Deep-cse-6-1 taught the models; lessons 20 to 22 here are about using them as a practitioner.

Phase 5, evaluation: This is not only computing accuracy. You ask: does the result meet the success criteria from phase 1? Is it good enough to change the decision? Did we make mistakes, like leaking future information into training? Are there groups where it fails badly? Would the people who must use it trust it? Only then do you decide to deploy, to iterate, or to stop. Stopping is a valid outcome; learning that the data cannot answer a question saves money.

Phase 6, deployment: The result is put to work. Deployment can be as simple as a one-page report sent to the manager, a weekly dashboard, a rule added to a process ("reorder when stock falls below 20"), or a live model inside an app. Deployment also means planning monitoring and maintenance: data changes, customers change, and a model that was good last year may quietly become bad. Finally you write down what was learned for the next project.

Why it loops: In the CRISP-DM picture, arrows go back and forth between phases, and a big circle surrounds them all. That circle says the end of one project is often the start of the next question. A dashboard shows a new pattern, the team asks why, and a new cycle begins. Expect to loop; plan time for it.

What each phase produces: A useful trick is to name the small document or artifact each phase leaves behind, so you know when a phase is done. Business understanding ends with a one-page project brief: the decision, the owner, the success criteria and the constraints. Data understanding ends with a data report: sources, row counts, date ranges, missing values and known problems. Data preparation ends with a rerunnable script and a clean dataset, plus a short log of every cleaning choice. Modeling ends with the baseline and the candidate models, each with its scores. Evaluation ends with a go or no-go note that compares results to the brief. Deployment ends with the working report, dashboard or service, a monitoring plan and a handover note saying who owns it now. If you cannot point to the artifact, the phase is probably not finished.

OSEMN, a lighter map: Another popular map, from Hilary Mason and Chris Wiggins in 2010, is OSEMN, pronounced like "awesome". It stands for obtain (get the data), scrub (clean it), explore (look at it), model (build models) and interpret (explain the results). It skips business understanding and deployment as named steps, so it fits small analyses, but in real companies the CRISP-DM phases at both ends are often what decide success. Some teams also use TDSP, Microsoft's Team Data Science Process, which adds roles and templates on top of similar phases.

Where the time goes, with numbers: Suppose a project has 8 weeks. A realistic split might be 1 week of business understanding, 1.5 weeks of data understanding, 3 weeks of preparation, 1 week of modeling, 0.5 week of evaluation and 1 week of deployment and handover. Add them: 1 + 1.5 + 3 + 1 + 0.5 + 1 = 8 weeks. Modeling is only 1 of 8 weeks, or 12.5 percent. Exact numbers vary a lot by project, but the pattern, preparation heavy and modeling light, is very common.

A walked example, a pharmacy chain: Imagine an invented pharmacy chain, "ShasthoPlus", with 40 branches in Dhaka. Customers complain that common medicines like paracetamol syrup and ORS are often out of stock. In business understanding you learn the decision: how much of each item each branch orders every week. Success: cut stock-out days for the top 100 items by half within three months without raising total stock value by more than 10 percent. Constraint: only sales and delivery data, no customer personal data.

The example continued: In data understanding you find two years of daily sales per branch and item, and weekly deliveries. Problem: a stock-out is never recorded directly. But you notice that zero sales of a normally popular item on a day right before a delivery strongly suggests a stock-out. You agree with the managers to use that as a proxy and accept it is imperfect. In data preparation you fix branch names spelled three ways, remove test transactions, add features like day of week and days to Eid, and build one row per branch, item and week.

The example finished: In modeling, your baseline forecast is "next week equals the average of the last four weeks". A slightly smarter model adds a seasonal Eid effect and branch size. In evaluation you replay the last six months: with the new forecast plus a safety buffer, simulated stock-out days fall from 1,200 to 550, a 54 percent cut, while stock value rises 7 percent. That meets the criteria. In deployment, each Thursday branch managers get a suggested order list in a simple spreadsheet, and a dashboard tracks actual stock-outs. Three months later you check whether real stock-outs fell, which starts the next loop.

Checking the arithmetic: The fall from 1,200 to 550 is 650 days. Divide 650 by 1,200 and you get about 0.54, which is 54 percent, more than the 50 percent target. The 7 percent stock increase is under the 10 percent limit. Writing the criteria first made this evaluation a simple comparison rather than an argument.

Real-life example 2, a mobile operator: A telecom team wants to reduce prepaid customers leaving. Business understanding reveals the real decision is which customers get a retention offer by SMS, with a budget of 50,000 offers a month. Data understanding shows "leaving" is not recorded for prepaid users, since they just stop recharging, so the team defines churn as no recharge for 60 days. Preparation builds usage features; modeling ranks customers by churn risk; evaluation checks whether offers to the top-ranked customers actually keep more of them than random offers, using an experiment like the ones in lesson 17; deployment sends the monthly list to the marketing system.

Why projects fail: Studies and industry surveys keep finding that many data projects never reach use. The usual causes are a vague goal ("do something with AI"), data that cannot answer the question, results that are never connected to a real process, and people who do not trust or understand the output. Notice that a weak algorithm is rarely the main cause. The life cycle exists to catch these problems early, in phases 1, 2 and 5.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Common mistakes are skipping business understanding, treating the cycle as a straight line, evaluating only with a model metric, and thinking deployment is the end instead of the start of monitoring. Exams usually ask you to name and explain the six CRISP-DM phases in order, draw the cycle with its loops, compare CRISP-DM with OSEMN, and apply the phases to a scenario such as churn or sales forecasting.

Recap: A data project is a recipe with six phases: understand the business, understand the data, prepare it, model it, evaluate against the real goal, and deploy with monitoring. You will loop between phases, and that is healthy. Most of the time goes into preparation, and most failures come from the ends of the cycle, not the middle. Next lesson we zoom into the very first phase and learn how to turn a vague wish into a sharp question with the right metric.
key_points: CRISP-DM has six phases: business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modeling, evaluation, deployment.
The arrows loop back; discoveries in later phases often send you back to earlier ones.
OSEMN is a lighter map: obtain, scrub, explore, model, interpret.
Business understanding fixes the decision, the success criteria and the constraints before any code.
Evaluation judges the result against the business goal, not only against a model metric.
Deployment can be a report, a dashboard, a rule or a live model, and it needs monitoring.
Projects usually fail from a vague goal, unusable data or no one acting on the result, not from a weak algorithm.
lessons.tip: Before you open any data, write one sentence for each CRISP-DM phase on a single page. That page becomes your project plan, and you will be surprised how often the business understanding line is the hardest to write.
lessons.task: Take a problem you know, like long queues at your college canteen. Write the six CRISP-DM phases as headings and fill each with two or three lines: the decision, the data you would need, the cleaning you expect, a simple model or analysis, how you would judge success, and how the result would be used every day.

quiz.q: In CRISP-DM, which phase comes right before modeling?
quiz.explain: The order is business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modeling, evaluation, deployment.

quiz.q: During data understanding you find the sales table has no record of stock-outs at all. What is the most sensible next step?
options: Go back and adjust the question or find a new data source
quiz.explain: CRISP-DM loops back. If the data cannot answer the question, change the question or get better data.

quiz.q: A model has an excellent accuracy score, but the shop managers say it does not help them order better. Which phase should have caught this?
options: Evaluation, checking against the business goal
quiz.explain: Evaluation asks whether the result meets the business success criteria, not just a technical metric.

quiz.q: What does the S in OSEMN stand for?
quiz.explain: OSEMN is obtain, scrub, explore, model and interpret.

quiz.q: Which is the most common reason data science projects fail?
options: The algorithm was not the newest one
The goal was vague, the data unusable, or nobody acted on the result
quiz.explain: Most failures are about the problem framing, data and adoption rather than the algorithm.

lessons.title: Asking Good Questions and Choosing Metrics
lessons.content:
Imagine your younger cousin says, "Tell me about cricket." Where do you even start? Rules? History? Players? Now imagine she says, "Why does Bangladesh lose more wickets in the last five overs than other teams?" Suddenly you know exactly what to look at. Data works the same way. A vague request gives vague answers; a sharp question tells you which data to get, which number to compute and what to do with the result. This lesson is about the most underrated skill in data science: turning a fuzzy wish into a sharp, answerable question with the right metric.

What a good question is: A good data question is specific, measurable, tied to a decision, and answerable with data you can actually get. "Improve sales" is a wish. "Which 10 products had the biggest drop in weekly sales in Chattogram branches between January and March, and was the drop bigger where the new competitor opened?" is a question. It names a population (Chattogram branches), a time window (January to March), a metric (weekly sales) and a comparison (near the competitor versus not).

Why it matters: Data is huge and time is short. Without a sharp question you will wander through tables, make many charts, and find "interesting" patterns that nobody can use. Worse, if you look at enough things you will find something that looks significant by pure luck, a trap we meet again in lesson 17. A sharp question also makes the project easy to explain and easy to judge: either you answered it or you did not.

The decision test: The best single test of a question is: what will someone do differently depending on the answer? If the answer is "nothing", the question is trivia. For example, "what percentage of our users are left-handed?" is fun but changes nothing for a grocery app. "Do users who see delivery time on the home screen order more often?" can change what the home screen shows. Always find the person who owns the decision and ask them directly.

From vague to sharp, step by step: Start with the wish: "we want fewer late deliveries". Ask who and where: all of Dhaka or only some zones? Ask how late is late: more than 10 minutes after the promised time? Ask the unit: per order. Ask the window: last 8 weeks. Ask the comparison: by zone, time of day and restaurant. Now the question is "Over the last 8 weeks, what share of orders arrived more than 10 minutes after the promised time, broken down by zone, hour and restaurant, and which combination accounts for most late orders?" Every word now tells you what data and calculation you need.

Unit of analysis: The unit of analysis is the thing each row represents in your final table: a customer, an order, a shop-day, a patient visit. Choosing it is a big decision. "Average spending per customer" and "average spending per order" are different numbers. Suppose 2 customers place orders: Rina places 1 order of 1,000 taka, Karim places 4 orders of 250 taka each. Per order, the average is (1,000 + 4 x 250) / 5 = 2,000 / 5 = 400 taka. Per customer, the average is (1,000 + 1,000) / 2 = 1,000 taka. Same data, different unit, very different answer. Always state the unit.

Analytics type again: Remember the ladder from lesson 01. Decide early whether your question is descriptive, diagnostic, predictive or prescriptive. "How many late orders?" is descriptive and needs counting. "Why are they late?" is diagnostic and needs comparison and maybe experiments. "Which orders will be late tomorrow?" is predictive and needs a model. "How many riders should we schedule per zone per hour?" is prescriptive and needs a model plus an optimisation. The type decides the tools and the time.

Metrics and KPIs: A metric is any number you track: number of orders, average delivery time, app crashes per day. A KPI, or key performance indicator, is one of the small set of metrics directly tied to a goal, which leaders watch closely. A company may track 500 metrics but only 5 to 10 KPIs. A good metric is clearly defined (exact formula, exact time window), sensitive (it moves when things really change), hard to game, and understandable by the people who use it.

Defining a metric precisely: "Delivery time" sounds clear but is not. From when? Order placed, order confirmed, or food picked up? To when? Rider arrives at the building or customer marks received? Do cancelled orders count? A precise definition might be: "minutes from order confirmation to the rider marking delivered, for completed orders only, reported as the median per day". Notice we chose the median, because a few orders stuck for two hours would pull the mean far up (recap of deep-cse-2-6 lesson 03).

Counts versus rates: Raw counts often mislead because they ignore size. Suppose zone A had 50 complaints last month and zone B had 30. Zone A looks worse. But zone A handled 10,000 orders and zone B only 3,000. Per 1,000 orders, zone A had 50 / 10,000 x 1,000 = 5 complaints, while zone B had 30 / 3,000 x 1,000 = 10 complaints. Zone B is actually twice as bad. Whenever you compare groups of different sizes, divide by the right denominator: per order, per customer, per 1,000 people, per day. And think carefully about which denominator: complaints per order and complaints per customer can tell different stories, which is the unit-of-analysis lesson again.

Leading and lagging metrics: A lagging metric tells you the result after it has happened, like monthly customer churn or yearly profit. It is the final score, but by the time you see it, it is too late to change. A leading metric moves earlier and predicts the lagging one, like late deliveries this week, app crash rate, or how many users opened the app but did not order. Good dashboards show both: leading ones to act on, lagging ones to confirm the actions worked.

Proxy metrics: Often the thing you care about cannot be measured directly. You cannot measure "customer happiness", so you use proxies: star ratings, repeat orders, complaints. You cannot measure "learning", so a school uses test scores. A proxy is fine as long as you remember it is a stand-in and check that it actually moves with the real thing.

Goodhart's law: Economist Charles Goodhart observed that a measure used for control tends to stop behaving; it is popularly phrased as "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure". If a call centre rewards short calls, agents hang up on hard customers. If a hospital is judged only on short waiting times, it may rush patients. If a team is judged on the number of bugs fixed, they may create small bugs to fix. The defence is to use several metrics together and to keep asking whether the number still reflects the real goal.

North star and guardrails: Many product teams pick one north star metric that best captures the value customers get, for example "orders delivered on time per week" for a delivery app. Around it they set guardrail metrics, numbers that must not get worse, such as cancellation rate, rider complaint rate and refund cost. If a change pushes the north star up but breaks a guardrail, it is not a real win. We will use exactly this pattern when designing A/B tests in lesson 17.

Success criteria and hypotheses up front: Before touching the data, write what result would count as success and what you expect to find. "We expect late orders to be concentrated in 3 zones at dinner time; if those 3 zones account for over 40 percent of late orders, we will move 20 riders there." Writing this first protects you from the very human habit of seeing what you want in results and calling it the goal all along. It also makes it clear when the data surprises you, which is where learning happens.

Fermi estimation: Sometimes before collecting any data you need a rough size, to check whether a question is worth answering at all. Fermi estimation, named after physicist Enrico Fermi, breaks a big unknown into small guesses. Example: how many online grocery orders might there be per day in Dhaka? Assume about 2 crore people, that is 20,000,000. With about 4 people per household, that is 50 lakh households. Suppose 5 percent order groceries online once a week: 5 percent of 5,000,000 is 250,000 orders per week. Divide by 7 and you get about 35,700 orders per day. The real number could be half or double, but now you know the market is tens of thousands of orders a day, not hundreds or millions, and that is enough to decide whether to start.

Real-life example 1, a school: A head teacher says, "Our results are bad." The data scientist asks which results, which classes, compared with what. The sharp question becomes: "In the last 3 years of SSC results, which subjects have the lowest pass rate for our students compared with the district average, and did students who attended the extra coaching class do better in those subjects?" The unit is the student-subject, the metric is pass rate, the comparison is coaching versus not. A careful analyst also notes that students who chose coaching may differ from those who did not, which is a causation trap for lesson 18.

Real-life example 2, a mobile wallet: A wallet company wants "more active users". Active must be defined: a user with at least one money-moving transaction in the last 30 days. North star: 30-day active users. Guardrails: fraud rate and failed-transaction rate. A leading metric: share of new users who complete their first send-money within 7 days of sign-up. The team then asks a sharp question: "Among users who signed up in the last 3 months, which onboarding steps do those who never transact drop out at?" That points straight at the screens to fix.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Common mistakes are answering a question nobody asked, using vague metrics like "engagement" without a formula, mixing units of analysis, choosing a metric that is easy to game, and deciding the success criteria after seeing the numbers. Exams ask you to turn a vague business problem into a data question, define a metric precisely, distinguish metrics from KPIs and leading from lagging indicators, explain Goodhart's law with an example, and do a short Fermi estimate.

Recap: A good question is specific, measurable, tied to a decision and answerable. Fix the unit of analysis, the population, the time window and a precisely defined metric. Pair a north star with guardrails, prefer leading metrics for action, and remember that any metric turned into a target can be gamed. Write success criteria and hypotheses before you look. With a sharp question in hand, the next step is understanding what shape your data takes, which is lesson 04.
key_points: A sharp question names the decision, the population, the unit of analysis, the time window and the metric.
A metric is any number you track; a KPI is one of the few metrics tied directly to a goal.
Leading metrics move early and can be acted on; lagging metrics confirm results later.
Proxy metrics stand in for what you cannot measure directly, and Goodhart's law warns they break when they become targets.
A north star metric captures value for customers; guardrail metrics make sure you are not causing harm elsewhere.
Write the success criteria and hypotheses before looking at results.
Fermi estimation breaks a big unknown into small guessable pieces and checks whether a question is even worth asking.
lessons.tip: When someone hands you a vague request, ask "what will you do differently depending on the answer?" If they cannot say, the question is not ready yet, and that one question can save weeks of work.
lessons.task: Choose a goal from your life, like "study better" or "spend less on transport". Rewrite it as a sharp question with a unit of analysis, a time window and one metric. Then add one guardrail metric and write down, before measuring anything, what result would make you change your behaviour.

quiz.q: Which is the sharpest version of "we want happier customers"?
options: Did the share of orders rated 4 or 5 stars rise from March to June for Dhaka customers after the new packaging?
quiz.explain: It names the population, time window, metric and the change being judged.

quiz.q: A call centre is rewarded for short call times, and agents start hanging up on hard calls. What is this an example of?
options: Goodhart's law: a measure that becomes a target stops being a good measure
quiz.explain: Once the number became the target, people optimised the number instead of the real goal.

quiz.q: For a food delivery app, which is a leading metric for monthly customer loss?
options: Number of customers lost last month
Rise in late deliveries this week
quiz.explain: Late deliveries show up early and can be fixed before customers actually leave.

quiz.q: Why should success criteria be written before analysis?
options: So you cannot move the goalposts after seeing the results
quiz.explain: Deciding in advance what counts as success protects you from fooling yourself.

quiz.q: What is the unit of analysis in "average spending per customer per month"?
quiz.explain: Each row you average over is one customer in one month.

lessons.title: Data Types, Tidy Data and File Formats
lessons.content:
Imagine two friends each keep a record of the family's monthly electricity bills. One writes in a notebook: "January was high, around 2k, Feb lower, March forgot." The other keeps a neat table with three columns, month, units used and bill in taka, one row per month, every number filled in. Six months later, which record can answer "how much did we spend in summer compared with winter?" Obviously the second. The data is the same family, the same bills, but the shape and type of the record decide what you can do with it. This lesson is about those shapes and types, and the file formats that carry them.

Structured, semi-structured and unstructured: Structured data fits neatly into rows and columns with fixed meanings, like a bank's transaction table or a school's marks sheet. Semi-structured data has some organisation but flexible fields, like JSON from an app where one order has 2 items and another has 15, or where some customers have an email field and others do not. Unstructured data has no table shape at all: Facebook posts, customer voice calls, X-ray images, CCTV video. Most classic data science works on structured data, so a big part of the job is turning the other two kinds into tables, for example by counting words in reviews or extracting the date and amount from scanned receipts. Deep learning, NLP and computer vision (deep-cse-8-1, 8-2, 8-3) go deep on unstructured data.

Why types matter: The type of a variable decides which calculations make sense. You can average order amounts, but averaging district names is nonsense. You can sort customer ratings from poor to excellent, but sorting blood groups has no meaning. Getting the type wrong leads to silent errors: a model that treats district codes 1 to 64 as numbers will think district 64 is "bigger" than district 2, which is meaningless.

Numeric variables: Numeric variables are measured or counted numbers. Discrete numeric variables are counts that jump in whole steps, like number of children or number of orders. Continuous variables can take any value in a range, like weight, temperature or delivery time in minutes. Statisticians also split numeric data into interval scale, where differences mean something but zero is arbitrary (temperature in Celsius: 30 degrees is not twice as hot as 15), and ratio scale, where zero means none and ratios make sense (income: 40,000 taka is twice 20,000). Recall these scales from deep-cse-2-6 lesson 01.

Categorical variables: Categorical variables put things into groups. Nominal categories have no order: district, payment method (bKash, Nagad, card, cash), blood group. Ordinal categories have an order but unequal or unknown gaps: education level (primary, SSC, HSC, graduate), customer rating (poor, fair, good, excellent), T-shirt size (S, M, L, XL). For ordinal data the median makes sense but the mean is risky, because the gap between poor and fair may not equal the gap between good and excellent.

Numbers that are not numbers: Some columns look numeric but are really labels. Mobile numbers, national ID numbers, postcodes like 1216 for Mirpur, student roll numbers and product codes are all categorical. Two warnings follow. First, never do maths on them: the average postcode means nothing. Second, store them as text, because tools that read 01712345678 as a number will drop the leading zero and you will get 1712345678, which no longer matches other tables.

Datetime, text and boolean: Datetime variables record a moment or a date, and they are rich: from one timestamp you can get year, month, day of week, hour, whether it was a holiday, and how long ago it was. They are also full of traps: time zones, different formats like 03/04/2024 meaning 3 April in Bangladesh but March 4 in the United States, and Bangla versus Gregorian calendars. Text variables are free writing, like product reviews or complaint notes. Boolean variables are yes or no, true or false, like "is_premium_customer". Store booleans as true and false or 1 and 0, not as a mix of "Y", "yes", "1" and "TRUE".

Tidy data: In 2014 statistician Hadley Wickham described tidy data with three rules. Each variable is a column. Each observation is a row. Each type of observational unit is its own table. It sounds obvious, but most real spreadsheets break it. The payoff is huge: tidy data can be filtered, grouped, joined, plotted and fed to models with the same small set of tools, while messy data needs custom code every time.

Breaking the rules, example 1: A spreadsheet has columns district, Jan, Feb, Mar, with rainfall in millimetres in each cell. Here "month" is a variable, but it is hiding in the column headers, and "rainfall" is spread across three columns. This is called wide form. The tidy, long form has three columns: district, month, rainfall_mm. Two districts and three months become 6 rows: Dhaka Jan 7, Dhaka Feb 20, Dhaka Mar 55, Sylhet Jan 6, Sylhet Feb 35, Sylhet Mar 150, and so on. Now "average rainfall by month" is one grouping, and adding April is adding rows, not changing the table's structure.

Breaking the rules, example 2: A column called "name_age" holds values like "Rina_23". Two variables are squeezed into one column; the fix is to split it into name and age. Another common break is one cell holding several values, like "phones: 017..., 018...". Another is mixing two observational units in one table, for example repeating the customer's address on every order row. If the customer moves, you must update hundreds of rows, and you will miss some. The tidy fix is a customers table and an orders table linked by customer_id, the same idea as normalisation in database design (deep-cse-4-2).

Wide versus long, when each is useful: Long form is usually best for analysis, grouping and plotting. Wide form is often best for humans reading a report, and some models expect a wide feature table with one row per customer and one column per feature. So you will reshape back and forth; pandas has melt to go wide to long and pivot to go long to wide, which we use in lesson 09. Neither shape is wrong; the question is which shape fits the next step.

CSV files: CSV, comma-separated values, is the most common way to share tables. It is plain text, so any tool can open it. But it has traps. It stores no types, so every reader must guess whether "01712345678" is text or a number. Values that contain commas, like "Mirpur 10, Dhaka", must be wrapped in quotes or the row breaks into extra columns. There is no single standard for dates, decimal marks or missing values: one file writes NA, another leaves the cell empty, another writes 0, which is the most dangerous because it looks like a real value.

JSON files: JSON stores data as nested key-value pairs and lists, and it is what most web APIs return. An order might look like: {"order_id": 501, "customer": {"id": 77, "city": "Dhaka"}, "items": [{"sku": "RICE5", "qty": 2}, {"sku": "OIL1", "qty": 1}]}. This is great for apps but not yet a table. To analyse it you flatten it: one row per order with customer_id and city as columns, and a separate items table with one row per order and item. Deciding how to flatten is part of tidying.

Excel files: Excel is everywhere in offices, and you will receive many files from it. Traps include merged cells, several tables on one sheet, totals rows mixed into data rows, colours used to mean something ("red rows are cancelled"), numbers stored as text, and automatic conversion of things that look like dates. A famous problem in biology was gene names like SEPT2 being turned into dates by spreadsheet software, so much that some gene names were officially changed. Treat Excel files as input to clean, and never let colour carry information that is not in a column.

Parquet and columnar formats: For large data, formats like Parquet store data column by column instead of row by row, keep the data types, and compress each column. If a table has 50 columns and you need only 3, a columnar reader can read just those 3, skipping most of the file. Compression works well because one column has similar values, like many repeats of "Dhaka". The trade-off is that you cannot open Parquet in a text editor, so CSV remains common for small, human-shared files. Big data systems (deep-cse-7-2) rely heavily on columnar storage.

Text encoding and Bangla: Computers store text as bytes, and the encoding says how characters map to bytes. Use UTF-8 everywhere; it can store every script. English letters take 1 byte each in UTF-8, but Bangla characters take 3 bytes each, so the 5-character word বাংলা takes 15 bytes. If a file is opened with the wrong encoding you see garbage like Ã¦ symbols, often called mojibake. Another subtle trap: the same-looking Bangla letter য় can be stored as one code point or as two (য followed by a nukta sign). They look identical on screen but compare as different strings, so a search for a district name might miss half the rows. The fix is to apply one Unicode normalisation consistently during cleaning.

The data dictionary: Every dataset you build or receive should come with a data dictionary: for each column, its name, meaning, type, unit, allowed values or range, how missing values are written, and where it came from. For example: "delivery_min, integer, minutes from order confirmation to delivered, 0 to 300, empty if cancelled, from the rider app". It is the cheapest insurance in data science. Metadata like when the file was made, by whom, and which date range it covers belongs with it.

Real-life example 1, a survey: An NGO runs a household survey in Rangpur and gets an Excel file with one sheet per upazila, merged header cells, and a column "family members (M/F)" holding values like "3/2". The analyst stacks the sheets into one long table with an upazila column, splits the M/F column into male_members and female_members as integers, converts the "monthly income" column from text like "8,000 tk" to numbers, and writes a data dictionary. Only then can she compare upazilas fairly.

Real-life example 2, an e-commerce app: A shopping app logs every order as JSON. The data team flattens it nightly into three tidy tables: customers, orders and order_items, stored as Parquet. An analyst asking "which product categories sell most in Khulna on weekends?" joins orders to order_items, uses the order timestamp to make a weekday column, and gets the answer in seconds, because the shape was settled once instead of in every analysis.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include treating ID numbers as numeric, averaging ordinal ratings without thinking, letting tools guess types silently, keeping wide tables when analysis needs long ones, using 0 to mean missing, and ignoring encoding until Bangla turns into garbage. Exams ask you to classify variables by type and scale, state Wickham's three tidy data rules, convert a small wide table to long form, compare CSV, JSON, Excel and Parquet, and explain structured versus semi-structured versus unstructured data.

Recap: Know your data's shape before you analyse it. Classify each column's type, because type decides valid maths and charts. Keep data tidy: variables in columns, observations in rows, one table per kind of thing. Choose file formats for the job, use UTF-8, and write a data dictionary. Next we look at where data comes from in the first place, and how the way it is collected can quietly bias everything after.
key_points: Structured data fits rows and columns; semi-structured data like JSON has flexible nested fields; unstructured data is text, images, audio and video.
Variables are numeric (discrete or continuous), categorical (nominal or ordinal), datetime, text or boolean, and the type decides which summaries and charts make sense.
Numbers that are labels, like phone numbers and postcodes, are categorical, not numeric.
Tidy data: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, each type of observational unit is a table.
Wide and long are two shapes of the same data; long is usually easier to group, plot and model.
CSV is simple but loses types; JSON handles nesting; Excel hides traps; Parquet is columnar, typed and compressed.
Use UTF-8 everywhere; Bangla characters take 3 bytes each and the same-looking text can be stored in different ways.
lessons.tip: Before any analysis, write a tiny data dictionary: one line per column with its meaning, type, unit and allowed values. It takes ten minutes and prevents most "wait, what does this column mean?" bugs later.
lessons.task: Open your phone's contacts or a class result sheet and list five columns it has. For each, write its variable type (nominal, ordinal, discrete, continuous, datetime, text or boolean). Then sketch the same small table in both wide and long form on paper and decide which is tidy.

quiz.q: Which variable is ordinal?
options: Customer rating: poor, fair, good, excellent
quiz.explain: Ordinal categories have a natural order but the gaps between them are not measured numbers.

quiz.q: Why should a column of Bangladeshi mobile numbers like 01712345678 be stored as text?
options: Numbers cannot be longer than 8 digits
As a number the leading zero is lost and averages of phone numbers mean nothing
quiz.explain: Phone numbers are labels. Stored as numbers they lose the leading 0 and invite meaningless maths.

quiz.q: A table has columns district, Jan, Feb, Mar holding rainfall. Which statement is true?
options: It is wide; the tidy long form would have columns district, month, rainfall
It must be converted to JSON first
quiz.explain: Month is a variable hiding in the column headers. Long form makes month its own column.

quiz.q: What is a main advantage of Parquet over CSV for large analytics data?
options: Humans can read it in Notepad
It stores data by column with types and compression, so reading a few columns is fast
quiz.explain: Columnar storage lets tools read only the columns needed, and types are kept.

quiz.q: In UTF-8, how many bytes does the 5-character Bangla word বাংলা take?
quiz.explain: Bangla characters each take 3 bytes in UTF-8, so 5 characters take 15 bytes.

lessons.title: Collecting Data: Surveys, Logs, APIs and Scraping
lessons.content:
Imagine you want to know how many students at your college skip breakfast. You stand at the canteen at 8 AM and ask everyone who walks in. By 9 AM you have asked 200 students, and only 10 percent say they skip breakfast. Great news? Not really. You stood in the canteen, so you mostly met students who were going to eat. The ones who skip breakfast were somewhere else. Your answer was decided by where you stood, not by the truth. This lesson is about collecting data, and the big lesson inside it is that how you collect decides what you can conclude.

Primary and secondary data: Primary data is collected by you, for your own question: a survey you run, an experiment you design, a sensor you install. You control the definitions, but it costs time and money. Secondary data was collected by someone else for another purpose: government statistics, a company's sales records, a public dataset. It is cheap and often large, but the definitions may not match your question, and you must learn how it was collected before trusting it. Most real projects mix both.

Why collection matters so much: Every later step, cleaning, exploring, modeling, assumes the data represents the world you want to talk about. If it does not, no amount of clever analysis can fix it. Statisticians have a saying that you cannot fix by analysis what you bungled by design. A model trained on biased data learns the bias; a chart of biased data shows the bias beautifully.

Surveys: A survey asks people questions. It is the main way to learn opinions, habits and anything not recorded elsewhere, like how much a household spends on medicine. Surveys can be done face to face, by phone, on paper or online. Each mode reaches different people: an online survey misses people without internet, a phone survey misses people who never answer unknown numbers, and a face-to-face survey costs the most but reaches the widest group.

Writing good questions: Wording changes answers. A leading question pushes people: "Don't you agree the new road has made life easier?" A neutral version is "How has the new road changed your travel time?" A double-barrelled question asks two things at once: "How satisfied are you with the price and speed of delivery?" Split it into two. Vague words like "often" or "recently" mean different things to different people; ask "how many times in the last 7 days?" instead. Sensitive questions about income or illness get more honest answers with ranges and privacy. Always pilot a survey on 10 to 20 people first; you will find confusing questions you never imagined.

Sampling recap: You rarely survey everyone, so you take a sample. Deep-cse-2-6 lesson 18 covered simple random, stratified, systematic and cluster sampling. The core idea: in a random sample every member of the population has a known chance of being chosen, which is what lets you generalise. A convenience sample, asking whoever is easy to reach, like your canteen survey, has no such guarantee.

Sampling bias, three kinds: Selection bias happens when the way you pick people favours some groups, like the canteen. Non-response bias happens when the people who answer differ from those who do not; for example, very busy or very unhappy customers may skip a feedback form. Survivorship bias happens when you only see the cases that survived some filter. In World War II, statistician Abraham Wald studied bullet holes on bombers that came back and argued that armour should go where returning planes had no holes, because planes hit there did not return. In business, studying only current customers to learn why customers leave is the same mistake.

The Literary Digest lesson: In 1936 the American magazine Literary Digest mailed about 10 million ballots, mostly to people from its subscriber lists, telephone directories and car registrations, and got about 2.4 million back. It predicted Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt won in a landslide, with about 61 percent of the popular vote. In 1936, people with phones and cars were richer than average and leaned against Roosevelt, and those who bothered to return ballots were not typical either. Meanwhile George Gallup, with a far smaller but better designed sample, called the winner correctly. The lesson: size does not cure bias. A million biased answers are still biased.

How big a sample: For a simple random sample estimating a proportion, the 95 percent margin of error is about 1.96 times the square root of p(1 - p) / n. The worst case is p = 0.5. With n = 384 that gives about 0.05, or plus or minus 5 percentage points. With n = 1,000 it is about 3.1 points; with n = 2,400 about 2 points. Notice that to halve the error you need four times the sample, because of the square root. Also notice that population size barely matters once it is much larger than the sample, which is why national polls of about 1,000 people can work, if the sample is truly random. We return to this in lesson 16.

Experiments: Sometimes you do not just observe; you change something on purpose and measure the effect. Giving half the customers a new app screen at random and comparing their orders is an experiment. Experiments are the strongest way to learn cause and effect, because randomisation balances everything else between the groups. Lessons 17 and 18 cover A/B testing and causation in detail.

Logs and instrumentation: Apps and websites record events: app opened, product viewed, item added to cart, payment failed. These logs are the richest data many companies have. But they only contain what someone decided to record. If the app never logs "searched and found nothing", you can never study failed searches. Good teams write an event plan before launching a feature: the event name, when exactly it fires, which fields it carries (user id, time, screen, product id) and who owns it. Watch for changes too: if an app update renames an event, a chart can show a fake drop to zero.

Sensors and machines: Weather stations, smart electricity meters, GPS trackers on delivery bikes and factory machines produce streams of measurements. Sensor data has its own problems: a device can drift out of calibration, lose power and send nothing, or send obviously wrong values like a temperature of 999. Time stamps from different devices may not agree. Treat sensor data with the same suspicion as survey data.

Internal databases and warehouses: In a company, the first place to look is usually the data it already has. Operational databases run the business: orders, payments, stock, customers. They are built for fast small updates, so heavy analysis queries on them can slow the live app. That is why companies copy data every night or every hour into a data warehouse, a separate database designed for big analytical queries, often holding years of history. Data engineers build these copy pipelines (deep-cse-7-11). As a data scientist you mostly query the warehouse, and you must learn its timing: if the copy runs at 2 AM, today's orders are not there yet, and a chart of "today" will look like sales collapsed. Always ask how fresh each table is and which system is the source of truth.

Measurement error: Even unbiased collection can measure badly. Scales may be off by half a kilo, people round their age to 30 or 40, and phone surveys get different answers from face-to-face ones on sensitive topics. Know the likely errors of each source and record them in the data dictionary.

Open and public data: Many organisations publish data freely: national statistics offices such as the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics, the World Bank's open data, the World Health Organization, weather agencies, and research datasets on sites like Kaggle. Public data is perfect for practice and for adding context, like population per district. Always read the documentation: what is counted, the time period, and how missing areas are handled.

APIs: An API, application programming interface, lets your program request data from a service in a structured way, usually returning JSON. In Python a call looks like: response = requests.get(url, params={"city": "Dhaka", "page": 1}, headers={"Authorization": "Bearer KEY"}), then data = response.json(). Three practical details matter. Keys: most APIs need an access key; never put it in shared code. Pagination: results come in pages; if each page holds 100 records and you need 25,000, you need 250 requests. Rate limits: the service may allow, say, 60 requests per minute, so 250 requests take a little over 4 minutes, and your code should wait and retry politely when told to slow down.

Web scraping: When no API exists, people sometimes scrape: download web pages and extract the data from the HTML. It is fragile, because a small website redesign breaks your code, and it raises legal and ethical questions. Before scraping, check the site's terms of use and its robots.txt file, which says which parts automated programs should not visit. Prefer an official API or dataset if one exists. Scrape slowly so you do not overload the site, and never collect personal data you have no right to use. Copyright, privacy law and computer misuse laws can all apply.

Real-life example 1, crop prices: A student wants to study how vegetable prices in Dhaka change through the year. Secondary data: government market price bulletins, which list daily prices for common items. She checks the documentation and learns prices are collected from a set of markets on working days only, so Fridays are missing by design, not by error. She adds rainfall data from a public weather source to look for links. Knowing how the data was collected stops her from calling Friday gaps "missing values" to be filled.

Real-life example 2, a customer survey that went wrong: A food delivery company emails a satisfaction survey and gets 8 percent replies. Average rating: 4.6 out of 5. The product manager celebrates. A data scientist checks who replied: mostly long-time, frequent customers. Customers who ordered once and never returned barely replied. She runs a small phone follow-up with a random sample of 200 one-time customers and finds their average experience was far worse, with late deliveries as the top complaint. Non-response bias had hidden the problem.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include trusting big samples without checking how they were drawn, writing leading or double-barrelled questions, forgetting who is missing, assuming logs record everything, changing event definitions silently, and scraping without permission. Exams ask you to distinguish primary and secondary data, name and explain types of sampling bias with examples, critique and rewrite survey questions, explain the Literary Digest poll, and compute a margin of error or required sample size.

Recap: Data is made, not found. Decide what to collect from your question, design surveys and logs carefully, sample randomly where you can, and always ask who is missing. Use APIs and public data responsibly and scrape only when allowed. With data in hand, the next step is pulling exactly the slice you need, and in most companies that means SQL, which is lesson 06.
key_points: Primary data is collected by you for your question; secondary data was collected by someone else for another purpose.
Survey wording changes answers; avoid leading, double-barrelled and vague questions.
Sampling bias (selection, non-response, survivorship) cannot be fixed by collecting more of the same biased data.
The 1936 Literary Digest poll had over 2 million replies and still picked the wrong winner.
Logs and instrumentation record what users do; define events carefully before the app ships.
APIs return structured data with keys, pagination and rate limits; scraping reads web pages and must respect terms, robots.txt and privacy.
A random sample of about 1,000 gives roughly a 3 percent margin of error for a proportion.
lessons.tip: For every dataset, ask "who is missing from this data, and why?" before asking what it says. The people or events that never made it into the table often matter more than the ones that did.
lessons.task: Write a five-question survey about how classmates travel to college. Rewrite any question that is leading, double-barrelled or vague. Then list three ways your sample could be biased if you only asked friends in your own section.

quiz.q: Which survey question is double-barrelled?
options: How many days a week do you take the bus?
How satisfied are you with the price and speed of our delivery?
Which district do you live in?
How old are you in years?
quiz.explain: It asks about two things, price and speed, so one answer cannot describe both.

quiz.q: A magazine polls its own readers by mail and gets 2 million replies, but its prediction is badly wrong. What is the main problem?
options: The sample was biased, so its size could not fix it
quiz.explain: A huge biased sample stays biased. That was the Literary Digest's mistake in 1936.

quiz.q: An app team wants to study why users stop ordering, but only has data from users who still order. What bias is this?
options: Measurement error from a broken sensor
quiz.explain: The users who left are missing, so the data only shows survivors.

quiz.q: An API returns 100 records per page and you need 25,000 records. How many requests do you need at least?
quiz.explain: 25,000 divided by 100 is 250 pages, one request each.

quiz.q: What is the best first step before scraping a website?
options: Scrape as fast as possible before being blocked
Check the site's terms, robots.txt and whether an official API or dataset exists
Collect all personal data you can find
Hide your identity with many accounts
quiz.explain: Respect the site's rules and prefer official sources. Scraping personal data or ignoring terms can be illegal and unethical.

lessons.title: SQL for Data Science
lessons.content:
Imagine a giant library with ten million index cards, one for every sale a supermarket chain ever made. You need the total sales in Khulna last Ramadan. You could carry all ten million cards home and count them on your bed, or you could hand the librarian a precise note: "Please add up the amounts on cards from Khulna between these dates and tell me the total." The librarian works right next to the cards and gives you one number. SQL is that precise note. It is the language for asking databases questions, and in most companies it is the first tool a data scientist reaches for every single day.

What SQL is: SQL, Structured Query Language, is a declarative language: you describe what result you want, and the database decides how to get it efficiently. It works on relational tables, which you studied in deep-cse-4-2: tables with rows and columns, linked by keys. Here we focus on the querying side that data work needs, not on designing schemas or transactions.

Why data scientists need it: Company data lives in databases and warehouses, often far too large to download. SQL lets you filter, join and summarise next to the data and pull back only the slice you need, maybe a few thousand rows ready for pandas. It is also a shared language: analysts, engineers and many managers can read a SQL query and check its logic. In interviews for data jobs, SQL questions are almost guaranteed.

Our example tables: Let us use two small tables. Table orders has columns order_id, customer_id, city, amount and order_date, with six rows: order 1 by customer 101 in Dhaka for 500 taka on 1 May; order 2 by 102 in Dhaka, 1,200 on 1 May; order 3 by 101 in Dhaka, 300 on 2 May; order 4 by 103 in Khulna, 800 on 2 May; order 5 by 104 in Sylhet, 450 on 3 May; order 6 by 103 in Khulna, 200 on 3 May. Table customers has customer_id and name: 101 Rina, 102 Karim, 103 Mitu, 104 Sabbir, 105 Joy. Joy has signed up but never ordered.

The basic query: The skeleton is SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY column LIMIT n. For example: SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders WHERE city = 'Dhaka' AND amount >= 500 ORDER BY amount DESC; returns order 2 with 1,200 and order 1 with 500. WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. ORDER BY sorts, DESC means largest first, and LIMIT keeps only the first n rows, which is handy for a quick look at a huge table.

Aggregation with GROUP BY: Most data questions are summaries. SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS sales, AVG(amount) AS avg_order FROM orders GROUP BY city; splits rows by city and summarises each group. Dhaka has 3 orders with sales 500 + 1,200 + 300 = 2,000 and an average of about 666.67. Khulna has 2 orders, sales 1,000, average 500. Sylhet has 1 order of 450. Every column in SELECT must either be in GROUP BY or be inside an aggregate function; otherwise the database does not know which row's value to show.

WHERE versus HAVING: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. To list cities whose total sales exceed 500: SELECT city, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY city HAVING SUM(amount) > 500; returns Dhaka 2,000 and Khulna 1,000, and drops Sylhet with 450. You cannot write WHERE SUM(amount) > 500, because when WHERE runs, the sums do not exist yet.

The logical order of a query: We write SELECT first, but the database logically processes clauses in this order: FROM and JOIN (which tables), WHERE (which rows), GROUP BY (make groups), HAVING (which groups), SELECT (which columns and calculations), ORDER BY (sort), LIMIT (cut). Knowing this order explains many errors, like why a column alias defined in SELECT often cannot be used in WHERE: WHERE has already run.

Joins: Data is split across tables, so you combine them with joins on a key. An INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match in both tables: SELECT c.name, o.amount FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id; gives six rows, and Joy disappears because she has no orders. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills the right side with NULL where there is no match: with customers on the left, Joy appears once with NULL amount. Use INNER when you only care about matches, LEFT when you must not lose anyone from the left side, for example when counting customers who never ordered.

Counting with LEFT JOIN, a trap: To count orders per customer including Joy: SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.name; gives Joy 0, Karim 1, Mitu 2, Rina 2, Sabbir 1. If you write COUNT(*) instead, Joy gets 1, because COUNT(*) counts the row itself, and her row exists even though its order part is NULL. COUNT(column) skips NULLs, so it gives the correct 0.

Join fan-out, the biggest trap: Suppose a payments table records how each order was paid, and order 2 was split: 700 taka by bKash and 500 by card, so it has two payment rows. Total sales from orders alone are 500 + 1,200 + 300 + 800 + 450 + 200 = 3,450. Now someone writes SELECT SUM(o.amount) FROM orders o JOIN payments p ON o.order_id = p.order_id; and gets 4,650. The join repeated order 2's row once per payment, so its 1,200 was counted twice: 3,450 + 1,200 = 4,650. This is called fan-out. The fixes: aggregate each table to the right level before joining, sum the payment amounts instead if that is what you mean, and always compare row counts before and after a join.

NULL traps: NULL means unknown, not zero and not empty text. Any comparison with NULL is not true, so WHERE city <> 'Dhaka' silently drops rows where city is NULL; you must add OR city IS NULL if you want them. You test for NULL with IS NULL, never with = NULL. AVG ignores NULLs, which is usually right, but if NULL really means zero sales, the average will be too high. COALESCE(amount, 0) replaces NULL with 0 when that is the correct meaning.

Common table expressions: Long queries get messy. A CTE, written with WITH, names an intermediate result so you can build a query in readable steps: WITH city_sales AS (SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS sales FROM orders GROUP BY city) SELECT city, sales FROM city_sales WHERE sales > 500; This reads like a recipe: first make city_sales, then use it. CTEs are also the clean way to aggregate before joining, avoiding fan-out.

CASE, DISTINCT and dates: A few more tools cover most daily work. CASE WHEN builds categories inside a query: CASE WHEN amount >= 1000 THEN 'big' WHEN amount >= 400 THEN 'medium' ELSE 'small' END labels order 2 big, orders 1, 4 and 5 medium, and orders 3 and 6 small. Put a CASE inside SUM to count conditionally: SUM(CASE WHEN city = 'Dhaka' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) gives Dhaka's 2,000 in the same row as other totals, which is handy for building a wide summary. COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) counts unique customers: 4 in our orders table, though there are 6 orders. Date functions, whose exact names differ between databases, extract the month or weekday from order_date or truncate timestamps to the day or week, which is how you group sales by week. When a query must run on a different database, check that database's date functions first; they are the least standard part of SQL.

Window functions: Sometimes you want a calculation across rows without collapsing them into one row per group. Window functions do that, with OVER. A running total of daily sales: daily totals are 1,700 on 1 May, 1,100 on 2 May and 650 on 3 May. SUM(daily_sales) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) gives 1,700, then 2,800, then 3,450. LAG(daily_sales) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) gives the previous day's value, so day-over-day change is 1,100 minus 1,700 = -600 on 2 May and 650 minus 1,100 = -450 on 3 May. RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_spend DESC) ranks customers by spend: Karim 1,200 first, Mitu 1,000 second, Rina 800 third, Sabbir 450 fourth. PARTITION BY restarts the window per group, for example ranking customers within each city.

Pushing work to the database: A good habit is to let the database do filtering, joining and heavy aggregation, then pull a modest result into Python for exploration, charts and modeling. Moving 50 million rows over a network to sum them in pandas wastes minutes or hours; the database can return the same sum in seconds. On the other hand, complex statistics and models are easier in Python, so the skill is choosing where each step lives.

Real-life example 1, a supermarket chain: The manager asks, "Which 10 products lost the most sales in Khulna branches this Ramadan compared with last Ramadan?" The analyst writes a CTE that sums sales per product for each Ramadan period in Khulna branches, joins the two summaries on product_id with a LEFT JOIN from last year (so products that vanished entirely are kept, using COALESCE to turn their NULL into 0), computes the difference, orders by it and keeps 10 rows. The final download is 10 rows, not millions.

Real-life example 2, user retention: A mobile app team wants to know how many users who signed up each week were still active four weeks later. The query groups users by signup week, LEFT JOINs to an activity table filtered to the fourth week after signup, and counts distinct users on both sides. Distinct counts matter here: a user active on five days in that week must count once, so COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) is used, not COUNT(*).

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Typical mistakes: confusing WHERE and HAVING, selecting a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated, using INNER JOIN and silently losing rows, fan-out double counting, testing NULL with =, using COUNT(*) where COUNT(column) or COUNT(DISTINCT column) was needed, and dumping huge tables into Python. Exams ask you to write queries for a small schema, predict the output of a GROUP BY or a join by hand, explain inner versus left joins, explain the logical order of clauses, and use a window function for ranking or running totals.

Recap: SQL lets you ask the database for exactly the data you need. Filter rows with WHERE, summarise with GROUP BY, filter groups with HAVING, combine tables with joins, and use CTEs and window functions for readable, powerful queries. Watch for NULLs and fan-out, check row counts after every join, and push heavy work to the database. Next lesson we move to Python, where the slice you pulled gets explored, cleaned and modelled.
key_points: SQL asks a database for exactly the slice you need: SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition.
GROUP BY with SUM, COUNT and AVG summarises groups; HAVING filters groups after aggregation, WHERE filters rows before.
Logical order: FROM and JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
INNER JOIN keeps matching rows only; LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table and fills NULL where there is no match.
Joining one-to-many tables then summing can double count; aggregate before joining or check row counts.
NULL is unknown: comparisons with NULL are not true, and COUNT(column) skips NULLs while COUNT(*) does not.
Window functions like running SUM, RANK and LAG compute across rows without collapsing them.
lessons.tip: After every join, check the row count against what you expected. A join that silently multiplies rows is the most common way analysts report wrong totals with total confidence.
lessons.task: On paper, make the small orders and customers tables from this lesson. By hand, compute total sales per city, the result of a LEFT JOIN from customers to orders, and the running total by date. Then, if you have a computer, type them into any free online SQL playground and check your answers.

quiz.q: Which clause filters groups after aggregation, such as cities with total sales above 500?
quiz.explain: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the grouped results.

quiz.q: A LEFT JOIN from customers to orders includes Joy, who has no orders. What does COUNT(o.order_id) give for Joy?
quiz.explain: COUNT of a column skips NULLs, and Joy's order_id is NULL, so the count is 0. COUNT(*) would wrongly give 1.
