quiz.q: Total sales are 3,450 taka, but after joining orders to a payments table (one order paid in two parts) the SUM of amount is 4,650. Why?
options: The payments table has wrong numbers
The join repeated the split order's row, so its amount was counted twice
quiz.explain: One-to-many joins repeat the "one" side. Sum before joining, or sum the payment amounts instead.

quiz.q: Daily sales are 1,700, 1,100 and 650. What does a running total window function return on day three?
quiz.explain: Running total adds all days so far: 1,700 + 1,100 + 650 = 3,450.

quiz.q: Why is it often better to aggregate in the database than to download all rows into Python?
options: The database works next to the data and sends back only the small summary
SQL results are always more accurate
quiz.explain: Moving millions of rows is slow; the database can summarise near the data and return a few rows.

lessons.title: Python, Notebooks and NumPy
lessons.content:
Imagine you have to calculate VAT for 10 lakh items in a shop's sales file. With a calculator you would be pressing buttons for months. With a spreadsheet it is quicker, but the file becomes slow and fragile. With a few lines of Python it takes well under a second, and tomorrow you can rerun it on the new file without touching anything. That is why data scientists write code: not because code is fancy, but because it is fast, repeatable and checkable. This lesson covers the working environment of most data scientists: Python, Jupyter notebooks and NumPy, the library that makes numbers fly.

Why Python: Python was created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991. It became the most common language in data science for three reasons. Its syntax is simple and reads almost like English, so analysts who are not software engineers can learn it. It is general purpose, so the same language can fetch data from an API, clean it, train a model and run a web service. And it has a huge ecosystem of free libraries: NumPy for arrays, pandas for tables, matplotlib and seaborn for charts, scikit-learn for machine learning, and many more. You learned programming basics in earlier courses; here we focus on what matters for data work.

Jupyter notebooks: A notebook is a document made of cells. A code cell holds Python; when you run it, its output, a number, a table or a chart, appears right below. A text cell holds notes written in Markdown. Behind the notebook runs a kernel, a live Python process that keeps every variable in memory. This makes exploration wonderful: load data once, then try a dozen ideas, each in its own cell, seeing results instantly. It also makes notebooks a natural lab report: question, code, result and explanation side by side. JupyterLab, VS Code and cloud services like Google Colab all run notebooks.

The hidden state trap: Because the kernel remembers everything, the order you run cells matters, not the order they appear on the page. Example: cell 1 says x = 5, cell 2 says y = x * 2, and shows 10. Later you edit cell 1 to x = 10 and run it, but forget cell 2. The page now shows x = 10 next to y = 10, which looks like a bug in maths but is really stale output. Worse, you might delete a cell that defined a variable; everything still works today because the variable lives in memory, but tomorrow, after a restart, the notebook crashes. The fix is a habit: regularly use "restart kernel and run all", and never share a notebook that does not run cleanly from top to bottom.

Notebook versus script: Notebooks are best for exploring, explaining and teaching. Scripts, plain .py files run from top to bottom, are better for code that must run every day, be tested and be reviewed. A healthy pattern is to explore in a notebook, then move stable pieces, like the cleaning function, into a script or module that the notebook imports. That way the important logic is in one tested place, not copied across ten notebooks.

NumPy, the foundation: Python's built-in lists can hold anything, a number, a string, another list, in any mix. That flexibility makes them slow for maths, because Python must check each item's type every time. NumPy provides the ndarray: a block of memory holding many values of one type, like 64-bit floats, packed side by side. Operations on the whole array run in compiled code. Almost every data library, including pandas and scikit-learn, is built on top of NumPy arrays.

Vectorisation: Vectorisation means writing an operation once for the whole array instead of looping. With a Python list you would write a loop: for each price, multiply by 1.15 and append. With NumPy you write prices * 1.15 and it is done. For prices [100, 250, 40] the result is about [115, 287.5, 46]. On millions of numbers, vectorised code is often tens of times faster than a Python loop, and it is shorter and clearer too. A rule of thumb for data work: if you are writing a for loop over rows, look for a vectorised way first.

Memory, with numbers: A float64 takes 8 bytes. Ten million of them in a NumPy array take 80,000,000 bytes, about 80 MB. In a Python list each number is a separate object of about 24 bytes plus an 8-byte pointer, so roughly 32 bytes each, around 320 MB for the same numbers. This four-times difference is one reason pandas and NumPy can handle datasets that would choke plain Python.

Broadcasting: Broadcasting lets NumPy combine arrays of different shapes when it makes sense. Multiplying an array by a single number is the simplest case: the number is "broadcast" to every element. A more useful case: three shops sold two items, quantities [[2, 1], [0, 3], [5, 2]], one row per shop, and the item prices are [50, 120]. quantities * prices multiplies each column by its price: [[100, 120], [0, 360], [250, 240]]. Summing each row gives revenue per shop: 220, 360 and 490 taka. No loops, and the shapes explain the logic. If shapes do not line up, NumPy raises an error rather than guessing, which is good.

Reading errors: When code fails, Python prints a traceback, a list of the function calls that led to the error. Beginners panic at its length, but the trick is simple: read the last line first. It names the error type and a message. If you try to multiply the 3-by-2 quantity table by a list of three prices, NumPy says something like "ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (3,2) (3,)". That tells you exactly what is wrong: the shapes do not line up, because three prices cannot match two columns. A KeyError usually means a column or dictionary key name is misspelled; a TypeError often means you mixed text and numbers, like adding "500" to 20. Then look one or two lines up the traceback to find which line of your own code triggered it. Printing the shape, dtype and first few values of the arrays involved solves most data bugs in a minute.

Indexing and boolean masks: You can select parts of an array by position, like a[0] for the first item or a[1:3] for the second and third. More powerful is boolean masking: prices > 100 gives an array of True and False, and prices[prices > 100] keeps only the matching values. This same idea powers filtering in pandas, which we use in the next lesson.

Data types and NaN: Every array has a dtype: int64, float64, bool, and so on. Integers cannot represent "missing", so missing numeric values are usually stored as NaN, a special floating point value meaning "not a number". NaN spreads: the mean of [10, 20, NaN] is NaN. That is a feature, it stops you from silently ignoring gaps, but you must decide what to do; np.nanmean ignores NaN and gives 15. Another oddity: NaN is not equal to itself, so testing x == NaN never works; use np.isnan(x). In classic pandas, an integer column with a single missing value is turned into floats for this reason.

Floating point surprises: Computers store most decimals approximately in binary. In Python, 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, and 100 * 1.15 gives 114.99999999999999. These tiny errors rarely matter for analysis, but they matter for comparisons and money. Never test floats with ==; compare with a small tolerance, for example np.isclose. For accounting, store money as whole poisha or use a decimal type, and round only for display.

Randomness and seeds: Data science uses randomness everywhere: random samples, train-test splits, bootstrap, model initialisation. Computers generate pseudo-random numbers from a starting value called a seed. Fix the seed, for example rng = np.random.default_rng(42), and the same "random" numbers come out every run, so your results can be reproduced and checked. Change the seed and see whether conclusions hold; if a result only appears with one seed, it is probably luck.

Environments and versions: Libraries change. Code that worked last year may break or, worse, give slightly different results with a new version. A virtual environment, made with tools like venv or conda, keeps each project's packages separate. A requirements file lists the packages and versions, so a colleague can recreate your setup. Recording versions is part of honest, reproducible work, just like recording your data source.

Other tools and when to use them: R is another excellent language for data analysis, especially strong in statistics and in the ggplot2 plotting system; many statisticians and researchers prefer it. Excel is fine for small tables and quick checks, and managers know it, but it handles at most 1,048,576 rows per sheet and makes reproducible work hard. SQL, from lesson 06, is best for pulling and summarising data in databases. BI tools like Power BI build dashboards, lesson 15. Julia aims at fast numerical computing. Pick the tool for the job; many real projects use SQL plus Python plus a BI tool together.

Real-life example 1, a VAT check: A shop's accountant suspects some invoices have wrong VAT. The analyst loads 2 lakh invoice lines into a NumPy array of prices and another of VAT charged, computes expected = prices * 0.15 in one line, and flags rows where the absolute difference from the VAT charged is more than 1 taka, using a tolerance instead of exact equality. It finds 312 suspicious lines in under a second, and the notebook shows the code, the count and a sample of bad rows, so the accountant can check them.

Real-life example 2, a simulation: A clinic wants to know how often more than 30 patients will arrive in an hour if on average 22 arrive. The analyst simulates 100,000 hours with NumPy's random Poisson generator using a fixed seed, counts the hours above 30, and divides by 100,000. Vectorisation makes 100,000 simulated hours take a moment, and the seed means a colleague who reruns the notebook gets the same estimate. Probability distributions like Poisson were covered in deep-cse-2-6 lesson 13.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include trusting a notebook that was run out of order, looping over rows when a vectorised operation exists, comparing floats with ==, forgetting that NaN spreads or is not equal to itself, not fixing seeds, and not recording package versions. Exams ask why Python dominates data science, what a notebook kernel is and why hidden state is dangerous, the difference between a list and a NumPy array, what vectorisation and broadcasting are with a worked example, and how to make an analysis reproducible.

Recap: Python plus notebooks is the data scientist's workbench. Notebooks are great for exploring but keep hidden state, so restart and run all often and move stable code into scripts. NumPy arrays store one type in packed memory, which makes vectorised maths and broadcasting fast and clear. Respect NaN and floating point quirks, fix seeds, and record your environment. Next, we build on NumPy with pandas, the library that turns arrays into labelled tables.
key_points: Python is the most common language for data science because of its simple syntax and its libraries: NumPy, pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, scikit-learn.
Jupyter notebooks mix code, output and notes in cells run by a kernel that keeps state in memory.
Running cells out of order creates hidden state; always restart and run all before trusting or sharing a notebook.
A NumPy array holds one data type in one block of memory, so vectorised operations run far faster than Python loops.
Broadcasting stretches smaller arrays to match bigger ones, for example multiplying every row by a price vector.
NaN marks missing floats; it spreads through calculations, and floating point has tiny rounding errors.
Reproducibility needs a fixed random seed, a recorded environment and code that runs from raw data.
lessons.tip: Before you share any notebook, click "Restart kernel and run all". If it does not run cleanly from top to bottom, it is not finished, no matter how good the outputs look.
lessons.task: Without a computer, write the NumPy-style result of multiplying the quantity table [[2, 1], [0, 3], [5, 2]] by the price list [50, 120], then sum each row. If you have a computer, open a free online notebook, type it in with NumPy and check. Then run the cells out of order on purpose and see how the answer can go wrong.

quiz.q: In a notebook, cell 1 sets x = 5 and cell 2 computes y = x * 2. You change cell 1 to x = 10 and run it, but do not re-run cell 2. What is the risk?
options: Outputs on screen may come from older values, so the notebook no longer matches its code
There is no risk at all
quiz.explain: Notebooks keep state in memory. Outputs depend on the order cells were run, not on their order on the page.

quiz.q: Why is a NumPy operation like prices * 1.15 usually much faster than a Python for loop?
options: It runs one compiled operation over a block of same-typed numbers
It skips half of the numbers
quiz.explain: Vectorised NumPy code runs in compiled loops over contiguous memory, avoiding Python's per-item overhead.

quiz.q: Quantities [[2, 1], [0, 3], [5, 2]] are multiplied by prices [50, 120] with broadcasting. What is the first row of the result?
quiz.explain: Each column is multiplied by its price: 2 x 50 = 100 and 1 x 120 = 120.

quiz.q: What is np.mean of the array [10, 20, NaN]?
quiz.explain: NaN spreads through ordinary calculations. np.nanmean would ignore it and give 15.

quiz.q: Which practice best makes an analysis reproducible?
options: Editing the raw data by hand and saving over it
Fixing a random seed, recording package versions and running code from raw data
Running cells in whatever order works today
quiz.explain: Same code, same data, same environment and same seed should give the same results for anyone.

lessons.title: pandas Fundamentals
lessons.content:
Think of a school's result register. Each row is a student, each column is a subject, and the roll numbers down the left side let you find any student quickly. You can run your finger down the Maths column to find the highest mark, or across one student's row to see all their marks. pandas gives Python exactly this kind of register, but one that can hold millions of rows and answer questions in a single line. It was created by Wes McKinney, starting in 2008, and today it is the most used tool for working with tables in Python.

What pandas is: pandas is a Python library for labelled, tabular data. It is built on NumPy, so columns are fast arrays, but it adds labels for rows and columns, mixed column types (text in one, numbers in another, dates in a third), missing value handling, and hundreds of ready functions for loading, cleaning, grouping and reshaping data. If NumPy is a powerful calculator for grids of numbers, pandas is a spreadsheet you control with code.

Why we need it: Real data is rarely a neat grid of floats. It has names, dates, categories and gaps. Before pandas, people wrote long, error-prone loops to read files, match rows and count things. pandas turns those loops into short, readable, fast commands, and because it is code, every step is recorded and repeatable. That is the big difference from clicking around in Excel. A colleague can read your notebook and see exactly which rows you removed and why, something a clicked spreadsheet can never show. pandas does have limits: it works in memory on one machine, so tables much bigger than your RAM need a database, a columnar tool or a distributed system instead.

Series and DataFrame: A Series is a one-dimensional labelled array: values plus an index. For example, a Series of revenues with order ids as the index. A DataFrame is a table: several Series sharing the same index, one per column. df["qty"] gives one column as a Series; df[["qty", "unit_price"]], with a list inside, gives a smaller DataFrame. The index is the row label. By default it is 0, 1, 2 and so on, but you can set a meaningful one like order_id.

Our example table: We will use an eight-row shop table with columns order_id, date, branch, product, qty and unit_price. Rows: order 1 on 1 June 2024 at Mirpur, Rice 5kg, 2 bags at 450; order 2, 1 June, Uttara, Oil 1L, 3 at 180; order 3, 2 June, Mirpur, Eggs 12, 1 at 150; order 4, 2 June, Dhanmondi, Rice 5kg, 1 at 450; order 5, 3 June, Uttara, Rice 5kg, 4 at 450; order 6, 3 June, Mirpur, Oil 1L, 2 at 180; order 7, 4 June, Dhanmondi, Eggs 12, 5 at 150; order 8, 4 June, Uttara, Eggs 12, 2 at 150.

Loading data: df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv") reads a CSV into a DataFrame. read_csv has many useful options: dtype={"phone": str} keeps phone numbers as text so leading zeros survive; parse_dates=["date"] turns date strings into real dates; na_values=["NA", "-", "n/a"] tells pandas which strings mean missing; usecols picks only the columns you need, saving memory. Similar functions read Excel, JSON, Parquet and SQL query results, for example pd.read_sql(query, connection), which connects lesson 06 to this one.

The first look: Always start with the same few commands. df.shape gives (rows, columns), here (8, 6). df.head() shows the first five rows so you see real values. df.info() lists each column's dtype and how many non-missing values it has, the fastest way to spot a number column read as text or a column full of gaps. df.describe() gives count, mean, standard deviation, min, quartiles and max for numeric columns. df["branch"].value_counts() counts each category: Mirpur 3, Uttara 3, Dhanmondi 2.

Adding a column: New columns are computed for the whole column at once, just like NumPy: df["revenue"] = df["qty"] * df["unit_price"]. Our revenues are 900, 540, 150, 450, 1,800, 360, 750 and 300, a total of 5,250 taka. df["revenue"].describe() would show mean 656.25 and median 495. The mean is above the median because one big order of 1,800 pulls it up, the same lesson about skew you met in statistics.

Selecting with loc and iloc: loc selects by label and iloc by position. df.loc[3, "product"] gives the product in the row whose index label is 3. df.iloc[0:3] gives the first three rows by position, positions 0, 1 and 2, because like Python slicing the end is excluded. A surprise worth remembering: loc slices by label include the end, so df.loc[0:3] gives four rows when the index is 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on. When the index is the default numbers, loc and iloc look similar, but after sorting or filtering they differ, so be deliberate.

Boolean masks for filtering: Filtering uses the same masks as NumPy. df["revenue"] > 500 makes a True/False Series; df[df["revenue"] > 500] keeps matching rows: orders 1, 2, 5 and 7. Combine conditions with & for and, | for or, and ~ for not, with brackets around each part: df[(df["branch"] == "Mirpur") & (df["qty"] >= 2)] keeps orders 1 and 6. Plain Python and or words do not work here, and forgetting the brackets is a classic error. df[df["branch"].isin(["Mirpur", "Uttara"])] checks membership in a list.

Sorting and ranking: df.sort_values("revenue", ascending=False) puts order 5 with 1,800 first. You can sort by several columns, like branch then revenue. df.nlargest(3, "revenue") is a shortcut for the top three: orders 5, 1 and 7. Sorting does not change the index labels, which is why loc and iloc can give different rows afterwards.

Dtypes and conversion: Many problems come from wrong dtypes. If a price column contains "450 tk" in a few rows, pandas reads the whole column as object, meaning text, and arithmetic fails or gives nonsense. Fix it by cleaning the text, then converting: pd.to_numeric(df["price"].str.replace(" tk", ""), errors="coerce"). errors="coerce" turns values that still fail into NaN, so you must then count and inspect them rather than ignoring them. Dates: pd.to_datetime(df["date"]). Categories with few distinct values, like branch, can use the category dtype to save memory.

The .str and .dt accessors: For text columns, .str gives vectorised string methods: df["product"].str.lower(), .str.strip() to remove spaces, .str.contains("Rice"), .str.split(" "). For date columns, .dt extracts parts: df["date"].dt.day_name() gives Saturday, Sunday, Monday and Tuesday for 1 to 4 June 2024; .dt.month, .dt.hour and so on. These are the building blocks of cleaning (lessons 10 and 11) and feature engineering (lesson 19).

apply versus vectorised: df.apply(function, axis=1) runs a Python function once per row. It is flexible but slow, because it loses NumPy's compiled speed. df["qty"] * df["unit_price"] does the same multiplication over whole columns in compiled code. On a few thousand rows you will not notice; on millions, the difference can be minutes versus seconds. Use apply only when no vectorised method exists, and for simple if-else logic look at np.where or .map with a dictionary.

Method chaining: Instead of creating many temporary variables, you can chain steps: (df.assign(revenue=lambda d: d["qty"] * d["unit_price"]).query("revenue > 500").sort_values("revenue", ascending=False)). Each line is one step, read top to bottom like a recipe. Chains are easy to review and do not leave half-finished DataFrames lying around in a notebook's memory.

Copy versus view warning: If you filter a DataFrame and then change the result, pandas may warn with a SettingWithCopyWarning, because it cannot be sure whether you meant to change the original. Example: mirpur = df[df["branch"] == "Mirpur"] then mirpur["qty"] = 0. The safe patterns are: change the original directly with df.loc[df["branch"] == "Mirpur", "qty"] = 0, or say clearly that you want a separate table with mirpur = df[df["branch"] == "Mirpur"].copy(). Newer pandas versions are moving to copy-on-write behaviour that removes much of this confusion, but the explicit habits still make your intent clear.

Working with the index: The index is more than row numbers. df.set_index("order_id") makes order ids the row labels, so df.loc[5] fetches order 5 directly, and when two Series are added together pandas lines them up by index label, not by position. That alignment is powerful but surprising: adding two Series with different labels gives NaN wherever a label exists in only one of them. df.reset_index() turns the index back into an ordinary column, which you often need after grouping. When results look shifted or full of unexpected NaN, check the index first.

A first look at missing values: df.isna().sum() counts missing values per column, and it belongs in your first-look routine next to info(). df.dropna() removes rows with any missing value and df.fillna(0) fills them, but both are decisions, not defaults: dropping can throw away most of a table, and filling with 0 can invent fake sales. Lesson 11 covers how to choose properly.

Saving results: df.to_csv("clean_sales.csv", index=False) writes a CSV without the extra index column; df.to_parquet("clean_sales.parquet") keeps dtypes intact for the next step. Never save over the raw file. Keep raw data read-only, and write cleaned outputs to new files with clear names, so you can always rerun from the start.

Real-life example 1, a pharmacy's daily file: A pharmacy exports 30,000 sales lines daily. The analyst writes a short notebook: read_csv with phone as text and dates parsed, info() to check types, a revenue column, a filter for returns (negative quantities) which are moved to a separate table, and value_counts on product to list the top sellers. The notebook runs in seconds every morning, and the head pharmacist gets the same checks every day, without anyone copying and pasting in Excel.

Real-life example 2, exam results: A college has a CSV of 1,200 students' marks in six subjects. With pandas the teacher reads it, uses describe() to see each subject's mean and spread, filters students below 33 in any subject with a mask combined using |, sorts by total marks with nlargest(10, "total") for the merit list, and uses .str.strip() and .str.title() to fix names typed with extra spaces and mixed case. What used to take a day of manual work takes an afternoon to write once and seconds to rerun next term.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include skipping info() and missing a wrong dtype, using and or or instead of & and |, forgetting brackets around conditions, mixing up loc and iloc after sorting, using apply for simple arithmetic, ignoring values turned to NaN by errors="coerce", and modifying slices. Exams and interviews ask you to explain Series versus DataFrame, write code to load, filter, add a column and sort, explain loc versus iloc, predict the output of a small filter, and explain why vectorised code is faster.

Recap: pandas gives Python a labelled, typed table with fast columns. Load with read_csv and the right options, look first with shape, head, info, describe and value_counts, select with loc, iloc and boolean masks, add vectorised columns, fix dtypes early, and use .str and .dt for text and dates. Prefer vectorised operations and chains, and be explicit about copies. Next lesson we go from single tables to grouping, joining and reshaping, where most real questions get answered.
key_points: A Series is a labelled one-dimensional array; a DataFrame is a table of Series sharing one index.
read_csv loads files; head, info, describe, shape and value_counts are the first look at any table.
Select columns with df["col"], rows and columns by label with loc, by position with iloc, and rows by condition with boolean masks.
New columns are vectorised: df["revenue"] = df["qty"] * df["unit_price"].
Check and fix dtypes early; use .str for text and .dt for dates.
Prefer vectorised operations over apply with Python functions, and chain steps for readable pipelines.
Modifying a filtered slice can trigger a copy-versus-view warning; use loc on the original or make an explicit copy.
lessons.tip: Make df.shape, df.info() and df.head() your reflex after every step that changes a DataFrame. Most pandas bugs show up as an unexpected row count or a column with the wrong dtype.
lessons.task: Copy the eight-row shop table from this lesson onto paper. By hand, add the revenue column, find the mean and median revenue, count orders per branch, and list the rows with revenue above 500. If you can, repeat it in pandas and check each number.

quiz.q: What does df.loc[df["branch"] == "Mirpur", ["product", "qty"]] return?
options: The first two rows of the table
Only Mirpur rows, with the product and qty columns
An error, because loc only takes numbers
quiz.explain: loc selects by label: the boolean mask chooses rows and the list chooses columns.

quiz.q: For revenues 900, 540, 150, 450, 1,800, 360, 750 and 300, which is true?
options: The mean is 656.25 and the median is 495
The mean and median are both 495
quiz.explain: Sum 5,250 / 8 = 656.25. Sorted, the middle two values are 450 and 540, median 495. The large 1,800 pulls the mean up.

quiz.q: A price column was read as text because some cells say "450 tk". What is the right fix?
options: Leave it as text and compute averages anyway
Strip the text, then convert with pd.to_numeric, checking which values failed
quiz.explain: Clean the strings, convert to numbers, and inspect values that could not be converted instead of hiding them.

quiz.q: What is df.iloc[0:3] ?
options: Rows where the value is below 3
The first three rows by position
quiz.explain: iloc is position based and, like Python slicing, excludes the end, so 0:3 gives positions 0, 1 and 2.

quiz.q: Why is df["qty"] * df["unit_price"] preferred to df.apply(lambda r: r.qty * r.unit_price, axis=1)?
options: The vectorised version runs in fast compiled code over whole columns
Multiplication is not allowed inside apply
There is no difference at all
quiz.explain: apply with axis=1 calls a Python function once per row, which is much slower on big tables.

lessons.title: Grouping, Joining and Reshaping in pandas
lessons.content:
Imagine your class teacher has every student's marks in one long list and the principal asks, "What is the average marks of each section?" The teacher splits the list into sections A, B and C, works out each section's average, and writes the three answers in a small table. That three-step move, split, apply, combine, is behind most questions you will ever ask a dataset. This lesson covers it, plus the two other everyday moves: joining tables together and reshaping them between long and wide.

Split-apply-combine: The statistician Hadley Wickham named this pattern in 2011, and pandas implements it with groupby. You split the rows by one or more keys, apply a function to each group (sum, mean, count, or something custom), and combine the results into a new table. In pandas: df.groupby("branch")["revenue"].sum(). It reads like the question: group by branch, take revenue, sum it.

Our running example: We continue with the eight-row shop table from lesson 08, with its revenue column: order 1 Mirpur Rice 900; order 2 Uttara Oil 540; order 3 Mirpur Eggs 150; order 4 Dhanmondi Rice 450; order 5 Uttara Rice 1,800; order 6 Mirpur Oil 360; order 7 Dhanmondi Eggs 750; order 8 Uttara Eggs 300. Dates run from 1 to 4 June 2024. The grand total is 5,250 taka.

A worked groupby: df.groupby("branch")["revenue"].sum() gives Dhanmondi 1,200, Mirpur 1,410 and Uttara 2,640. Check by hand: Mirpur is 900 + 150 + 360 = 1,410, Uttara is 540 + 1,800 + 300 = 2,640, Dhanmondi is 450 + 750 = 1,200. They add up to 5,250, which is a check you should always do: group totals must equal the grand total. Grouped by product instead, Rice is 900 + 450 + 1,800 = 3,150, Oil is 540 + 360 = 900, and Eggs is 150 + 750 + 300 = 1,200, again 5,250 in total.

Several summaries at once with agg: Usually you want more than one number per group. df.groupby("branch").agg(orders=("order_id", "count"), revenue=("revenue", "sum"), avg_order=("revenue", "mean"), items=("qty", "sum")) gives a tidy summary with named columns. For Mirpur: 3 orders, 1,410 revenue, average 470, 5 items. Uttara: 3 orders, 2,640, average 880, 9 items. Dhanmondi: 2 orders, 1,200, average 600, 6 items. Named aggregation like this makes the output self-explaining, which matters when someone reads your notebook later.

Grouping by several keys: df.groupby(["branch", "product"])["revenue"].sum() gives one row per branch and product combination that actually occurs: seven rows here, because Dhanmondi sold no oil. The result has a two-level index, which you can flatten with reset_index() to get ordinary columns again. Grouping by time parts is common too: df.groupby(df["date"].dt.day_name())["revenue"].sum() gives sales by weekday.

transform for group-wise columns: Sometimes you want a group result attached to every original row. transform does that. df["branch_total"] = df.groupby("branch")["revenue"].transform("sum") puts 1,410 on every Mirpur row, 2,640 on every Uttara row and 1,200 on every Dhanmondi row. Then df["share"] = df["revenue"] / df["branch_total"] gives each order's share of its branch's sales: order 5 is 1,800 / 2,640, about 68 percent of Uttara's sales. transform is also how you fill missing values with a group's median, which we use in lesson 11.

What a group summary hides: A mean per group hides two things you should always look at alongside it: the count and the spread. Dhanmondi's average order of 600 rests on just 2 orders, so one unusual order would swing it a lot, while a branch with 2,000 orders has a stable average. Add a count and a standard deviation to every agg you show, and be careful ranking groups with tiny counts; the "best" and "worst" groups in any ranking are often just the smallest ones, because small groups vary the most by chance.

Hidden groupby details: By default groupby drops rows whose key is missing, so sales with no branch recorded simply vanish from the summary and the group totals no longer add up to the grand total. Pass dropna=False to keep them as their own group and see how big the problem is. Results are sorted by key by default; sort=False keeps the order of first appearance. With category dtype keys, pandas may also show categories that have no rows, which you control with the observed argument.

Running and rolling calculations within groups: Many questions are about order within a group. groupby("branch")["revenue"].cumsum() gives each branch's running total over time; groupby("customer_id")["date"].diff() gives days since the same customer's previous order, a key feature for churn models; groupby("branch")["revenue"].shift(1) gives the previous value in the same branch. On a daily series, rolling(7).mean() gives a 7-day moving average, which smooths out weekday swings; we use it in lesson 13. Always sort by date first, or "previous" will mean the wrong row.

filter and custom functions: groupby(...).filter(lambda g: len(g) >= 3) keeps only groups with at least three rows, here Mirpur and Uttara. You can apply your own function to each group with apply, but as with rows, it is slower than built-in aggregations, so use it when nothing simpler fits.

Joining tables with merge: Data lives in several tables. Suppose a branches table has branch, manager and area in square feet: Mirpur, Rahim, 1,200; Uttara, Nusrat, 1,500; Dhanmondi, Tanvir, 1,000; Bashundhara, Farhana, 1,800. Bashundhara is new and has no sales yet. sales.merge(branches, on="branch", how="left") attaches each sale's manager and area. The how argument works like SQL from lesson 06: inner keeps matches only, left keeps all left rows, right keeps all right rows, outer keeps everything with NaN where there is no match.

Checking merges: The most common merge bug is a duplicate key on the side that should be unique. If the branches table accidentally lists Mirpur twice, each of the 3 Mirpur sales matches 2 rows, so the left merge produces 8 + 3 = 11 rows instead of 8, and Mirpur's revenue doubles in every later total. Two defences: compare len(df) before and after merging, and pass validate="many_to_one", which tells pandas that many sales map to one branch and raises an error if a branch key is duplicated. indicator=True adds a column saying whether each row came from both tables or only one, great for spotting unmatched keys, like misspelled branch names.

Many-to-many merges: The worst case is joining two tables that both have repeated keys. Suppose customer 103 has 2 orders and also 3 saved delivery addresses. Merging orders with addresses on customer_id gives 2 x 3 = 6 rows for that customer, every order paired with every address, which is almost never what you want. If a customer has 50 orders and 10 addresses, that becomes 500 rows. Usually the fix is to decide which single row of the second table applies, such as the address used for each order or the default address, before merging. validate="one_to_one" or "many_to_one" will refuse a many-to-many join and force you to think.

A merge that answers a question: Big branches naturally sell more, so is Uttara really the best? Merge branch totals with the branches table and divide: Mirpur 1,410 / 1,200 is about 1.18 taka per square foot, Uttara 2,640 / 1,500 = 1.76, Dhanmondi 1,200 / 1,000 = 1.2. Uttara is still best, but Dhanmondi now edges past Mirpur, which the raw totals hid. This is the counts-versus-rates lesson from lesson 03, made possible by a join.

concat for stacking: When you have the same kind of table in several pieces, like one file per month, pd.concat([jan, feb, mar]) stacks them into one table. Check that the columns match exactly; a column named "Branch" in one file and "branch" in another becomes two half-empty columns. Add a column saying which file each row came from, so you can trace problems later.

pivot_table, long to wide: For reports, a wide summary is often clearer. df.pivot_table(index="branch", columns="product", values="revenue", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0) gives a grid: Mirpur Rice 900, Oil 360, Eggs 150; Uttara Rice 1,800, Oil 540, Eggs 300; Dhanmondi Rice 450, Oil 0, Eggs 750. Each row adds to its branch total and each column to its product total. fill_value=0 is right here because no sale means zero revenue; for something like average price, an empty cell should stay NaN, because "no data" is not "zero". margins=True adds totals.

melt, wide to long: melt reverses the pivot. pivot.reset_index().melt(id_vars="branch", var_name="product", value_name="revenue") gives 9 rows, one per branch and product, including Dhanmondi Oil with 0. This is how you fix the wide rainfall table from lesson 04, and how you prepare data for plotting libraries that want long data, which we use in lesson 15.

Time resampling: When the index is a datetime, resample groups by time periods. df.set_index("date")["revenue"].resample("D").sum() gives daily sales: 1,440 on 1 June, 600 on 2 June, 2,160 on 3 June and 1,050 on 4 June. "W" gives weeks and "MS" months starting on the first day. Unlike a plain groupby on dates, resample also creates rows for days with no sales, which keeps time series charts honest.

Real-life example 1, a garments factory: A factory records defects per sewing line per hour. The quality manager wants defect rate per line per week. The analyst merges the defects table with a production table (pieces made per line per hour) on line and hour, validates one-to-one, resamples to weeks, and computes defects per 1,000 pieces with groupby and agg. A pivot table with lines as rows and weeks as columns becomes the weekly report, and a melt of the same table feeds a line chart.

Real-life example 2, upazila health data: A health programme has a visits table (one row per patient visit) and an upazila table with population. Grouping visits by upazila and month and merging population lets the team compute visits per 1,000 people, then rank upazilas with the lowest coverage. Using indicator=True reveals three upazila names spelled differently in the two tables, which would have quietly dropped those areas from the report.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include forgetting that group totals should add up to the grand total, merging without checking row counts or using validate, filling every empty pivot cell with 0 even when the value is an average, concatenating tables with mismatched column names, and using apply where agg would do. Exams and interviews ask you to explain split-apply-combine, write groupby with several aggregations, explain agg versus transform, predict the row count of a merge with duplicate keys, and convert a small table between long and wide by hand.

Recap: groupby with agg summarises groups, transform attaches group results to rows, merge joins tables like SQL with validation and row-count checks, concat stacks pieces, pivot_table and melt switch between wide and long, and resample groups by time. With these moves you can answer most business questions, as long as you keep checking that totals still add up and row counts still make sense after every step. But all of them assume the data is clean, and real data almost never is, which is why the next two lessons are about cleaning.
key_points: Split-apply-combine: split rows into groups, apply a summary to each, combine the results.
groupby with agg can compute several summaries at once, with clear names for each output column.
transform returns a value for every original row, useful for shares of group totals and group-wise filling.
merge joins tables on keys; choose how (inner, left, right, outer) and always check row counts.
validate="many_to_one" and similar checks catch duplicate keys that would silently multiply rows.
pivot_table turns long data into a wide summary; melt turns wide data back into long.
resample groups time-indexed data into days, weeks or months.
lessons.tip: Before every merge, say out loud what kind of relationship it is: one-to-one, many-to-one or many-to-many. Then pass validate= to merge and let pandas shout if the data disagrees with you.
lessons.task: Using the eight-row shop table from lesson 08, compute by hand the total revenue per branch and per product, then build the branch by product pivot table with 0 for empty cells. Check that every row and column of your pivot adds up to the grand total of 5,250 taka.

quiz.q: Branch revenues are Mirpur 1,410 from 3 orders, Uttara 2,640 from 3 orders and Dhanmondi 1,200 from 2 orders. What is Uttara's mean order revenue?
quiz.explain: 2,640 divided by 3 orders is 880 taka.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between agg and transform after groupby?
options: agg returns one row per group; transform returns a value for every original row
quiz.explain: transform broadcasts the group result back to each row, so it lines up with the original table.

quiz.q: A sales table with 8 rows is left-merged with a branches table that accidentally lists Mirpur twice. Mirpur has 3 sales rows. How many rows does the result have?
quiz.explain: Each of the 3 Mirpur rows matches 2 branch rows, adding 3 extra rows: 8 + 3 = 11.

quiz.q: Which function turns a table with columns branch, Rice, Oil, Eggs into columns branch, product, revenue?
quiz.explain: melt unpivots wide columns into long rows, one per branch and product.

quiz.q: Why compute sales per square foot by merging branch sizes instead of just comparing total sales?
options: Bigger branches naturally sell more, so dividing by size gives a fairer comparison
Square feet are easier to graph
quiz.explain: A rate adjusts for size. Uttara's 2,640 over 1,500 sq ft is 1.76 per sq ft, still the best, but the gap narrows.

lessons.title: Data Cleaning I: Types, Formats and Duplicates
lessons.content:
Imagine you are sorting a sack of rice that has small stones, husks and a few broken grains mixed in. If you cook it as it is, someone will bite a stone. So before cooking you spread it on a kula and pick out the bad bits, patiently, handful by handful. Data cleaning is that kula work. It is not glamorous, it takes time, and it is the difference between a meal people enjoy and one that breaks a tooth. In this lesson we handle the first half of cleaning: wrong types, messy formats, inconsistent categories and duplicates. Lesson 11 handles missing values and outliers.

What data cleaning is: Data cleaning, also called data cleansing or wrangling, means finding and fixing problems in data so it accurately represents what it should. Problems arise everywhere: people type differently, systems change formats, files are merged badly, sensors glitch, test records leak into real tables. Cleaning is not about making data look pretty; it is about making sure every later number means what you think it means.

Why it matters so much: A model or chart cannot tell that "Dhaka" and "dhaka " are the same city; it treats them as two. A price stored as text cannot be summed. A duplicate customer makes your customer count too high and your average spend too low. These errors are silent: no error message appears, just wrong answers presented confidently. That is why experienced data scientists spend so much of their time here, and why skipping it is the most expensive shortcut in the field.

Data quality dimensions: It helps to name what "dirty" means. Accuracy: values match reality (the recorded age is the person's real age). Completeness: required values are present. Consistency: the same thing is recorded the same way everywhere (one spelling of a district; totals in two tables agree). Timeliness: data is up to date for its use. Validity: values follow the rules of their type and range (an age of 250 is invalid). Uniqueness: each real-world entity appears once. When you report a data problem, naming the dimension makes it easier for others to understand and fix.

Inspect before you fix: Never start fixing blindly. First look: df.info() for dtypes and non-missing counts, df.describe() for strange minimums and maximums, value_counts() on every categorical column to see all spellings, df.sample(10) to see random real rows, and df.duplicated().sum() for exact duplicates. Write down what you find. This list becomes your cleaning plan, and often it reveals that a problem comes from one source, like one branch's new software, which you can then fix at the source.

Fixing types: The first job is getting each column into the right type, because almost every later step depends on it. Numbers stored as text, dates stored as text, IDs stored as numbers, booleans stored as "Y", "yes", "1" and "TRUE" all need converting. Do it explicitly with pd.to_numeric, pd.to_datetime and a mapping for booleans, and always count how many values failed to convert. If 3 out of 10,000 prices fail, look at those 3; if 3,000 fail, your parsing rule is wrong.

Standardising text: Text columns hide endless variety. Start with mechanical clean-up: .str.strip() removes leading and trailing spaces, .str.lower() or .str.title() makes case consistent, and collapsing repeated spaces turns "Mirpur  10" into "Mirpur 10". Then handle real variants with an explicit mapping. For a city column with "Dhaka", "dhaka ", " DHAKA", "Dhk", "Dacca", "Chittagong", "Chattogram" and "Ctg", after strip and lower you map {"dhaka": "Dhaka", "dhk": "Dhaka", "dacca": "Dhaka", "chittagong": "Chattogram", "chattogram": "Chattogram", "ctg": "Chattogram"}. Anything not in the mapping should be flagged and inspected, not silently kept or dropped.

Why explicit mappings beat guessing: It is tempting to use clever fuzzy matching to merge all similar strings automatically. But "Barisal" and "Barishal" are the same district, while "Rajshahi" and "Rajbari" look similar and are different districts. An explicit mapping, reviewed by someone who knows the domain, is boring and safe. Fuzzy matching is fine for suggesting candidates, which a human then confirms, and the confirmed pairs go into the mapping table for next time.

Parsing messy numbers: Prices arrive as "5,000 tk", "Tk 450", "450/-", "1.2k" and sometimes in Bangla digits like ৫০০. A cleaning function for this removes currency words and symbols, removes thousands separators, converts Bangla digits to Latin with a translation table mapping ০ to 0 through ৯ to 9, handles known shorthands like k for thousand, and then converts to a number. So "৫০০ টাকা" becomes 500 and "5,000 tk" becomes 5000. Anything that still fails becomes NaN and goes on the inspection list. Watch the decimal mark too: some sources write 1.250 meaning one thousand two hundred fifty, and others mean one point two five.

Parsing dates: Dates are notorious. The same day may appear as "03/04/2024", "2024-04-03", "3 Apr 2024" and "03-04-24". In Bangladesh, 03/04/2024 means 3 April, but software built for the United States reads it as March 4. Never let a parser guess silently. Give pd.to_datetime an explicit format for each known pattern, or at least dayfirst=True, and check the result: are there dates in the future, before the business existed, or a suspicious pile-up on the 1st of a month, which often means unknown days were filled with 1? Also decide on a time zone; mixing UTC timestamps from a server with local Bangladesh time, 6 hours ahead, shifts late-night orders into the next day.

Units: The same quantity may be recorded in different units: grams and kilograms, taka and lakh taka, minutes and hours. Bangladesh adds traditional units, like rice recorded in mon, where one mon is about 37.3 kg, so 2 mon is about 74.6 kg. Choose one unit per column, convert everything into it, and name the column with the unit, like weight_kg. Then check plausibility: if a 5 kg rice bag column has values like 5,000, someone entered grams.

Exact duplicates: Exact duplicates are rows identical in every column, often caused by a file being loaded twice or an app retrying a request. df.duplicated() marks them and df.drop_duplicates() removes them. But first ask whether identical rows can be real: two customers can buy the same item for the same price in the same minute. Usually a unique id, like order_id, decides; duplicates in the id column are the real problem. df.duplicated(subset=["order_id"]) checks just that column.

Near duplicates: Harder are records of the same thing that differ slightly: "Md. Rahim Uddin, 01712345678" and "Rahim Uddin, 01712345678 " are clearly one person. Strategies: normalise first (strip, lower, remove titles like "Md."), then match on a strong key such as phone number or national ID, and use fuzzy string similarity for names. Edit distance counts the minimum single-character insertions, deletions or substitutions to turn one string into another: "Rahim" to "Raheem" is 2 (change i to e, insert another e). A small distance suggests a match, but a human should review candidate merges, because merging two different people is worse than leaving a duplicate.

Validation rules: Validation rules state what must be true and catch what cleaning missed. Examples: age between 0 and 120; delivery minutes at least 0; delivery time after order time; quantity a positive whole number; order date not in the future; a Bangladeshi mobile number matching the pattern ^01[3-9]\d{8}$, which means 01, then a digit from 3 to 9, then 8 more digits, 11 in total. Rows that fail are not automatically deleted; they are counted, inspected and either fixed, set to missing or excluded with a reason. Tools exist to write such rules as tests that run every time new data arrives.

Test and junk records: Real tables often contain test orders made by developers, staff accounts, demo branches and records like "test test" or a customer called "asdf". They inflate counts and distort averages. Find them by known test ids, internal email domains, zero prices or obviously fake names, confirm with the people who run the system, and exclude them with a documented filter.

Keep raw data and a cleaning log: Two habits make cleaning trustworthy. First, never modify the raw file; read it, clean in code, and write a new cleaned file. Second, keep a log of every step with row counts. For example: raw 10,000 rows; removed 120 exact duplicates, leaving 9,880; removed 45 test orders, leaving 9,835; set 30 impossible ages to missing; mapped 14 city spellings to 8 cities; 6 prices could not be parsed and were set to missing. Anyone can now see what happened, question a decision, and rerun everything when next month's data arrives.

Fix at the source when you can: Cleaning downstream is a repair, not a cure. If the same messy values arrive every month, talk to whoever owns the form or app: a dropdown list of districts instead of free text, a date picker instead of typed dates, a phone field that only accepts 11 digits. One small change at the source can remove a whole cleaning step forever and make the data more trustworthy for everyone who uses it, not only you.

Real-life example 1, a microfinance survey: An NGO's field officers enter borrower data on tablets in several districts. The analyst finds district names in English and Bangla, loan amounts like "১৫,০০০" and "15k", dates in two formats depending on the tablet's settings, and the same borrower entered twice when a sync failed. She writes a cleaning script: normalise and map district names, convert Bangla digits and shorthand, parse dates with explicit formats per tablet batch, and flag possible duplicates by matching phone number and village, which a supervisor reviews. The log shows 2.3 percent of rows were affected, and the field team fixes the tablet setting that caused the date problem.

Real-life example 2, a delivery company's address field: Customers type addresses freely: "House 12, Road 5, Dhanmondi", "h-12 r-5 dhanmondi", "Dhanmondi R/5 H/12". To analyse deliveries by area, the analyst does not try to perfect full addresses. She extracts the area name with a list of known Dhaka areas and their variants, maps them to standard names, and validates against the delivery zone the rider app recorded. Rows where the two disagree go to an inspection list, which reveals a few zones whose boundaries were drawn wrongly in the app.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include cleaning by hand in Excel without a record, letting parsers guess types and date formats, auto-merging fuzzy matches without review, deleting rows that fail validation without counting them, mixing units, and overwriting raw data. Exams ask you to list and explain data quality dimensions, describe steps to clean a given messy column, explain exact versus near duplicates, write simple validation rules or a regular expression, and explain why a cleaning log and untouched raw data matter.

Recap: Cleaning starts with inspection, then fixes types, standardises text with explicit mappings, parses numbers, dates and units carefully, removes exact duplicates and reviews near ones, and enforces validation rules. Do it in code, keep the raw data, and log counts at every step. Next lesson tackles the two problems that need the most judgment: missing values and outliers.
key_points: Data quality has dimensions: accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity and uniqueness.
Inspect before fixing: dtypes, unique values, value counts and a few sample rows show what is wrong.
Standardise text with strip and lower, then map known variants to one canonical value and flag anything unmapped.
Parse numbers by removing currency words and commas and converting Bangla digits; parse dates with an explicit format.
Convert all values to one unit, and check that the conversion is plausible.
Remove exact duplicates, and find near duplicates with keys like phone number and fuzzy matching, reviewing before merging.
Validation rules catch impossible values; keep raw data and a cleaning log with counts for every step.
lessons.tip: Never clean by hand in the raw file. Write every fix as code, keep the raw file untouched, and print a before-and-after row count for each step. Your future self, and your reviewer, will thank you.
lessons.task: Write ten messy versions of your own district's name the way people might type them (spaces, capitals, short forms, old spellings, Bangla). Then write a mapping table that turns all of them into one standard name, and one validation rule that would catch a value your mapping missed.

quiz.q: Which data quality dimension is broken when the same customer appears three times with slightly different names?
quiz.explain: Uniqueness means each real-world thing is recorded once. Duplicates break it.

quiz.q: A city column has "Dhaka", "dhaka ", " DHAKA" and "Dhk". What is the best first step?
options: Delete all rows that are not exactly "Dhaka"
Leave them; they mean the same anyway
Strip spaces and lower-case, then map known variants like "dhk" to "Dhaka" and flag anything unmapped
quiz.explain: Standardise first, then map variants explicitly, and look at whatever is left over instead of guessing.

quiz.q: A date "03/04/2024" comes from a Bangladeshi form. What should the parser be told?
options: Day comes first, so it is 3 April 2024
Month comes first, so it is 4 March 2024
quiz.explain: Bangladesh writes day first. Give the parser an explicit format or dayfirst so it does not guess.

quiz.q: A raw file has 10,000 rows. You remove 120 exact duplicates and then 45 test orders. How many rows remain?
quiz.explain: 10,000 - 120 = 9,880, then 9,880 - 45 = 9,835. Logging each step's count makes errors visible.

quiz.q: Which regular expression checks an 11-digit Bangladeshi mobile number starting with 013 to 019?
quiz.explain: 01, then a digit from 3 to 9, then 8 more digits makes 11 digits in total.

lessons.title: Data Cleaning II: Missing Values and Outliers
lessons.content:
Imagine you are a class captain collecting lunch money. A few students have not paid yet, and one student wrote "10,000 taka" next to his name instead of "100". If you just add everything up, the total is nonsense. If you ignore the unpaid students, you will think lunch is cheaper per head than it is. To do this right you need two kinds of judgment: what to do about the blanks, and what to do about the number that looks impossible. That is this lesson: missing values and outliers, the two cleaning problems where there is no single correct button to press.

What missing values are: A missing value is a cell where a value should exist but does not. In pandas it usually appears as NaN or None, but real files disguise it: empty strings, "N/A", "-", "unknown", and the dangerous ones, numbers like 0, -1 or 999 that some systems use to mean "not recorded". A survey where the age 999 means "refused" will make the average age look enormous unless you convert 999 to missing first. So the first step is to find every disguise and turn it into a proper NaN, then count: df.isna().sum() per column and df.isna().mean() for the share missing.

Why missing data is a problem: Most calculations and models cannot use NaN directly; many models refuse to run. More importantly, the rows with missing values may be different from the others. If you drop them or fill them carelessly, your results describe a different group than the one you think. The key question is never "how do I get rid of NaN?" but "why is it missing, and what does that imply?"

Three kinds of missingness: Statisticians, following Donald Rubin's work in the 1970s, use three categories. MCAR, missing completely at random: the chance of being missing has nothing to do with any data, like a few survey sheets lost in the rain. MAR, missing at random: missingness depends on other observed columns, for example older respondents skip the email question more often, but within each age group it is random. MNAR, missing not at random: missingness depends on the missing value itself, for example people with very high or very low incomes skip the income question. MCAR is harmless except for losing data, MAR can be handled using the other columns, and MNAR is hard; no method fully fixes it, so you must state the risk.

Looking at missingness: Before choosing a method, explore the pattern. Which columns have gaps? Do gaps cluster in certain rows, dates, branches or survey interviewers? Compare rows with and without a missing value on other columns: if customers with missing age spend far less, the missingness is not random. A heatmap of df.isna() often shows patterns instantly, like a whole month of missing sensor readings after a power cut.

Option 1, dropping: df.dropna() removes rows with any missing value; dropna(subset=["income"]) removes only rows missing that column. Dropping is simple and fine when few rows are affected and the data is MCAR. But it adds up fast: if 10 columns each have 5 percent missing at random, independently, only about 0.95 to the power 10, roughly 60 percent of rows are complete, so dropping loses 40 percent of the data. And if missingness is not random, dropping biases the result. You can also drop a column that is mostly empty, if it is not essential.

Option 2, simple imputation: Imputation means filling missing values with estimates. Mean imputation fills with the column's average, median imputation with the middle value, mode imputation with the most common category. Worked example: observed incomes in thousand taka are 12, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25 and 90, and two are missing. The mean is 202 divided by 7, about 28.9; the median is 20. The mean is higher than 5 of the 7 observed incomes because the 90 pulls it up, so filling with 28.9 invents two fairly rich people. The median is the better single fill for skewed data. Remember that any single-value fill shrinks the spread, because all filled values are identical, which makes the data look more certain than it is.

Option 3, group-wise imputation: A smarter fill uses related information. If income differs a lot by district, fill a missing income with the median income of the person's own district: df["income"] = df["income"].fillna(df.groupby("district")["income"].transform("median")). This is the transform trick from lesson 09. It works well when data is MAR with respect to the grouping column. More advanced methods predict the missing value from many columns with a model, or create several plausible filled datasets (multiple imputation) to reflect uncertainty; deep-cse-6-1 lesson 03 touched on the simple versions.

Option 4, a missing indicator: Sometimes the fact that a value is missing is itself informative. A loan applicant who leaves "monthly income" blank may be riskier. Add a column like income_missing with 1 for missing and 0 otherwise, then impute the value. The model can now learn from both. In surveys, "refused to answer" can be its own category instead of being forced into a number.

Time series filling: For data ordered in time, nearby values carry information. Forward fill, ffill, copies the last known value forward; it suits values that persist, like a product's price or a stock level, which stays the same until it changes. It is wrong for flows like daily sales: a missing sales day should not copy yesterday's sales. Interpolation draws a straight line between known neighbours, which suits smooth measurements like temperature. Always limit how far you fill, for example at most 2 days, so a month-long gap is not invented.

What outliers are: An outlier is a value far from the rest. It might be an error, like a typo of 1800 for 180, a real but rare extreme, like a wedding order of 300 biryani boxes, or exactly what you are hunting, like a fraudulent transaction. Statistics alone cannot tell which; the domain and investigation must decide. Outliers matter because they distort means, standard deviations, correlations and many models, especially linear regression.

The IQR rule, worked: The interquartile range method from deep-cse-2-6 lesson 04 is the standard first tool. Take ten delivery times: 22, 25, 28, 30, 31, 33, 35, 38, 40 and 180 minutes. Using the common linear interpolation method, Q1 is 28.5 and Q3 is 37.25, so the IQR is 8.75. The lower fence is 28.5 minus 1.5 times 8.75, which is 15.375; the upper fence is 37.25 plus 13.125, which is 50.375. Only 180 lies outside, so it is flagged. The rule works because quartiles barely move when one extreme value is added; it is robust. Box plots draw exactly these fences as whiskers.

The z-score rule and masking: The z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean: z = (x - mean) / standard deviation. A common rule flags |z| > 3. For the same data, the mean is 46.2 and the sample standard deviation is about 47.3, so the z-score of 180 is about 2.83, below 3. The rule misses the most obvious outlier! The reason is masking: the outlier itself pulled the mean up and stretched the standard deviation. Without 180, the mean of the other nine is about 31.3. Lesson: z-scores work for large, roughly normal data, but robust rules based on medians and quartiles are safer for small or skewed data.

Error or real: When a value is flagged, investigate. Check impossible values against domain rules: a delivery time of -5 minutes or an age of 250 is an error. Look at the raw record: was 1800 a typo for 180? Is the 180-minute delivery real, perhaps during a hartal or flooding? Ask the people who know. Errors get fixed if the true value is knowable, or set to missing if not. Real extremes usually stay, because removing them makes the world look calmer than it is.

Handling real extremes: When real extremes distort a summary or a model, you have options that keep the information. Report the median and IQR instead of the mean and standard deviation. Cap or winsorise: set values above a high percentile, like the 99th, to that percentile, which limits their pull without deleting the rows. Transform: a log transform squeezes large values, which lesson 12 shows with numbers. Use robust methods: median-based statistics, or models and losses less sensitive to extremes, like the Huber loss from deep-cse-6-1 lesson 07. Or analyse extremes separately, because a wedding order and a family dinner order are different businesses.

Document every decision: Missing value and outlier choices change results, sometimes a lot. Write them down: "income: 4.1 percent missing, MAR by district, filled with district median, indicator added"; "delivery_min: 23 values above the IQR fence, 3 were typing errors and were corrected, 20 were real hartal-day deliveries and kept; median reported." Better still, check sensitivity: run the key analysis with and without the extremes, or with mean versus median fill. If conclusions do not change, say so; if they do, say that too.

Real-life example 1, a hospital's patient records: A Dhaka hospital wants average length of stay by ward. Discharge date is missing for 6 percent of records. Investigation shows most are patients still admitted, not data errors, so they are MNAR in a sense: their stays are long and ongoing. Dropping them would make stays look shorter. The analyst separates current patients, reports completed stays with the median, and notes how many long stays are still in progress. One stay of 2,000 days turns out to be a typo in the admission year and is corrected.

Real-life example 2, mobile wallet fraud: A wallet company sees a handful of transactions 50 times larger than the customer's usual amount. Treating them as noise to delete would be a disaster; in fraud work, outliers are the signal. The team flags transactions above a customer-specific IQR fence, combines them with other signals like a new device, and sends them for review. Here outlier detection is not cleaning but the product itself, which we revisit in lesson 22 on anomaly detection.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include missing disguised codes like 999, dropping rows without checking how many and which, filling everything with the mean, forward-filling flows like sales, deleting outliers automatically, trusting z-scores on small skewed samples, and not recording decisions. Exams ask you to define MCAR, MAR and MNAR with examples, compare deletion and imputation methods, compute mean and median imputation, apply the IQR rule to a small dataset, compute a z-score, and discuss whether to remove a given outlier.

Recap: Find every disguise of missing values, ask why they are missing, then drop, impute (median, group-wise, with an indicator) or fill over time with care. Flag outliers with robust rules like the IQR fence, investigate before acting, fix errors, keep real extremes, and use robust summaries, capping or transforms when they distort. Write every decision down. With clean data in hand, we can finally start exploring it properly in lesson 12.
key_points: Missing values hide as NaN, empty strings, 0, -1, 999 or "N/A"; find them all before counting.
MCAR is missing purely by chance, MAR depends on other observed columns, MNAR depends on the missing value itself.
Dropping rows is safe only when few are missing and the missingness is random; otherwise it biases results.
Median imputation resists skew better than mean; group-wise imputation and a missing indicator column keep more information.
The IQR rule flags values below Q1 - 1.5 IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 IQR, and it is robust to the outliers themselves.
A big outlier inflates the standard deviation and can hide itself from a z-score rule.
An outlier can be an error to fix, a real extreme to keep, or the very thing you are looking for; document every decision.
lessons.tip: Before filling a single missing value, ask "why is it missing?" and before removing a single outlier, ask "could this be real?" Those two questions turn cleaning from a mechanical chore into real analysis.
lessons.task: Write down ten delivery times in minutes from your imagination, including one very large value. By hand, find Q1, Q3, the IQR and the upper fence, and check whether your big value is flagged. Then compute the mean with and without it and write one sentence on which number you would report to a manager and why.

quiz.q: A survey's income question is skipped mostly by high earners. What kind of missingness is this?
options: MAR, explained fully by another column
MNAR, missing not at random, because it depends on the income itself
quiz.explain: When the chance of being missing depends on the unseen value, the data is MNAR, the hardest case.

quiz.q: Observed incomes in thousand taka are 12, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25 and 90. Which value is the better single fill for two missing incomes, and why?
options: The median 20, because the mean of about 28.9 is pulled up by the 90
The mean 28.9, because it is always more accurate
quiz.explain: With skew, the median represents a typical person better. The mean is higher than 5 of the 7 observed incomes.

quiz.q: Delivery times have Q1 = 28.5 and Q3 = 37.25 minutes. What is the upper IQR fence?
quiz.explain: IQR = 8.75, so the fence is 37.25 + 1.5 x 8.75 = 50.375 minutes.

quiz.q: Why did the z-score of a 180-minute delivery come out below 3 in a 10-value sample?
options: The outlier itself inflated the mean and standard deviation, masking itself
z-scores only work on negative numbers
quiz.explain: Mean and standard deviation are not robust. One huge value stretches the standard deviation so its own z-score shrinks.

quiz.q: A bank finds a few transactions 50 times larger than usual. What is the best response?
options: Investigate them; they may be errors, real large payments or fraud worth flagging
Ignore them because they are rare
quiz.explain: In fraud detection the outliers are the target. Check the cause before deciding.

lessons.title: Exploratory Data Analysis I: One Variable at a Time
lessons.content:
Imagine you move to a new neighbourhood and want to know it. You do not start by writing a report. You walk around: which shops are busy, where children play, which road floods in rain, where the tea stall gossip happens. Only after walking around do you know which questions are worth asking. Exploratory data analysis, EDA, is that walk around the data. In this lesson we walk through one variable at a time; in lesson 13 we look at how variables relate to each other.

What EDA is: The statistician John Tukey made exploratory data analysis famous with his 1977 book of that name. He argued that before testing hypotheses, analysts should look at data openly, with simple summaries and especially pictures, to see what is there: patterns, oddities, errors and surprises. Tukey contrasted it with confirmatory analysis, which tests specific claims. EDA generates questions; confirmatory analysis answers them. Both are needed, and EDA comes first.

Why EDA matters: EDA catches problems cleaning missed, like a column where 30 percent of values are exactly 0. It tells you which methods fit: a model that assumes symmetric data will struggle with heavy skew. It shows which variables matter and which are nearly constant and useless. And it produces many of the most valuable findings directly; plenty of business insights come from a good histogram rather than a complex model.

The EDA mindset: Be curious and suspicious at once. For every column ask: what does it measure, what values should be possible, and what do I actually see? Keep a notebook section of "observations" and "questions". Do not try to confirm what you hoped; try to be surprised. When something looks odd, find out why before moving on, because the oddity is often either an error or the most interesting thing in the data.

Number summaries recap: For a numeric variable, compute count, missing count, mean, median, standard deviation, minimum, maximum and quartiles, all from deep-cse-2-6 lessons 03 and 04. In pandas, describe() gives most of them. Each number has a job. Mean and median describe the centre. Standard deviation and IQR describe the spread. Minimum and maximum reveal impossible values. Comparing the mean with the median hints at skew. Count versus number of rows reveals missing values.

Shape: Two variables can share the same mean and spread but have very different shapes. Symmetric data, like heights of adult men, looks the same on both sides of the centre. Right-skewed data has a long tail of large values, very common in money and time: incomes, order values, delivery delays, number of followers. Left-skewed data has a long tail of small values, like exam scores on an easy test where most students score high. Bimodal data has two peaks, which usually means two different groups mixed together. Data can also show spikes at round numbers, like ages heaped at 30, 40 and 50 because people round, or prices clustered at 99 and 499.

The histogram: A histogram splits the range into equal bins and draws a bar for how many values fall in each, as you learned in deep-cse-2-6 lesson 02. It is the main picture of shape. Bin width matters: too few bins hide structure, too many make random noise look like structure. Sturges' rule suggests about 1 + log2(n) bins, roughly 11 bins for 1,000 values; the Freedman-Diaconis rule uses a width of 2 times IQR divided by the cube root of n, which suits skewed data better. In practice, try two or three widths and see which features survive.

The box plot: A box plot draws the median as a line, the quartiles as a box, whiskers to the most extreme points within 1.5 IQR, and individual dots beyond, using the IQR fences from lesson 11. It hides detail like bimodality, but it is excellent for comparing many groups side by side, such as delivery time by zone for 20 zones. Use histograms to see one distribution in detail and box plots to compare many.

Density plots: A kernel density estimate, KDE, draws a smooth curve instead of bars, as if each data point spreads a small hill and the hills are added up. It looks nicer and makes overlaying two groups easy, but the smoothing amount, called bandwidth, can create or hide bumps just like bin width, and the curve can spill into impossible values like negative delivery times. Treat it as a sketch, not a fact.

Mean versus median under skew, worked: Take 13 monthly household incomes in thousand taka from a village survey: 8, 9, 10, 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 15, 18, 25, 60 and 150. The median, the 7th value in order, is 12. The mean is 353 divided by 13, about 27.2. The mean is more than double the median because two large incomes, 60 and 150, pull it up. Only 2 of the 13 households earn more than the mean. If a report says "average income is 27,000 taka", most readers will picture a typical household that does not exist. For skewed data, report the median as the typical value, and the mean only when totals matter, like total spending power.

The log transform, worked: When data is right-skewed and spans several orders of magnitude, a log transform often helps. log10 turns 10 into 1, 100 into 2 and 1,000 into 3: each tenfold step becomes one equal step. For our incomes, log10 values run from about 0.90 for 8 up to about 2.18 for 150, and the histogram of these logs is far more balanced. The mean of the logs is about 1.23, and 10 to that power is about 16.9 thousand taka, which is the geometric mean, a typical value between the median and the arithmetic mean. Logs need positive values; for data with zeros, people use log(1 + x). Logs also make charts readable: plotting order values on a log axis lets you see both 100-taka and 100,000-taka orders.

Percentiles for business questions: Averages answer "what is typical?" but many decisions are about the tail. A delivery company promises "30 minutes"; what matters is how many orders break that promise. The 90th percentile, p90, is the value below which 90 percent of observations fall. If p50 delivery time is 28 minutes but p90 is 55, one order in ten takes almost twice the promise, and those customers are the ones who complain and leave. Web teams track p95 and p99 page load times for the same reason. In pandas, df["delivery_min"].quantile([0.5, 0.9, 0.99]) gives them in one line. Reporting a few percentiles, not just the mean, gives decision makers a far more honest picture of a skewed variable.

Categorical variables: For categories, the summary is a frequency table: counts and percentages, from value_counts(normalize=True). Look for an unexpected dominant category, like 70 percent "Other", which means the category list is broken. Look for rare categories: a district column with 64 values where 40 each have under 1 percent of rows. Rare categories make noisy averages and cluttered charts; for display or modeling you may group them, for example into "Other" or by division, but keep the detailed column too. Check also for categories that should not exist, like a payment method "test".

Dates and time variables: For datetime columns, look at the range (first and last date), counts per day or month to spot gaps and spikes, and distributions of hour of day and day of week. A sudden drop to zero on certain dates usually means a logging problem, not a business collapse. A histogram of order hour often shows lunch and dinner peaks, the bimodal pattern again.

Anscombe's quartet: In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe published four small datasets of 11 points each. All four have the same mean of x (9), nearly the same mean of y (about 7.50), the same variance of x (11), nearly the same variance of y (about 4.12), the same correlation (about 0.816) and the same best-fit line, roughly y = 3 + 0.5x. Yet when plotted, one is a normal scatter around a line, one is a smooth curve, one is a perfect line with one outlier, and one is a vertical stack with a single far point that creates the whole correlation. The message became a motto of data science: never trust summary statistics without looking at the picture.

A one-variable EDA checklist: For each important numeric column, record count and missing share, min, max, mean, median and IQR, a histogram at two bin widths, any spikes or impossible values, and whether a log scale helps. For each categorical column, record the number of categories, the top categories with percentages, rare categories and suspicious labels. For each date column, record the range, gaps and spikes. Write one line of interpretation per column, in plain words, such as "order value is heavily right-skewed; median 420 taka, p90 1,900 taka; 3 percent are exactly 0 and need checking". This sounds slow but takes an hour for a typical table and saves days later.

Real-life example 1, a ride-hailing company: Analysing trip fares in Dhaka, an analyst sees the mean fare is far above the median and the histogram has a long right tail. On a log scale, she sees a second small bump: airport trips, which are much longer. She also sees a spike of fares at exactly 0, which turn out to be cancelled trips logged as completed. EDA, not a model, revealed two segments and a data bug.

Real-life example 2, SSC marks: A school plots the histogram of Bangla first paper marks and sees a strange pile-up right at 33, the pass mark, and almost nobody at 31 or 32. This is a known pattern in many exam systems where borderline scripts get re-checked or rounded up. It is not an error to delete, but an important fact about how the data is produced, and any analysis of "pass rates" needs to mention it.
