Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include reporting the mean for skewed money data, judging shape from one bin width, using KDE curves without noticing they spill into impossible values, ignoring rare or suspicious categories, skipping plots because the summary "looks fine", and treating spikes as natural when they reveal how data was recorded. Exams ask you to define EDA and its purpose, describe shapes from a histogram, explain the relationship between mean and median under skew, interpret a box plot, explain what a log transform does, and explain Anscombe's quartet.

Recap: EDA is the curious walk through your data before formal analysis. Summarise each variable with numbers and pictures, read its shape, compare mean and median, try log scales for skewed data, inspect categories and dates, and always plot because summaries can hide everything. Next lesson we look at two or more variables together: relationships, comparisons, and the traps that come with them.
key_points: EDA, named by John Tukey, means looking at data openly to understand it, find problems and form questions before formal testing.
For each numeric variable check centre, spread, shape, gaps and extreme values.
Shapes: symmetric, right-skewed (long tail of big values), left-skewed, bimodal (two peaks), and with spikes at round numbers.
In right-skewed data the mean is above the median; report the median for a typical value.
Histogram bin width changes the picture; try a few widths, and use box plots to compare groups.
A log transform turns multiplicative spread into additive spread and often makes right-skewed data symmetric.
Anscombe's quartet shows four datasets with almost identical summaries but very different pictures: always plot.
lessons.tip: For every important column, look at a number summary and a picture together. Numbers tell you how much; pictures tell you what shape. Either one alone will fool you sooner or later.
lessons.task: Ask 13 people (family, friends, classmates) how many minutes they spent on their phone yesterday. Compute the mean and the median, draw a rough histogram on paper with 5 bins, and decide whether the data is skewed. Then take log10 of each value and see whether the histogram becomes more symmetric.

quiz.q: Monthly incomes (thousand taka) in a sample have mean 27.2 and median 12. What does that tell you?
options: The data is right-skewed: a few large incomes pull the mean up
quiz.explain: When the mean is well above the median, a long right tail of large values is pulling the mean.

quiz.q: What does Anscombe's quartet teach?
options: Datasets with the same summary statistics can look completely different, so always plot
Four is the best sample size
quiz.explain: Its four datasets share means, variances, correlation and regression line, yet the plots differ wildly.

quiz.q: A histogram of order times shows two clear peaks, around 1 PM and 9 PM. What shape is this?
quiz.explain: Two peaks mean two common values, here lunch and dinner. Treating it as one group would hide that.

quiz.q: What does a log10 transform do to the values 10, 100 and 1,000?
options: Turns them into 1, 2 and 3, equally spaced
quiz.explain: Each tenfold step becomes a step of 1, so huge ranges are squeezed into an even scale.

quiz.q: A district column has 64 categories, and 40 of them each have under 1 percent of rows. A good EDA step is to:
options: Treat district as a number from 1 to 64
Look at the counts, and for charts or models consider grouping rare districts into "Other" or by division
quiz.explain: Rare categories make noisy charts and estimates. Grouping them, with care, keeps the information usable.

lessons.title: Exploratory Data Analysis II: Relationships and Comparisons
lessons.content:
Imagine a doctor looking at one patient's temperature. Useful, but limited. Now imagine she looks at temperature together with how many days the fever has lasted, the patient's age and whether there was recent rain in the area. Suddenly patterns appear: fevers that last over three days in the monsoon, in young adults, suggest dengue more than flu. Most real insight comes from looking at variables together. This lesson is about exploring relationships between two or more variables, and about the traps that make relationships lie.

Why relationships matter: Business and science questions are almost always about relationships. Do customers who get faster deliveries order again more often? Do branches with more staff sell more? Does rainfall come before dengue cases? EDA of relationships tells you which links exist, how strong and what shape they are, and which surprising comparisons need a closer look, before you build models or run experiments.

Scatter plots: For two numeric variables, the scatter plot is the main tool: one variable on each axis, one dot per observation. Read four things. Form: is the pattern a straight line, a curve, or clusters? Direction: does y tend to rise or fall as x rises? Strength: are dots tightly packed around the pattern or loosely scattered? Outliers: are there dots far from the rest? With thousands of points, dots pile on top of each other; make them semi-transparent, use small dots, or plot a random sample, so dense areas show up as darker.

Pearson's correlation, recap with a warning: Pearson's r, from deep-cse-2-6 lesson 24, measures the strength of a linear relationship, from -1 to +1. Five students who studied 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 hours and scored 40, 50, 55, 65 and 70 give r of about 0.99, a very strong positive line. Now add a sixth student who studied 6 hours but was ill on exam day and scored 20. Pearson's r falls to about -0.09, as if there were no relationship at all. One point overturned the summary. This is why you never report r without looking at the scatter plot, and why r near 0 does not mean "no relationship"; a perfect U-shaped curve also has r near 0.

Spearman's rank correlation: Spearman's correlation replaces values with their ranks and then computes Pearson's r on the ranks. It measures any monotonic relationship, one that always goes up or always goes down, even if curved. For x = 1 to 5 and y = x cubed, that is 1, 8, 27, 64 and 125, Pearson's r is about 0.94 because the relationship is curved, but Spearman's is exactly 1, because y always increases with x. Spearman is also less affected by extreme values in many cases, though, as our sick student shows, no single number is fully safe from a badly placed point.

Binned summaries for big data: With a million rows, even a transparent scatter plot turns into a blob. Two tricks help. A hexbin or 2D histogram divides the plane into small cells and colours each cell by how many points fall in it, so you see where data is dense. A binned summary cuts x into ranges and plots the mean or median of y in each range: for example, group customers by delivery time in 10-minute bins and plot the share who ordered again within 30 days. If the line drops from 62 percent in the 20 to 30 minute bin to 41 percent above 60 minutes, you have a clear, readable relationship that a raw scatter of yes-or-no outcomes could never show. Include the count in each bin, because the last bins are often thin.

The correlation matrix: With many numeric columns, df.corr() gives the correlation of every pair, often shown as a heatmap. It is a quick map to find strongly related pairs, for example two columns that measure nearly the same thing, which matters for models. But treat it as a map, not the territory: each cell hides a scatter plot that might be curved, driven by an outlier or split into clusters. Plot the important pairs. And with 20 columns there are 190 pairs, so some moderate correlations will appear by pure chance.

Numeric versus categorical: To compare a numeric variable across groups, like delivery time by zone, use side-by-side box plots or several histograms, plus a group summary table with count, median, IQR and mean. Order the groups by their median so the chart is easy to read. Always show counts: a zone with 12 orders and a median of 50 minutes is weak evidence compared with a zone with 3,000 orders and a median of 40.

Two categorical variables: For two categories, like payment method and city, use a cross-tabulation: pd.crosstab(df["city"], df["payment"]). Raw counts mostly reflect how big each city is, so convert to row percentages with normalize="index". Suppose Dhaka has 10,000 orders, 60 percent bKash and 25 percent card, while Sylhet has 1,000 orders, 75 percent bKash and 5 percent card. In counts Dhaka has far more bKash orders, 6,000 against 750, but in percentages Sylhet relies on bKash more. Stacked 100 percent bar charts show such mixes well.

Simpson's paradox: Sometimes a relationship that holds in every subgroup reverses when the groups are combined. A famous real example is a 1986 study comparing two kidney stone treatments. For small stones, treatment A succeeded in 81 of 87 cases, 93 percent, and treatment B in 234 of 270, about 87 percent. For large stones, A succeeded in 192 of 263, 73 percent, and B in 55 of 80, about 69 percent. A was better in both groups. But overall, A succeeded in 273 of 350, 78 percent, and B in 289 of 350, about 83 percent, so B looks better when combined. How? Doctors gave treatment A mostly to large, hard stones and B mostly to small, easy ones. Stone size, a lurking variable, affects both which treatment is used and how likely success is.

Lessons from Simpson's paradox: Whenever you compare groups, ask what else differs between them. Branch A may have lower customer ratings than branch B overall, yet be better for both delivery and pickup orders, simply because A does far more deliveries, which get lower ratings everywhere. The fix is to split by the lurking variable and compare like with like, or to adjust for it, which connects to causal thinking in lesson 18. Which answer is "right" depends on the question: to choose a treatment for a patient with a known stone size, use the subgroup rates.

Three or more variables: Add a third variable to a scatter plot with colour or marker shape, for example colour each customer by city. Pair plots show a grid of scatter plots for every pair of a few numeric columns, with histograms on the diagonal, a fast overview of a small set of variables. Faceting, also called small multiples, draws the same chart once for each group, like one scatter plot per division, which often reveals that a relationship exists in some groups and not others.

Time series EDA: Data over time has its own patterns. Trend is a long-term rise or fall. Seasonality is a pattern that repeats on a fixed calendar, like weekly cycles in food orders, or yearly cycles in dengue and in sales before Eid. Irregular events are spikes or drops caused by things like hartals, floods or system outages. Plot the series as a line chart first. Then compare the same period across years, and look at averages by weekday or month to see seasonality.

Moving averages, worked: A moving average replaces each point with the average of nearby points, smoothing short-term noise so the trend is clearer. Take weekly dengue cases 40, 55, 70, 65, 90, 120 and 150. The 3-week moving average ending at week 3 is (40 + 55 + 70) / 3 = 55; ending at week 4 it is (55 + 70 + 65) / 3, about 63.3; then 75, about 91.7, and 120. The small dip at week 4 disappears and the rise is obvious. For daily data with weekly patterns, a 7-day moving average removes the weekday effect, because every window contains each weekday once. Remember that a trailing moving average lags behind sudden changes.

Lagged relationships: In time series, cause often comes before effect. Rainfall may relate to dengue cases two or three weeks later, not the same week. Compute the correlation of cases with rainfall shifted by 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 weeks and see where it is strongest. Be careful: both series may simply share the same seasonal pattern, which creates correlation at many lags without any direct link. Comparing year-over-year changes or removing seasonality first helps.

An EDA checklist for relationships: Plot the target, the thing you care about, against each important variable. Build a correlation matrix and plot the strongest pairs. Use row-percentage cross-tabs for categories. Compare groups with box plots and counts. For any surprising group difference, split by plausible lurking variables. For time data, plot trend, seasonality and lags. Write each finding as a plain sentence with a caveat, like "Late deliveries are 2.3 times more common in zone 7, but zone 7 also has more rain-day orders; needs splitting by weather."

Real-life example 1, a telecom churn study: Plotting churn rate against monthly data usage shows a U-shape: very low users and very high users churn most. Pearson's r is near 0, which would wrongly suggest usage does not matter. A cross-tab by package type reveals that heavy users on old packages churn the most, because competitors offer them better deals. EDA turned a "no correlation" into a specific retention target.

Real-life example 2, school results by area: Comparing pass rates of urban and rural schools shows urban schools ahead overall. Splitting by science and humanities streams shows the gap shrinks a lot within each stream, because urban schools have a larger share of science students, whose pass rates are higher everywhere. Part of the "urban advantage" was really a difference in stream mix, a Simpson-style lesson that changes where support should go.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include trusting r without plots, reading r near 0 as "no relationship", comparing raw counts across groups of different size, ignoring lurking variables, over-reading one of many correlations in a big matrix, and confusing shared seasonality with a causal link. Exams ask you to interpret scatter plots and correlations, compare Pearson and Spearman, compute row percentages, explain Simpson's paradox with a numerical example, and compute a simple moving average.

Recap: Relationships are where most insight lives. Use scatter plots, correlations with care, box plots with counts, and percentage cross-tabs. Watch for Simpson's paradox by asking what else differs between groups. For time data, separate trend, seasonality and events, smooth with moving averages and check lags. These pictures only help if they are drawn well, so the next lesson is about the principles of good visualization.
key_points: Scatter plots show the form, direction, strength and outliers of a relationship between two numeric variables.
Pearson's r measures linear relationship and is fragile to outliers; Spearman's rank correlation measures any monotonic relationship.
A correlation matrix is a quick map, but every important pair still needs its own plot.
For two categorical variables use a cross-tab with row or column percentages, not raw counts.
Compare groups with side-by-side box plots and group summaries that include counts.
Simpson's paradox: a trend in every subgroup can reverse when groups are combined, because of a lurking variable.
Time series EDA looks for trend, seasonality and unusual events; moving averages smooth out short-term noise.
lessons.tip: Whenever a comparison between two groups surprises you, ask "what else differs between these groups?" and split the data by that thing. Simpson's paradox is rare in textbooks but common in real business data.
lessons.task: Take five days of your own life and record hours of sleep and how tired you felt from 1 to 10. Draw a scatter plot on paper, guess the sign of the correlation, then write down one confounder (something that might affect both) and how you would check it.

quiz.q: Five students' study hours 1 to 5 and marks 40, 50, 55, 65 and 70 give r of about 0.99. A sixth student studied 6 hours and scored 20. What happens to Pearson's r?
options: It drops to about -0.09, showing how one point can dominate r
quiz.explain: Pearson's r is sensitive to outliers. Always look at the scatter plot before trusting r.

quiz.q: For x = 1 to 5 and y = x cubed, Pearson's r is about 0.94. What is Spearman's rank correlation?
options: 1.0, because y always increases with x
quiz.explain: Spearman uses ranks, so any perfectly increasing relationship scores 1 even if it is curved.

quiz.q: In the kidney stone study, treatment A had the higher success rate for both small and large stones but the lower overall rate. Why?
options: Treatment A was used mostly on harder, large-stone cases, and stone size affects success
Treatment B is better for every patient
Overall rates are always more reliable than subgroup rates
quiz.explain: This is Simpson's paradox. The mix of case difficulty differed between treatments, so the combined rate misleads.

quiz.q: Weekly dengue cases are 40, 55, 70, 65, 90, 120 and 150. What is the 3-week moving average ending at week 4?
quiz.explain: (55 + 70 + 65) / 3 is about 63.3. Moving averages smooth week-to-week bumps.

quiz.q: Why should a cross-tab of payment method by city usually be shown as row percentages?
options: Cities have different numbers of orders, so percentages make their mixes comparable
quiz.explain: Raw counts mostly reflect city size; row percentages show each city's payment mix fairly.

lessons.title: Data Visualization Principles
lessons.content:
Imagine you are lost in a new city and ask two people for directions. The first gives you a long paragraph: "go straight, then after the third or maybe fourth lane, near a blue shop, turn..." The second draws a quick map on a piece of paper with one arrow and a big X. You understand the map in two seconds. A good chart is that quick map: it turns numbers into shapes the eye reads instantly. A bad chart is worse than no chart, because it confidently points people the wrong way. This lesson is about the principles that make charts honest and clear.

What data visualization is: Data visualization means encoding data values as visual properties, such as position, length, angle, area, colour or shape, so that people can see patterns, compare values and remember messages. Every chart is a set of encodings. In a bar chart, value is encoded as bar length; in a scatter plot, two values are encoded as horizontal and vertical position; in a map, values may be encoded as colour. Choosing the right encoding is the core skill.

Why it matters: Humans are much better at spotting patterns in pictures than in tables of numbers. A table of 365 daily sales figures hides the weekly cycle and the Eid spike; a line chart shows both instantly. Charts are also how most decision makers meet your work: a manager may never read your notebook but will look at three charts in a meeting. If those charts are unclear or misleading, the analysis behind them is wasted or, worse, causes bad decisions.

Two purposes: exploring and explaining: Exploratory charts are for you, during EDA. They can be quick and rough, and you make dozens of them. Explanatory charts are for others, to communicate one finding. They need care: one message, clear labels, nothing distracting. Most bad charts in presentations are exploratory charts pasted in without being redesigned for the audience.

Choosing a chart by the question: Start from the question, not from the chart menu. To compare quantities across categories, use a bar chart, usually horizontal and sorted when category names are long. To show a distribution, use a histogram or box plot (lesson 12). To show a relationship between two numeric variables, use a scatter plot (lesson 13). To show change over time, use a line chart, with time on the x-axis running left to right. To show parts of a whole, use a stacked bar or a 100 percent stacked bar; a pie chart only works with two or three slices. To show geography, use a map, but only when location really matters.

Cleveland and McGill's ranking: In 1984 statisticians William Cleveland and Robert McGill ran experiments asking people to judge values from different encodings. People were most accurate with position along a common scale, like dots or bar ends on one shared axis. Next came position on separate but identical scales, then length, then angle and slope, then area, then volume, and colour shading and saturation were among the least accurate. This explains many design rules: bar charts beat pie charts because length on a common baseline beats angle; dot plots are excellent; bubble sizes are hard to compare; colour should show categories or rough levels, not precise amounts.

Bar charts versus pie charts: Try to tell from a pie chart whether a 23 percent slice is bigger than a 21 percent slice; it is nearly impossible. In a bar chart, the difference is clear. Pie charts get harder with each extra slice and fail completely with 8 or 12. If you must show parts of a whole with many parts, use a sorted bar chart of percentages. A pie can still work for a simple message with two or three parts, like "62 percent of payments are now digital".

Bars start at zero: In a bar chart, the reader judges the length of the bar, so the length must be proportional to the value. That means the value axis must start at zero. Line charts are different: they encode values by position and the slope between points, so zooming the axis to show change can be fine, as long as the axis is clearly labelled. For example, a line chart of exchange rates between 108 and 122 taka per dollar can start at 105; a bar chart of the same values must start at 0.

The lie factor, worked: Edward Tufte, in his 1983 book The Visual Display of Quantitative Information, defined the lie factor as the size of an effect shown in the graphic divided by the size of the effect in the data. Suppose branch A sold 95 lakh taka and branch B 100 lakh. The real difference is 5 divided by 95, about 5.3 percent. If the bar chart's axis starts at 90, branch A's bar is 5 units tall and B's is 10, so B looks 100 percent bigger. The lie factor is 100 divided by 5.26, about 19. The chart exaggerates the difference nineteen times. A lie factor near 1 is honest.

Other common distortions: Dual axes, two different y-axes on one chart, let the designer make any two lines appear to move together by choosing the scales; avoid them or use two aligned charts. 3D effects distort lengths and areas and hide bars behind each other. Cherry-picked time windows can turn a long-term fall into an apparent rise. Uneven intervals on the x-axis, like 2010, 2015, 2020, 2021, 2022 spaced equally, distort trends. Using area or icons that grow in both height and width makes a doubling look like a quadrupling.

Chartjunk and the data-ink ratio: Tufte also coined chartjunk for decoration that carries no information: heavy gridlines, background images, shadows, 3D bevels, unnecessary legends. His data-ink ratio asks what share of the ink on a chart actually shows data, and suggests raising it by erasing non-data ink. You do not need to be extreme, a light gridline can help reading, but every element should earn its place. A good test: remove an element and see whether the chart becomes harder to read. If not, leave it out.

Colour with purpose: Use colour to encode information, not to decorate. Sequential palettes go from light to dark in one hue and suit ordered values, like population density. Diverging palettes use two hues that meet at a neutral middle and suit values above and below a meaningful midpoint, like profit and loss, or temperature above and below average. Categorical palettes use clearly different hues for unordered groups, and work best with few groups, ideally under about eight. Avoid the rainbow palette for ordered data; its bright bands create false boundaries. Highlighting is powerful: draw everything in grey and one line in a strong colour to direct attention.

Colour-blind safety and accessibility: Red-green colour vision deficiency is common, affecting roughly 1 in 12 men in many populations. A chart that separates "good" and "bad" only with red and green may be unreadable for them. Use colour-blind safe palettes, vary lightness as well as hue, and add labels or patterns so colour is not the only cue. Also keep text large enough to read on a projector or a phone, and give enough contrast against the background.

Labels and titles: Label axes with names and units, like "Delivery time (minutes)". Label lines directly at their ends instead of forcing readers to match colours with a legend. Write the title as the finding: "Late deliveries doubled in Sylhet after the June floods" tells the reader what to look for, while "Delivery data" tells them nothing. Add a short subtitle for details like the date range, and a source line at the bottom. Round numbers sensibly: 23.4 percent, not 23.4187 percent.

Showing uncertainty: Many numbers on charts are estimates: survey percentages, forecasts, averages from samples. Drawing them as sharp points or bars hides how sure we are. Error bars show a range around each estimate, such as a 95 percent confidence interval from lesson 16; a shaded band around a forecast line shows the range of likely futures. Always say in the caption what the bars mean, because "plus or minus one standard deviation" and "95 percent confidence interval" are very different widths. If two survey results are 48 and 52 percent with error bars of plus or minus 3 points, the overlapping bars warn readers not to treat 52 as a clear winner. Honest uncertainty makes a chart less dramatic and much more useful.

Small multiples: When one chart has too many lines, a spaghetti chart, split it into small multiples: the same small chart repeated for each group, with the same axes, arranged in a grid. Eight divisions, each with its own small line chart of monthly sales on the same scale, are far easier to compare than eight tangled lines on one chart. Tufte championed this idea, and it is one of the most effective tools for comparing many groups.

Real-life example 1, a flood report: An NGO wants to show how many households in each of 10 upazilas lost crops in floods. The first draft is a 3D pie with 10 colours. The redesign is a sorted horizontal bar chart of the share of households affected, starting at zero, with the worst upazila highlighted in a strong colour and the rest in grey, and the title "Nearly half of households in Upazila X lost crops, twice the regional average". Donors understand it in seconds.

Real-life example 2, a stock price chart: A news post shows a company's share price dropping from 52 to 48 taka with the y-axis running from 47 to 53, making it look like a crash. As a line chart, zooming is acceptable, but the honest version adds the axis range clearly, shows a longer time window for context, and states the change in the title: "Share price fell 7.7 percent this week". The percentage, 4 divided by 52, gives readers the true size.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include pie charts with many slices, bar axes not starting at zero, dual axes, 3D charts, rainbow palettes for ordered data, red-green only colour coding, missing units, legends instead of direct labels, generic titles and overloaded charts. Exams ask you to choose a suitable chart for a given question, explain Cleveland and McGill's ranking, compute a lie factor, criticise and redesign a misleading chart, and explain sequential, diverging and categorical colour schemes.

Recap: Start from the question, pick the encoding people read best, usually position or length, keep bars at zero, compute the lie factor when in doubt, strip chartjunk, use colour with purpose and for everyone, label directly, and title with the finding. Use small multiples when one chart gets crowded. Next lesson turns these principles into practice with real tools: plotting libraries, BI tools and dashboards.
key_points: Pick the chart from the question: comparison (bar), distribution (histogram, box plot), relationship (scatter), change over time (line), part of a whole (stacked bar, sometimes pie).
Cleveland and McGill: people judge position most accurately, then length, then angle and slope, then area, volume and colour.
Bar charts must start at zero because the bar's length is the message; line charts may zoom in if clearly labelled.
Tufte's lie factor compares the size of an effect in the graphic with its size in the data; a truncated bar axis can exaggerate many times.
Remove chartjunk: 3D effects, heavy gridlines, needless colours and decorations.
Use sequential colours for ordered values, diverging for above and below a midpoint, categorical for groups, and check colour-blind safety.
Label directly, title with the finding, show units and sources, and use small multiples instead of crowded charts.
lessons.tip: Before drawing any chart, write its title as a full sentence stating the finding, like "Sylhet's late deliveries doubled after the floods". If you cannot write that sentence, you do not yet know what the chart is for.
lessons.task: Find one chart in a newspaper, TV news or social media post. Identify its chart type, what it encodes with position, length, colour or area, whether the axis starts at zero where it should, and what single message it sends. Then sketch a better version on paper with a title that states the finding.

quiz.q: You want to compare total sales across 12 branches. Which chart is usually best?
options: A line chart with branches on the x-axis
quiz.explain: Bars use length on a common baseline, which people judge accurately, and sorting makes ranking obvious.

quiz.q: Sales were 95 and 100. A bar chart's y-axis starts at 90, so the bars are 5 and 10 units tall. What is the lie factor?
quiz.explain: The data changes about 5.3 percent but the bars change 100 percent; 100 / 5.26 is about 19.

quiz.q: According to Cleveland and McGill, which encoding do people read most accurately?
quiz.explain: Position on a shared axis is the most accurately judged encoding, which is why dot plots and bars work well.

quiz.q: You map temperature anomalies, some above and some below the long-term average. Which colour scheme fits?
options: Categorical, a different colour for each district
Sequential from light to dark of one colour
Diverging, two colours meeting at a neutral midpoint
quiz.explain: Diverging palettes show direction and size of difference from a meaningful centre.

quiz.q: Which title best follows good practice?
options: Uttara overtook Mirpur in monthly sales from July 2024
quiz.explain: A finding-style title tells the reader what to see; the axis labels still carry the details.

lessons.title: Visualization Tools and Dashboards
lessons.content:
Think of the dashboard of a bus. The driver cannot read a report while driving through Gulistan traffic. Instead, a few dials show speed, fuel and engine temperature, and a warning light turns red if something is wrong. One glance tells the driver whether to act. A data dashboard is the same idea for a business: a small set of live numbers and charts that tell managers, at a glance, whether things are on track and where to look if they are not. In this lesson we cover the tools that draw charts, from code libraries to BI tools, and how to design dashboards people actually use.

Two families of tools: Charts are made either with code or with point-and-click tools. Code libraries, mainly in Python, give full control, live inside your analysis, and are reproducible: rerun the notebook and every chart updates. Business intelligence, or BI, tools let analysts and even managers build interactive reports by dragging fields onto a canvas, and share them with many people through a web portal. Most teams use both: code for exploration and one-off analyses, BI tools for recurring reports and dashboards.

matplotlib: matplotlib, started by John Hunter around 2003, is the foundation of plotting in Python. Its model has two key objects. A figure is the whole canvas, like a sheet of paper. An axes is one plotting area inside it, with its own x-axis and y-axis; a figure can hold one axes or a grid of many. Typical code is fig, ax = plt.subplots(), then ax.bar(branches, sales), ax.set_title("Uttara leads June sales"), ax.set_ylabel("Sales (taka)"). Almost anything can be customised, which is its strength and its weakness: good charts take some code, and defaults are not always pretty.

seaborn: seaborn, created by Michael Waskom, builds on matplotlib and focuses on statistical charts from tidy, long data, the shape from lesson 04. One line like sns.boxplot(data=df, x="zone", y="delivery_min") draws side-by-side box plots; adding hue="weather" splits each box by weather; sns.relplot(..., col="division") makes small multiples automatically. Its defaults look clean and it handles grouping and confidence bands for you. Because it returns matplotlib objects, you can still fine-tune details.

plotly and interactive charts: plotly produces interactive charts that run in a web browser: hover to see exact values, zoom into a time range, click legend items to hide lines. plotly express has a concise interface similar to seaborn. Interactivity is valuable for exploration and for dashboards, but it is not a substitute for a clear message; a static chart in a report must work without hovering. Other Python options include Altair, which describes charts declaratively, and Bokeh.

Saving and sharing charts: For reports and slides, save charts as image files with fig.savefig. Vector formats like SVG or PDF stay sharp at any size and suit printed reports; PNG at a sufficient resolution suits slides and chat apps. Write a small function that applies your team's fonts, colours and source line, so every chart looks consistent without repeating twenty lines of styling. Keep the code that made each chart next to the image, so when the data is updated next month you rerun one cell instead of redrawing by hand.

BI tools: Tools such as Microsoft Power BI, Tableau and Google's Looker Studio connect to databases, spreadsheets and cloud warehouses, let you define measures like total sales or on-time rate once, and build interactive dashboards with filters and drill-downs. They handle user access, scheduled refreshes and sharing. Their strengths are speed of building and ease for non-programmers. Their weaknesses are that complex logic can become hidden inside many clicked settings, version control is harder than with code, and licences cost money. The underlying principle is the same as in lesson 06: define logic once, in one place, and reuse it.

Maps and choropleths: A choropleth map colours regions, such as districts or upazilas, by a value. Maps are powerful when location matters, like flood exposure or delivery coverage. But a famous trap is mapping raw counts: a map of number of mobile banking agents, dengue cases or shops per district mostly shows where people live, so Dhaka and Chattogram are always darkest. Normalise first: agents per 10,000 people, cases per 100,000 people, or shops per square kilometre. Also remember that large rural districts dominate the map visually even if few people live there, so a bar chart of rates can be clearer for comparisons, with the map as context.

What a dashboard is for: A dashboard is a visual display of the most important information needed to monitor something, arranged on one screen so it can be read at a glance. Stephen Few, a well-known writer on dashboard design, stressed the "single screen" and "at a glance" parts. A dashboard is not a place to explore every question; it is for monitoring a known set of metrics and noticing when something needs attention. Deep investigation then happens in analysis, often starting from what the dashboard flagged.

Know the audience and decisions: Before designing, list who will use it, how often, and which decisions it supports. A rider operations manager checks every hour which zones are short of riders. A CEO checks weekly whether growth and costs are on target. These need different dashboards. For each metric, write the action it can trigger: "if on-time rate in a zone falls below 85 percent, move riders there." Metrics without a possible action are candidates for removal.

Layout: People read a screen from the top left, in a rough Z or F pattern. Put the few most important KPIs at the top as large numbers, each with context: a comparison with the target, the previous period or the same day last week, and a small arrow or colour showing good or bad. Below that, put trends over time, usually line charts. Below that, breakdowns that explain the KPIs, such as by zone, product or channel. Filters for date range and key segments go at the top or side. Keep it to roughly 5 to 9 elements; more than that turns a dashboard into a wall of charts.

Context makes numbers meaningful: "Orders today: 12,430" means little alone. "Orders today: 12,430, up 6 percent on last Tuesday, 3 percent below target" is useful. Always compare like with like: same weekday last week rather than yesterday, because Friday and Saturday patterns differ. Use colour sparingly for status, for example grey for normal and red only when a metric crosses a threshold, so red actually catches the eye.

Vanity versus actionable metrics: Vanity metrics look impressive and usually only go up, like total app downloads since launch or total registered users. They make good press releases but guide no decisions. Actionable metrics tie to behaviour you can change: weekly active users, share of new users completing a first order within 7 days, repeat purchase rate, on-time delivery rate. A dashboard full of vanity metrics makes everyone feel good while the business quietly struggles.

A delivery company dashboard, designed: Imagine an operations dashboard for a Dhaka food delivery company. Top row tiles: orders today versus the same weekday last week; on-time rate, defined as delivered within the promised time, against a 90 percent target; median delivery time; cancellation rate. Middle: a line chart of hourly on-time rate today against the average of the last four same weekdays, so the dinner rush is compared fairly. Bottom left: a sorted bar chart of late orders by zone, coloured red where on-time rate is below 85 percent. Bottom right: a table of the ten restaurants with the longest food preparation times today. Filters: date, zone and city. Every element answers a question a shift manager acts on.

Definitions and trust: Each metric on a dashboard needs a written definition, reachable from the dashboard itself, like an info icon: formula, data source, filters and refresh time. When two dashboards show different "on-time rates" because one counts cancelled orders and the other does not, people stop trusting both. Shared, documented metric definitions, sometimes called a semantic layer or metrics layer, prevent this. Display "Data updated at 10:15 AM" so nobody acts on stale numbers.

Performance and refresh: A dashboard that takes a minute to load will not be used. Do not let a dashboard query hundreds of millions of raw rows each time. Instead, pre-aggregate: a scheduled job builds a small summary table, like orders per zone per hour, and the dashboard reads that. Choose a refresh cadence that matches decisions: hourly for operations, daily for most business metrics, weekly for strategy. Real time costs much more and is only worth it when someone will act within minutes.

Maintaining dashboards: Dashboards decay. Business definitions change, source tables get renamed, and filters break. Each dashboard needs an owner who answers questions and fixes problems. Usage logs show which dashboards nobody opens; retire them, because a cluttered portal of 300 half-broken dashboards makes it hard to find the 10 that matter. When a dashboard number looks wrong, investigate like any data bug: check the definition, the source, the refresh time and the filters.

Real-life example 1, a district health dashboard: A district health office tracks immunisation coverage. KPI tiles show coverage for key vaccines against targets for the month; a line chart shows monthly coverage over two years; a choropleth shows coverage rate per union, not raw counts, with unions below 80 percent highlighted; a table lists unions whose reports are late. Health workers use the late-report table every Monday to call those unions, and supervisors plan outreach camps where the map shows low coverage.

Real-life example 2, a garments buyer dashboard: An apparel exporter's buyer-facing dashboard shows on-time shipment rate, defect rate per 1,000 pieces, and order fill rate against contract targets, with a weekly trend and a breakdown by factory line. A filter by buyer lets each client see only its orders. Because the dashboard reads a daily summary table, it loads in seconds, and the definition panel explains that "on-time" means shipped by the agreed ex-factory date.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include cramming 20 charts on one screen, showing numbers without comparisons, using vanity metrics, mapping raw counts, undefined or conflicting metric definitions, hiding stale data, slow dashboards built on raw tables, and dashboards with no owner. Exams ask you to compare code libraries and BI tools, explain matplotlib's figure and axes model, describe principles of dashboard design and layout, distinguish vanity from actionable metrics, explain why choropleths need normalisation, and design a dashboard for a given scenario.

Recap: Use matplotlib for full control, seaborn for quick statistical charts from tidy data, plotly for interactivity, and BI tools for shared, refreshed dashboards. Normalise maps. Design dashboards for specific users and decisions: KPIs with context at the top, trends, then breakdowns, few filters, clear definitions, visible freshness and fast pre-aggregated data. Charts and dashboards show what is happening; to judge whether differences are real or just noise, we now turn to statistics for decisions in lesson 16.
key_points: matplotlib draws any chart from figures and axes; seaborn adds statistical charts from tidy data; plotly adds interactivity for the web.
BI tools like Power BI, Tableau and Looker Studio connect to data and build interactive dashboards without much code.
Maps of raw counts mostly show where people live; normalise by population or area before drawing a choropleth.
A dashboard is for monitoring decisions: KPIs on top with comparisons, then trends, then breakdowns, with a few filters.
Prefer actionable metrics over vanity metrics that only go up.
Show data freshness, define every metric, and pre-aggregate large data so the dashboard stays fast.
Dashboards need owners and maintenance; unused or broken dashboards should be retired.
lessons.tip: Give every dashboard the five-second test: show it to someone for five seconds, hide it, and ask what they remember. If they cannot name the main number and whether it is good or bad, simplify.
lessons.task: Design on paper a one-screen dashboard for your college canteen manager. Choose four KPI tiles with comparisons, one trend chart, one breakdown chart and two filters. Write next to each element the question it answers and the action a manager might take after seeing it.

quiz.q: In matplotlib, what is the relationship between a figure and an axes?
options: A figure is the whole canvas and can contain one or more axes, each a single plot
Axes are only used for 3D charts
quiz.explain: The figure is the page; each axes is one plotting area with its own x and y axis.

quiz.q: A map shows the number of bKash agents per district, and Dhaka is darkest. What is the main risk in reading it?
options: The map mostly reflects population; agents per 10,000 people would compare districts fairly
quiz.explain: Raw counts follow population. Normalising turns a population map into an insight.

quiz.q: Which is a vanity metric for a learning app?
options: Share of new users who finish their first lesson in 7 days
Average lessons completed per active learner
quiz.explain: Cumulative downloads only go up and do not guide any decision; the others reveal whether learning happens.

quiz.q: Where should the most important KPIs usually go on a dashboard?
options: At the top, with comparisons to a target or previous period
At the bottom, after all the detail charts
quiz.explain: People read top-left first. Key numbers with context belong there.

quiz.q: A dashboard query scans 200 million raw rows every time someone opens it and takes two minutes. What is the usual fix?
options: Pre-aggregate the data into a smaller daily summary table that the dashboard reads
quiz.explain: Dashboards should read small, pre-computed summaries refreshed on a schedule.

lessons.title: Statistics for Decisions I: Estimation and Uncertainty
lessons.content:
Imagine you want to know whether a big pot of dal has enough salt. You do not drink the whole pot. You stir it and taste one spoon. If the spoon is salty, the pot probably is too. But one spoon could mislead a little: maybe you caught a bit where the salt had not mixed yet. Tasting three spoons from different places makes you more confident. Statistics for decisions is exactly this: learning about a whole pot, the population, from a few spoons, the sample, and being honest about how sure you can be. This lesson covers estimation and uncertainty; lesson 17 covers testing and A/B experiments.

What estimation is: An estimate is a number computed from a sample to approximate an unknown population value. The share of satisfied customers among the 400 we surveyed estimates the share among all 200,000 customers. The average delivery time in a sample of orders estimates the average across all orders. You studied point estimation in deep-cse-2-6 lesson 19 and confidence intervals in lesson 20; here we use them as everyday tools for business and policy decisions.

Why uncertainty matters: Every sample is a bit different by pure chance. If you surveyed another 400 customers, you would get a slightly different percentage. Decisions based on a single number without its uncertainty are dangerous. A manager who sees satisfaction drop from 67 percent last month to 64 percent this month may launch an expensive programme, when the change is well within normal sampling noise. Knowing the uncertainty tells you when a change is real enough to act on.

The sampling distribution, recap: Imagine drawing many samples of the same size and computing the mean of each. Those means form a distribution, called the sampling distribution. The central limit theorem (deep-cse-2-6 lesson 17) says that for reasonably large samples this distribution is approximately normal and centred on the true population value, even if the data itself is skewed. Its spread is the standard error. This is the bridge from one sample to statements about the population.

Standard error of a mean, worked: The standard error of the mean is s divided by the square root of n, where s is the sample standard deviation. Suppose 100 delivery times have mean 34 minutes and s = 12 minutes. The standard error is 12 divided by 10, which is 1.2 minutes. Notice the difference: s = 12 says individual deliveries vary a lot, by around 12 minutes; the standard error 1.2 says our estimate of the average is precise to about a minute. Confusing the two is a very common mistake.

A confidence interval for a mean: A 95 percent confidence interval is approximately the estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors. For our deliveries: 34 plus or minus 1.96 times 1.2, which is 34 plus or minus about 2.35, giving roughly 31.6 to 36.4 minutes. For small samples, under about 30, or when the population standard deviation is unknown and the data is close to normal, use the t distribution instead of 1.96; with n = 10 the multiplier is about 2.26, which widens the interval to reflect extra uncertainty.

A confidence interval for a proportion, worked: For yes-or-no data, the standard error of a proportion p is the square root of p(1 - p) / n. In a survey of 400 customers, 260 say they are satisfied, so p = 0.65. The standard error is the square root of 0.65 times 0.35 divided by 400, about 0.0238. The margin of error is 1.96 times 0.0238, about 0.047, so the 95 percent interval is about 0.603 to 0.697, or 60.3 to 69.7 percent. Reported honestly: "About 65 percent are satisfied, give or take about 5 points." This simple formula works well when n times p and n times (1 - p) are both comfortably above 10; for small samples or extreme proportions, use better methods such as the Wilson interval.

Reading an interval correctly: The 95 percent describes the method, not this particular interval. If you repeated the survey many times and built an interval each time, about 95 percent of those intervals would contain the true population value. It does not mean 95 percent of customers fall in the interval, and in classical statistics it does not mean the true value moves around. A practical reading is fine: "values in this range are consistent with our data; values far outside it are not." When two groups' intervals barely overlap, be careful; overlapping intervals do not automatically mean "no difference", which is why lesson 17 tests the difference directly.

An interval for a difference, worked: Decisions are usually about change, so estimate the difference directly. Return to the manager who saw satisfaction fall from 67 percent to 64 percent, each from a survey of 400. The difference is -3 points. The standard error of a difference between two independent proportions is the square root of the sum of their squared standard errors: the square root of 0.67 times 0.33 divided by 400 plus 0.64 times 0.36 divided by 400, about 0.0336. The 95 percent interval is -3 plus or minus 1.96 times 3.36 points, about -9.6 to +3.6 points. Zero is comfortably inside, so the data cannot tell whether satisfaction fell, stayed the same or even rose slightly. The expensive programme should wait for more evidence.

What intervals do not cover: A confidence interval only measures random sampling error. It says nothing about bias: if your survey only reached happy, long-time customers (lesson 05), the interval will be narrow and confidently wrong. It also ignores measurement errors, wrong definitions and data leakage. Always pair the interval with a sentence about how the data was collected.

The bootstrap: Formulas exist for means and proportions, but what about the median, a ratio, or a model's accuracy? The bootstrap, introduced by Bradley Efron in 1979, estimates uncertainty by simulation. Treat your sample as a stand-in for the population. Draw a new sample of the same size from it with replacement, so some values appear twice and some not at all, and compute your statistic. Repeat thousands of times. The spread of those results approximates the standard error, and the middle 95 percent of them gives a percentile confidence interval.

The bootstrap by hand: Take a tiny sample of five daily complaint counts: 5, 8, 12, 15 and 40, mean 16. One resample might be 8, 8, 12, 40, 5, mean 14.6. Another: 15, 5, 5, 12, 8, mean 9. Another: 40, 40, 12, 15, 8, mean 23. Another: 5, 12, 12, 8, 15, mean 10.4. Already you see the means swing widely, mainly depending on how many times the 40 is picked. With 10,000 resamples on a computer, the middle 95 percent of the means runs from about 7.6 to 28.6. That wide interval honestly reflects that five days, one of them extreme, tell us little. The bootstrap needs a reasonable sample to work well, but it is a powerful, general tool.

Margin of error and sample size, worked: Planning the sample size before collecting data saves money. For a proportion, the margin of error is 1.96 times the square root of p(1 - p) / n. Solving for n: n = 1.96 squared times p(1 - p) divided by the margin squared. With the worst case p = 0.5 and a desired margin of 3 percentage points, n = 3.8416 times 0.25 divided by 0.0009, about 1,067 people. For a 5 point margin, about 385. Because n grows with the square of the precision, halving the margin needs four times the sample. For subgroups, like each of 8 divisions, you need enough people in each group, which multiplies the total.

Practical versus statistical significance: With large data, even tiny differences become statistically clear. If 2 million users see two versions of an app screen and conversions are 5.00 percent and 5.05 percent, the difference may be statistically significant, meaning unlikely to be pure chance, yet it is only 0.05 percentage points. Whether it matters depends on business value: for a huge company it may be worth millions of taka; for a small one, it may not cover the cost of building the feature. Always report the effect size, the actual difference, with its confidence interval, and let the decision rest on whether the plausible range of effects is worth acting on.

Communicating uncertainty: Decision makers often dislike ranges, but ranges are the truth. Use plain words: "between 60 and 70 percent", "most likely around 65 percent". Show error bars or bands on charts (lesson 14). Avoid false precision like "64.87 percent" from a sample of 400. When an estimate is too uncertain to support a decision, say so and say how much more data would be needed.

Real-life example 1, a city satisfaction survey: A city corporation surveys 1,000 randomly chosen households about waste collection; 420 say service is good. The estimate is 42 percent with a margin of about 3 points, so between roughly 39 and 45 percent. Ward-level results, however, rest on only about 20 households each, with margins over 20 points, so the analyst warns against ranking wards from this survey and recommends a larger sample in the wards that matter most.

Real-life example 2, average basket size: An online grocery shop wants to know whether average basket size rose after a free delivery threshold of 999 taka was introduced. From a sample of 2,500 orders after the change, the mean basket is 1,140 taka with a standard deviation of 600, so the standard error is 600 divided by 50, which is 12 taka, and the 95 percent interval is about 1,116 to 1,164 taka. Because the distribution is skewed, the analyst also bootstraps the median basket. Before the change the mean was about 1,020 taka, far outside the interval, so the rise is not sampling noise; whether the threshold caused it is a causal question for lesson 18.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include reporting estimates without intervals, confusing standard deviation with standard error, saying "95 percent of people are in the interval", trusting narrow intervals from biased samples, ignoring small subgroup sizes, and treating statistically significant as important. Exams ask you to compute standard errors and confidence intervals for means and proportions, interpret an interval correctly, compute a required sample size, explain the bootstrap procedure, and distinguish practical from statistical significance.

Recap: Every estimate wobbles; the standard error measures how much. Build confidence intervals with about 1.96 standard errors, use t for small samples, read them as statements about a method, and remember they ignore bias. Use the bootstrap when no formula fits, plan sample sizes before collecting, and always judge effect size, not just significance. Next lesson uses these ideas to decide whether a change actually worked, through hypothesis tests and A/B experiments.
key_points: A sample estimate differs from the population value by chance; the standard error measures how much it typically wobbles.
Standard error of a mean is s divided by the square root of n; of a proportion, the square root of p(1 - p) / n.
A 95 percent confidence interval is roughly estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors; small samples use the t distribution.
The interval describes the method's reliability: 95 percent of intervals built this way would contain the true value.
The bootstrap estimates uncertainty by resampling the data with replacement many times.
Required sample size grows with the square of the precision you want; halving the margin needs four times the data.
Statistical significance is not practical importance; always report effect size with its interval.
lessons.tip: Never report an estimate without its uncertainty. "65 percent, give or take about 5 points" is a complete sentence; "65 percent" alone invites people to treat noise as fact.
lessons.task: Ask 20 classmates one yes-or-no question, such as whether they had breakfast today. Compute the proportion, its standard error and a 95 percent interval. Then compute how many people you would need to ask to get the margin of error down to 5 percentage points.

quiz.q: A sample of 100 delivery times has mean 34 minutes and standard deviation 12. What is the standard error of the mean?
quiz.explain: SE = s / sqrt(n) = 12 / 10 = 1.2 minutes.

quiz.q: In a survey of 400 customers, 260 are satisfied. What is the approximate 95 percent confidence interval?
quiz.explain: p = 0.65, SE is about 0.0238, margin is 1.96 x 0.0238, about 0.047, so roughly 60.3 to 69.7 percent.

quiz.q: Which interpretation of a 95 percent confidence interval is correct?
options: 95 percent of customers fall inside the interval
There is a 95 percent chance the sample mean is inside it
If we repeated the sampling many times, about 95 percent of intervals built this way would contain the true value
The true value changes 95 percent of the time
quiz.explain: The confidence is about the procedure. The interval is about the population value, not about individual people.

quiz.q: A poll wants a margin of error of 3 percentage points at 95 percent confidence, worst case p = 0.5. Roughly how many people are needed?
quiz.explain: n = 1.96 squared x 0.25 / 0.03 squared, about 1,067.

quiz.q: With 2 million users, a test shows conversion of 5.00 percent versus 5.05 percent, statistically significant. What should you say?
options: The difference is real but tiny; judge whether 0.05 points matters for the business
The test is wrong because significant results are always large
Statistical significance means it will triple revenue
quiz.explain: Huge samples make tiny effects significant. Report the effect size and its interval, and judge practical value.

lessons.title: Statistics for Decisions II: Hypothesis Tests and A/B Testing
lessons.content:
Imagine two tea stalls side by side at a bus stand. One owner thinks adding a little ginger makes customers come back. He tries ginger for a week and sales rise. Was it the ginger? Or was it colder weather, a holiday week, or just a lucky week? If he wants to really know, he could make ginger tea on random days and plain tea on others, and compare. Even then, he needs a way to tell a real difference from ordinary ups and downs. Hypothesis testing gives that way, and A/B testing is how modern apps and businesses use it every day to decide what actually works.

What a hypothesis test is: A hypothesis test asks whether the difference we see in data is bigger than what random chance alone would usually produce. We start with a null hypothesis, H0, usually "no effect": the new design converts at the same rate as the old one. The alternative hypothesis, H1, says there is an effect. We compute a test statistic that measures how far the data is from what H0 predicts, and then a p-value. You met the formal machinery in deep-cse-2-6 lessons 21 and 22; here we focus on using it correctly for real decisions.

The p-value, carefully: The p-value is the probability of seeing a difference at least as large as the one observed, if the null hypothesis were true. A small p-value means the data would be surprising under "no effect", which counts as evidence against it. It is not the probability that the null is true, not the probability the result is a fluke, and not the size of the effect. We compare it to a significance level alpha chosen in advance, usually 0.05. If p is below alpha, we reject H0; otherwise we fail to reject it, which is different from proving there is no effect.

Two kinds of errors: A Type I error, a false positive, is declaring an effect when there is none; its rate is alpha. A Type II error, a false negative, is missing a real effect; its rate is beta, and power, 1 minus beta, is the chance of detecting an effect of a given size. With alpha = 0.05, one in twenty tests of useless changes will still look like a win. With low power, many good ideas will look like failures. Both errors cost money.

What an A/B test is: An A/B test, also called a randomised controlled experiment, splits units, usually users, at random into a control group that sees the current version A and a treatment group that sees a new version B. Because assignment is random, the two groups are alike on average in everything else, such as age, phone type, city and mood, so a difference in outcomes can be credited to the change. That is why A/B tests are the gold standard for cause and effect in product decisions, a point we develop in lesson 18.

Designing the test: Decide the unit of randomisation: users are usual, but for a delivery pricing change you might randomise by zone or by day to avoid customers comparing prices. Choose one primary metric tied to the goal, like order conversion rate, and guardrail metrics that must not get worse, like cancellations, refunds and app crashes (lesson 03). Write the hypothesis, the minimum effect worth detecting, the sample size, the duration and the decision rule before launch. Run at least one full week, ideally two, so every weekday is covered, because behaviour on Friday differs from Tuesday.

The two-proportion z test, worked: Suppose control has 10,000 users with 500 conversions, a rate of 5.0 percent, and treatment has 10,000 users with 560 conversions, 5.6 percent. The difference is 0.6 percentage points. Under H0 both groups share one rate, estimated by pooling: 1,060 conversions out of 20,000 users is 0.053. The standard error of the difference is the square root of 0.053 times 0.947 times (1/10,000 + 1/10,000), about 0.00317. The z statistic is 0.006 divided by 0.00317, about 1.89. The two-sided p-value for z = 1.89 is about 0.058, just above 0.05. So, by the rule chosen in advance, we cannot reject "no effect", even though treatment did 12 percent better in relative terms.

Reading that result with an interval: The 95 percent confidence interval for the difference, using unpooled standard errors, runs from about -0.02 to +1.22 percentage points. This says more than the p-value: the effect could be essentially zero or worthwhile at about one point. The right conclusion is "promising but not conclusive", and the honest next step is to have planned a larger sample, not to declare victory or to tweak the analysis until p falls below 0.05.

Testing averages instead of rates: When the primary metric is an average, like order value in taka, the usual tool is a two-sample t test, which divides the difference in means by the standard error of that difference. Money metrics are heavily skewed, a few huge orders make averages jumpy, so these tests need larger samples than rate metrics. Common remedies are capping extreme values at a high percentile before testing, or bootstrapping the difference in means or medians (lesson 16). Decide which you will use before the test starts.

Sample size and power, worked: Before launching, decide the smallest effect worth detecting, the minimum detectable effect, and compute the sample needed for about 80 percent power. A common approximation for two proportions is n per group = (z for alpha + z for power) squared times (p1(1 - p1) + p2(1 - p2)) divided by (p2 - p1) squared. For alpha = 0.05 two-sided, z is 1.96; for 80 percent power, z is about 0.84. To detect a rise from 5.0 to 5.5 percent: (2.80) squared is about 7.85, times (0.0475 + 0.052) which is 0.0995, divided by 0.005 squared which is 0.000025, giving about 31,200 users per group. Small effects on small rates need large samples; that is why tiny apps struggle to A/B test small changes.

The peeking problem: It is tempting to check results every day and stop as soon as p dips below 0.05. But p-values wander up and down by chance during a test. If you check many times and stop at the first significant look, the real false positive rate rises well above 5 percent, sometimes several times higher. The fixes: decide the sample size or end date in advance and look only at the end, or use methods designed for continuous monitoring, such as sequential tests that adjust the thresholds for each look.

Multiple testing and Bonferroni, worked: Testing many metrics, segments or variants multiplies the chance of a false win. If you test 10 independent metrics at alpha 0.05 and nothing truly changed, the chance that at least one looks significant is 1 minus 0.95 to the power 10, about 40 percent. The Bonferroni correction divides alpha by the number of tests: 0.05 / 10 = 0.005 per test. It is simple and conservative. Better still, name one primary metric in advance, treat the rest as exploratory, and confirm surprising segment results with a new test. Searching through many slices until something is significant is called p-hacking, revisited in lesson 24.

Sample ratio mismatch: If you planned a 50/50 split and get 10,300 users in control and 9,700 in treatment out of 20,000, check it. A chi-square test for a 50/50 split gives a statistic of 18 and a p-value around 0.00002; such an imbalance almost never happens by chance. It usually means a bug: the treatment crashes on some phones and those users are not logged, or a redirect drops some users. Results from a test with sample ratio mismatch cannot be trusted until the cause is found.

Novelty, primacy and other traps: Users may click a new design simply because it is new, a novelty effect that fades; or resist change at first, a primacy effect. Run tests long enough and look at the effect over time. Seasonality matters: a test during Eid shopping may not generalise. Interference also matters: in a marketplace, giving treatment riders priority may slow control riders, so the comparison is biased; randomising by zone or time helps. Finally, very small changes repeated many times can add up; and big redesigns cannot always be tested piece by piece.

When not to A/B test: Some decisions cannot or should not be randomised. You cannot randomly give some patients a worse treatment, randomly raise prices for loyal customers in a way that feels unfair, or test changes when traffic is too small to ever reach the needed sample. Some changes are so obviously good, like fixing a broken payment button, that testing wastes time. In those cases use other evidence: before-and-after comparisons with care, natural experiments, or expert judgment, as lesson 18 discusses.

Real-life example 1, a checkout button: A Bangladeshi e-commerce app tests showing "Cash on delivery available" on the product page. Primary metric: orders per visitor. Guardrails: cancellation and return rates, because cash on delivery orders cancel more often. The planned sample is 40,000 visitors per group over two weeks. Orders rise from 3.1 to 3.5 percent with p well below 0.01, but cancellations also rise from 8 to 11 percent. After accounting for cancellations, net completed orders still rise, and the team launches with a plan to monitor cancellations by zone.

Real-life example 2, an SMS reminder for vaccination: A health programme wants to know if SMS reminders raise on-time child vaccination. Caregivers are randomised: half get reminders, half do not. The primary metric is the share vaccinated within a week of the due date. Because the programme serves many unions, randomisation is stratified by union so both groups include every area. The test shows a clear rise, and because assignment was random, the programme can credit the rise to the reminders and justify the cost of scaling up.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include reading the p-value as the probability the null is true, treating non-significant as proof of no effect, peeking and stopping early, testing many metrics without correction, ignoring guardrails and sample ratio mismatch, running tests for only a day or two, and changing the plan after seeing results. Exams ask you to state null and alternative hypotheses, explain p-values and Type I and II errors, carry out a two-proportion z test, compute a required sample size, explain the peeking and multiple testing problems with Bonferroni, and design an A/B test for a scenario.

Recap: Hypothesis tests ask whether a difference beats chance; p-values must be read carefully, alongside effect sizes and intervals. A/B tests randomise users so differences can be credited to the change. Plan the metric, guardrails, sample size and duration in advance, avoid peeking and metric fishing, and check sample ratio and novelty effects. Randomisation is the cleanest route to cause and effect; next lesson looks at causation more broadly, including what to do when you cannot randomise.
key_points: A hypothesis test asks whether an observed difference is larger than chance alone would usually produce.
The p-value is the probability of seeing a difference at least this large if there were truly no effect; it is not the probability the null hypothesis is true.
An A/B test randomly splits users between control and treatment and compares one primary metric, with guardrails.
The two-proportion z test compares conversion rates using a pooled standard error.
Plan sample size for a minimum detectable effect with about 80 percent power; small effects need very large samples.
Peeking and stopping early, or testing many metrics, inflates false positives; use fixed horizons and corrections like Bonferroni.
Check for sample ratio mismatch, novelty effects and seasonality before trusting a result.
lessons.tip: Write the experiment plan before launching: the hypothesis, the one primary metric, the guardrails, the sample size and the end date. Then do not peek at the result and stop early because it looks good.
lessons.task: Design an A/B test for a change you would like in an app you use, such as a new button text. Write the hypothesis, the unit of randomisation, the primary metric, two guardrail metrics, the minimum effect worth detecting and the planned duration. Then list two things that could make the result misleading.

quiz.q: Control converts 500 of 10,000 users (5.0 percent) and treatment 560 of 10,000 (5.6 percent). The two-sided p-value is about 0.058. At a 0.05 significance level, what do you conclude?
options: The evidence is not strong enough to rule out chance; the true effect could be zero or positive
quiz.explain: p = 0.058 is above 0.05. The 95 percent interval for the difference just includes zero, so more data may be needed.

quiz.q: What does a p-value of 0.03 mean?
options: There is a 3 percent chance the null hypothesis is true
If there were no real effect, a difference at least this large would appear about 3 percent of the time
The treatment wins 97 percent of the time
quiz.explain: The p-value assumes the null is true and asks how surprising the data would be. It is not the probability of the null.

quiz.q: You test 10 independent metrics, each at 0.05, and there is truly no effect. What is the chance at least one looks significant?
quiz.explain: 1 - 0.95 to the power 10 is about 0.40. Bonferroni would use 0.05 / 10 = 0.005 per metric.

quiz.q: A test meant to split users 50/50 ends with 10,300 in control and 9,700 in treatment out of 20,000. What should you do first?
options: Ignore it; small imbalances are normal
Investigate a sample ratio mismatch; such an imbalance is very unlikely by chance and suggests a bug
quiz.explain: A chi-square check gives a p-value around 0.00002. Something is wrong with assignment or logging, so results are untrustworthy.

quiz.q: Roughly how many users per group are needed to detect a rise from 5.0 to 5.5 percent conversion with 80 percent power at 0.05?
quiz.explain: Using the standard formula, n is about (1.96 + 0.84) squared x (0.0475 + 0.052) / 0.005 squared, about 31,200 per group.

lessons.title: Correlation, Causation and Causal Thinking
lessons.content:
Imagine a village where people notice that every year, when the mango trees flower, more children catch a cold. Some say mango flowers cause colds. A curious teacher thinks harder. Mango trees flower in late winter, when the weather swings between cold nights and warm days, and that is also cold season. The flowers and the colds move together, but both are driven by the season. Cutting down mango trees would not stop a single cold. This lesson is about the difference between things that move together and things that cause each other, the most important distinction in turning data into decisions.

Correlation and causation: Correlation means two variables tend to move together: when one is high, the other tends to be high (or low). Causation means that changing one would, by itself, change the other. Decisions are about causation: if we cut delivery fees, will orders rise? If we send reminders, will vaccination improve? Observational data, collected without intervening, mostly shows correlation. The art of causal thinking is judging when, and how far, a correlation can be trusted as a cause.

Why the difference matters: Acting on a false cause wastes money and can cause harm. A company might see that customers who use the app's wishlist feature spend more, and push everyone to use wishlists. But perhaps keen shoppers both use wishlists and spend more; forcing wishlists on casual users changes nothing. A health campaign based on a false cause can distract from the real one. Getting causation right is what separates useful analysis from decoration.

Confounding: A confounder is a third variable that affects both the supposed cause and the outcome, creating a correlation between them. Hot weather drives both ice cream sales and swimming, and swimming leads to drownings; so ice cream and drownings rise together without one causing the other. In business: customers in wealthier areas may both receive faster deliveries, because of better roads, and order more often, because of higher incomes; the delivery-speed and order-frequency correlation is partly income.

Reverse causation: Sometimes the arrow runs the other way. Areas with more police have more reported crime, but more crime leads to hiring more police. Hospitals with more doctors per bed may have higher death rates because they take the sickest patients. People who take vitamins may be less healthy if they start vitamins after feeling unwell. Time order helps: a cause must come before its effect, so look at what changed first.

Selection bias: If the data includes only a special group, correlations inside it can be misleading. Among startups featured in business magazines, those whose founders dropped out of university may look very successful, but you never see the many dropout-led startups that failed and were never featured. This is survivorship bias from lesson 05 in causal form. Comparing only customers who answered a survey, or only patients who reached a hospital, raises similar risks.

Chance and spurious correlations: With enough variables, some will correlate by pure luck. A well-known collection by Tyler Vigen shows amusing examples like the number of films an actor appeared in correlating with yearly swimming pool drownings in the United States. Two series that both trend upwards over time, like mobile phone users and average temperatures, will correlate strongly without any link. Always ask whether a mechanism makes sense and whether the pattern holds in new data.

Before-and-after traps: The simplest causal claim compares a number before and after a change: complaints were 120 last month, we retrained staff, and now they are 90. But many things change at once. The season may have shifted, a competitor may have closed, or the bad month may simply have been unusually bad. That last trap is called regression to the mean: if you act because a number was extreme, the next value tends to be closer to normal anyway, with or without your action. Branches picked for a programme because they had the worst month will usually "improve" the next month. A comparison group that did not get the change protects you from crediting luck.

Randomised experiments, the gold standard: If we randomly decide who gets a treatment, then on average the treated and untreated groups are alike in everything else, measured or not: income, motivation, health, phone type. Any difference in outcomes beyond chance can then be credited to the treatment. That is why randomised controlled trials are standard in medicine and A/B tests in tech (lesson 17). Randomisation does not need you to know what the confounders are; that is its magic.

Natural experiments: When we cannot randomise, sometimes the world does it for us. In London in 1854, John Snow studied cholera deaths among households supplied by two water companies, one drawing water from a sewage-polluted part of the Thames and one from a cleaner source upstream. Households on the same streets were served by different companies almost arbitrarily, so the groups were otherwise similar. Deaths were far higher among customers of the polluted supply, strong evidence that cholera spread through water. Modern natural experiments use lotteries, policy cut-off dates, or boundaries, like comparing households just inside and just outside a programme's eligibility line.

Difference-in-differences, worked: A common design compares changes over time between a treated group and a similar untreated group. Suppose a company introduces free delivery in Chattogram in March but not in Khulna, a similar city. Average daily orders in Chattogram rise from 1,000 in February to 1,300 in April, an increase of 300. Over the same period, Khulna rises from 900 to 1,000, an increase of 100, perhaps due to the season or general growth. The difference-in-differences estimate of the free delivery effect is 300 minus 100, that is 200 orders a day. The key assumption, called parallel trends, is that without the change Chattogram would have grown like Khulna. You check it by plotting both cities for several months before March: if their lines moved in parallel before, the assumption is more believable.

Regression with controls: Another approach is to measure likely confounders and adjust for them in a regression model. To estimate the effect of coaching on SSC marks, regress marks on a coaching indicator plus previous-year marks, family income and school. If the coaching gap shrinks from 12 marks to 4 after adding controls, part of the raw gap reflected who chose coaching. The remaining 4 is a better estimate, but only if all important confounders are measured; motivation, for example, is hard to measure and may still bias the result. Controls also must be chosen carefully: adjusting for something caused by the treatment, like hours of study that coaching itself increases, can hide part of the real effect.

Causal diagrams: A directed acyclic graph, or DAG, draws variables as nodes and causes as arrows. Hot weather points to ice cream sales and to swimming; swimming points to drowning. Drawing such a diagram makes your assumptions visible to others, and rules developed by Judea Pearl and others tell you which variables to adjust for and which not to, for example not to adjust for variables that lie on the causal path or are caused by both treatment and outcome. You do not need the full theory to benefit: simply drawing arrows before analysing often reveals a confounder you forgot.

Cut-offs as experiments: A neat natural experiment appears when a rule uses a sharp cut-off. Suppose a scholarship goes to every student scoring 80 or more on an exam. Students scoring 79 and 81 are almost identical in ability; a two-mark gap is mostly luck on the day.
