So comparing their later university results estimates the scholarship's effect for students near the line. This design is called regression discontinuity. It works only if people cannot precisely control which side of the line they land on, so always check whether suspiciously many cases sit just above the cut-off.

Judging observational evidence: When experiments are impossible, epidemiologists use questions like those listed by Austin Bradford Hill in 1965 when the link between smoking and lung cancer was debated. Is the association strong? Is it consistent across places and studies? Does the cause come before the effect? Is there a dose-response pattern, where more exposure means more effect? Is there a plausible mechanism? Does evidence from experiments, where possible, agree? No single question settles it, but together they help judge whether a correlation is likely causal.

Real-life example 1, a loyalty programme: A supermarket finds that loyalty card members spend 40 percent more than non-members and wants to credit the programme. But people who already shop a lot are the ones who bother to sign up: classic selection. A better design is to look at the same customers before and after they joined, compared with similar customers who joined later, a difference-in-differences style comparison. The estimated effect turns out to be around 8 percent: real, but far smaller than the naive 40.

Real-life example 2, a tubewell arsenic programme: Suppose a district finds that villages where wells were tested for arsenic and painted red or green show better health a few years later. Tested villages might also be closer to roads and clinics. Analysts compare villages just inside and just outside the programme's first-phase boundary, which was drawn by administrative lines rather than health, and use pre-programme health records to check that the groups were similar before. This turns a raw correlation into much stronger causal evidence for expanding testing.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include writing "causes" when data only shows association, ignoring confounders, missing reverse causation, forgetting selection effects, trusting a correlation found by searching many variables, assuming controls remove all bias, and assuming parallel trends without checking. Exams ask you to explain correlation versus causation with examples, identify confounders, reverse causation and selection bias in scenarios, explain why randomisation works, compute a difference-in-differences estimate, describe a natural experiment, and draw a simple causal diagram.

Language matters: Match your words to your evidence. From a randomised test you can say "the change caused an increase of about 0.6 points". From careful observational analysis say "is associated with" or "likely contributed to", and state the main assumptions. From a raw correlation, say only that two things move together. Precise language protects you and your audience from overconfident decisions. A good habit is to add one sentence naming the biggest assumption, for example "this assumes both cities would have grown alike without the change".

Recap: Correlation can come from causation, confounding, reverse causation, selection or chance. Randomised experiments are the clearest route to causes; natural experiments, difference-in-differences and regression with controls can help when randomisation is impossible, each with assumptions you must state. Draw causal diagrams, use Bradford Hill style questions, and choose your words to match your evidence. Next we return to the modeling side of the workflow, starting with the features that models learn from.
key_points: Correlation means two things move together; causation means changing one would change the other.
Correlations can come from confounders, reverse causation, selection bias or pure chance.
Randomised experiments break the link between treatment and confounders, so they are the gold standard for causal claims.
Natural experiments use events that assign treatment almost at random, like John Snow's water companies in 1854.
Difference-in-differences compares the change in a treated group with the change in a similar untreated group.
Regression with control variables adjusts only for measured confounders; unmeasured ones can still bias results.
Causal diagrams (DAGs) make assumptions explicit and show which variables to adjust for.
lessons.tip: For any claim that X causes Y, say three alternatives out loud: something else causes both, Y actually causes X, or the data only includes a special group. If you cannot rule them out, say "is associated with", not "causes".
lessons.task: Find a headline or social media post claiming that something causes something else, such as a food that "prevents" a disease. Draw a small causal diagram with arrows, add at least one possible confounder, and write how a randomised experiment or a natural experiment could test the claim.

quiz.q: Areas with more police officers have more reported crime. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Reverse causation: more crime leads cities to hire more police
quiz.explain: The arrow likely runs from crime to police numbers, not the other way round.

quiz.q: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise together. In a causal diagram, what is hot weather?
options: A result of ice cream sales
quiz.explain: Heat increases both ice cream sales and swimming, creating a correlation without a direct link.

quiz.q: Chattogram gets free delivery and daily orders rise from 1,000 to 1,300; similar Khulna without the change rises from 900 to 1,000. What is the difference-in-differences estimate?
quiz.explain: (1,300 - 1,000) - (1,000 - 900) = 300 - 100 = 200, assuming both cities would otherwise have followed parallel trends.

quiz.q: Why does randomly assigning a treatment support causal conclusions?
options: On average it balances all other factors, measured and unmeasured, between the groups
It removes the need for statistics
quiz.explain: Randomisation breaks the link between who gets treated and everything else that might affect the outcome.

quiz.q: Students who attend coaching score higher. An analyst adds previous-year marks as a control and the gap shrinks a lot. What is the best reading?
options: Coaching has no effect at all
The control proves coaching causes the full original gap
Previous marks are a confounder; some of the original gap reflected who chose coaching, and unmeasured factors may remain
Adding controls always removes bias completely
quiz.explain: Controls adjust for measured confounders only. The remaining gap is a better estimate but not proof.

lessons.title: Feature Engineering in Practice
lessons.content:
Think of a cricket selector choosing a batter. He does not just look at a raw list of every ball faced. He turns that list into useful summaries: average, strike rate, runs in the last five matches, record against spin, performance at home and away. Those summaries are features. A good selector with good summaries picks well; a brilliant selector staring at raw ball-by-ball data struggles. Machine learning models are the same. This lesson is about building good features from real business data, the step that often decides whether a model is useful.

What feature engineering is: A feature is an input column a model uses to make a prediction. Feature engineering is creating, transforming and choosing those columns from raw data. You met the basics in deep-cse-6-1 lesson 03: scaling, one-hot encoding and simple derived features. Here we go further with patterns data scientists use daily on tables of orders, users and events. A common saying in practice is that better data and features beat a fancier algorithm, and on tabular business data that is very often true.

Why it is needed: Raw data is shaped for storage, not learning. An orders table has one row per order with a timestamp, a customer id and an amount. A model predicting whether a customer will leave next month needs one row per customer with summaries of their behaviour. The patterns that matter, like "orders dropped after the price change" or "people order more on Friday evenings", are hidden until you compute them. Feature engineering is how your understanding of the business becomes numbers a model can use.

Date and time features: A timestamp like 2025-03-28 19:45 is almost useless to most models as raw text or a single big number. Break it into parts: hour (19), weekday (Friday), day of month (28), month (3), and whether it is a weekend. In Bangladesh the weekend is Friday and Saturday for most offices, so define the flag correctly. Add flags for special periods: the days before Eid ul-Fitr and Eid ul-Adha, Ramadan evenings when iftar orders spike, Pohela Boishakh, and national holidays. Because Eid follows the lunar calendar, its date moves about 11 days earlier each year, so build the flag from a holiday table, not a fixed month. Also compute durations: days since signup, days since last order, minutes between order and delivery.

Cyclical time: Hour 23 and hour 0 are one hour apart, but as numbers they look 23 apart. For models that read numbers directly, like linear models and neural networks, a common trick is to encode the hour as two features: the sine and cosine of 2 times pi times hour divided by 24. Then 23 and 0 land close together on a circle. Tree models can often handle raw hour fine, since they split at any point, so do not add complexity where it is not needed.

Aggregations and RFM, worked: Many problems need one row per entity summarising many events. The classic summary for customers is RFM. Recency is the number of days since the last purchase. Frequency is the number of purchases in a period. Monetary is total or average spend. Suppose a customer's last order was 10 days ago, they ordered 6 times this year, and spent 4,800 taka in total, an average of 800 per order. Their RFM is 10, 6 and 4,800. In pandas this is one groupby (lesson 09): group orders by customer, take the max date, the count and the sum. Add more: number of distinct categories bought, share of orders using cash on delivery, number of complaints, and spend in the last 30 days versus the 30 days before.

Windows and time cut-offs: Aggregations must respect time. If you predict at 1 April whether a customer will order in April, every feature must use only data up to 31 March. Build features with a cut-off date, then the label from the period after. Rolling windows such as "orders in the last 7, 30 and 90 days" capture recent change; a falling 30-day count compared with the 90-day average is often a strong sign of a customer drifting away.

Ratios and differences: Models, especially trees, find some relationships hard to build themselves. Give them directly. Cancellation rate = cancellations divided by orders: a customer with 3 cancellations out of 12 orders has 0.25. Average basket = total spend divided by orders. Price per kilogram lets you compare a 1 kg and a 5 kg bag of rice. Differences capture change: this month's orders minus last month's. Domain knowledge suggests which ratios matter; a delivery manager will tell you that orders per rider per hour drives lateness more than total orders.

Binning: Sometimes grouping a number into ranges helps. Age into bands like 18 to 24, 25 to 34 and so on; distance into under 2 km, 2 to 5 km and over 5 km. Bins make a feature robust to noisy values and easy to explain, and can capture step-like effects, like a delivery fee that jumps at 5 km. The cost is lost detail inside each bin, so do not bin by default; bin when the business itself thinks in ranges or when a linear model needs to capture a non-linear shape.

Log transforms, worked: Money, counts and durations are usually right-skewed: most orders are a few hundred taka, a few are tens of thousands. Taking the log turns multiplicative gaps into equal steps. With log base 10, 150 becomes about 2.18, 1,500 becomes 3.18, and 15,000 becomes 4.18. Now a tenfold jump is always one step, and the giant orders no longer dominate a linear model or a distance-based method like k-means. For values that can be zero, use log of 1 plus x. Trees do not need this, because splitting does not care about scale, but it rarely hurts.

Encoding categories with many values: One-hot encoding works for a handful of values, like payment method. But a column with thousands of values, like shop id or area name, would create thousands of mostly-zero columns. Frequency encoding replaces each category with how often it appears: popular shops get high values. Target encoding replaces each category with the average of the target for that category, such as the late-delivery rate of each zone. It is powerful but dangerous, as the next paragraph shows.

Target encoding safely, worked: A zone with only 4 orders, 2 of them late, has a raw late rate of 0.5, but that is mostly luck. Smoothing pulls small groups towards the overall rate. With overall rate 0.2 and a smoothing weight m = 10, the encoding is (4 times 0.5 plus 10 times 0.2) divided by (4 plus 10), that is 4 divided by 14, about 0.29. A zone with 200 orders and a 0.35 late rate gets (200 times 0.35 plus 10 times 0.2) divided by 210, about 0.34, close to its own rate because it has plenty of data. Compute these averages on training data only, and preferably out-of-fold: for each training row, use averages from the other folds so that a row's own label never feeds its feature. Otherwise the model sees a disguised copy of the answer.

Text basics: Product reviews, complaint notes and search queries hold valuable signal. Start simple: length, number of exclamation marks, whether certain words appear like "late", "broken" or "refund". The bag-of-words idea counts each word. TF-IDF, term frequency times inverse document frequency, weighs a word up when it is frequent in this text but down when it appears in almost every text, so "the" gets little weight and "refund" gets a lot. Bangla and mixed Banglish text needs care with spelling variants, such as "deri" and "dery" for late. Heavier methods like embeddings belong to NLP courses; simple counts often go surprisingly far.

Interactions: Sometimes two features matter together. Rain alone raises lateness a little, peak hour alone a little, but rain at peak hour a lot. A product feature, rain times peak flag, lets a linear model capture that. Tree models discover many interactions by themselves through successive splits, which is one reason gradient-boosted trees are so strong on tabular data. Add interactions when you have a domain reason, not every possible pair.

Feature selection: More features are not always better. Useless ones add noise, slow training, and make models harder to explain and maintain. Remove columns that are constant or almost constant, near-duplicates, and ones with mostly missing values that carry no signal. Use model-based importance or permutation importance (lesson 21) to find features that do not help, and check that removing them does not hurt validation scores. Keep a feature list with a one-line meaning for each.

Leakage through features: The most expensive feature mistake is leakage, using information that would not be available at prediction time. Predicting late delivery at order time with the rider's actual arrival time, or predicting churn with "account closed date", gives near-perfect validation scores and useless real predictions. Subtler leaks include aggregations computed over the whole dataset including future rows, target encodings computed with the test set, and IDs that happen to encode the outcome, like a refund ticket number existing only for problem orders. Always ask, for each feature, when its value becomes known.

Real-life example 1, predicting late grocery deliveries: A Dhaka grocery app builds features at order time: hour and weekday, Ramadan and pre-Eid flags, distance in km, items in the order, a rain flag from a weather feed, the store's open orders per available rider in the last 15 minutes, the smoothed late rate of the delivery zone from the previous month, and the log of order value. The riders-per-load ratio and the rain-at-peak interaction become the strongest features, and validation is done on later weeks than training.

Real-life example 2, a microfinance repayment model: A microfinance institution predicts missed instalments. Raw data is a ledger of payments. Features include days late on each of the last six instalments, the share of instalments paid on time, the trend in days late, loan size as a ratio of the borrower's reported monthly income, and a flag for flood-affected areas during the monsoon. Personal attributes that could be unfair, like religion, are excluded, a theme lesson 24 develops.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include leakage from future information, computing aggregations or encodings on the full dataset, ignoring holidays and local weekends, feeding raw timestamps or IDs to models, one-hot encoding thousands of categories, forgetting smoothing for small groups, and adding many unexplained features. Exams ask you to build date features, compute RFM, apply a log transform, explain frequency and target encoding with smoothing, describe TF-IDF in words, and spot leakage in a list of proposed features.

Recap: Feature engineering turns raw tables into columns that show a model the patterns that matter. Split dates into parts and holiday flags, summarise history with windows and RFM, add ratios, bins and logs where they help, encode many-valued categories with frequency or smoothed out-of-fold target encoding, and start text with counts or TF-IDF. Above all, guard against leakage by asking when each value is known. Next we turn features into models, starting with baselines.
key_points: Features are the inputs a model learns from; good features often matter more than the choice of algorithm.
Dates become useful through parts like weekday, month, hour and flags for holidays such as Eid.
Aggregations summarise history per entity, such as RFM: recency, frequency and monetary value.
Ratios, differences, bins and log transforms make patterns easier for models to learn.
High-cardinality categories can use frequency or smoothed target encoding, computed on training data only.
Text can start as simple counts or TF-IDF weights before using heavier methods.
Leakage through features, using information unavailable at prediction time, gives fake accuracy that collapses in production.
lessons.tip: For every feature, ask one question: "Would I know this value at the exact moment the model has to make its prediction?" If the answer is no, the feature is leakage, however good it looks.
lessons.task: Take a table of your own expenses for one month, or invent 20 rows with date, item, category and amount. Create five features: weekday, a weekend flag, days since the previous purchase, the share of spending per category, and the log of the amount. Write one sentence for each saying what pattern it might help a model find.

quiz.q: A customer's last order was 10 days ago; they ordered 6 times this year for a total of 4,800 taka. What are their recency, frequency and monetary values?
quiz.explain: Recency is days since the last order (10), frequency is the number of orders (6), and monetary is the total spend (4,800 taka).

quiz.q: Why apply a log transform to order values like 150, 1,500 and 15,000 taka?
options: To make multiplicative gaps into equal steps and tame a long right tail
quiz.explain: Log base 10 turns them into about 2.18, 3.18 and 4.18, equal steps, so a few huge orders do not dominate.

quiz.q: A zone has only 4 orders, 2 of them late (rate 0.5); the overall late rate is 0.2. With smoothing weight m = 10, what is the smoothed target encoding?
quiz.explain: (4 x 0.5 + 10 x 0.2) / (4 + 10) = 4 / 14, about 0.29. Small groups are pulled towards the overall rate.

quiz.q: To predict at order time whether a delivery will be late, which feature is leakage?
options: Number of items in the order
quiz.explain: Actual arrival is only known after delivery, so using it would fake accuracy.

quiz.q: Where should target encoding statistics be computed?
options: On the whole dataset including the test set
On the training data only, ideally out-of-fold
quiz.explain: Computing them with test rows, or with each row's own label, leaks the answer into the feature.

lessons.title: Modeling in Practice I: Framing, Baselines and the Loop
lessons.content:
Imagine a new cook in a busy hotel kitchen. Before inventing fancy dishes, the head chef asks one thing: can you make plain rice and dal that customers are happy with? Only once the basics are right does experimenting with biryani make sense, and every new dish is judged against what the kitchen already serves well. Building models at work is similar. Frame the problem clearly, know what a simple approach achieves, then improve step by step, always checking that each change really helps. This lesson is about that practical loop.

What modeling in practice means: Deep-cse-6-1 taught how algorithms work: linear and logistic regression, trees, ensembles, neural networks, and how to evaluate them. In data science work, the harder part is around the algorithm: deciding what exactly to predict, when, with what data, how to measure success, and how to know the model actually beats simpler options. Good practice here prevents the common failure of a clever model that solves the wrong problem.

Framing the problem: First decide the type. Regression predicts a number, like delivery minutes or next month's sales. Classification predicts a category, like late or on time, fraud or not. Forecasting predicts future values of a time series, like daily orders for the next 14 days. Clustering groups similar items without labels, like customer segments (lesson 22). Ranking orders items, like which products to show first. The same business question can be framed in different ways: "reduce late deliveries" could be classification at order time, or regression of delivery minutes with a threshold.

Target, moment and unit: Define the target precisely: "late" means delivered more than 10 minutes after the promised time. Define the prediction moment: when the order is placed, before a rider is assigned. Define the unit: one row per order. These three choices decide which features are allowed (lesson 19) and which data you can use. Writing them down in one sentence, "At order placement, predict whether this order will arrive more than 10 minutes late", prevents months of confusion.

Choosing the metric: Pick metrics that match the decision. For regression, MAE, mean absolute error, is easy to explain: "on average we are off by 4 minutes". RMSE punishes big errors more. For classification with rare positives, accuracy misleads; use precision, recall, F1 or the area under the precision-recall curve (deep-cse-6-1 lesson 13). Write the business version too: "we want to catch at least 70 percent of late orders while flagging no more than 15 percent of all orders."

Baselines, worked: A baseline is the simplest sensible prediction, and every model must beat it. For regression, predict the training mean for everyone. If test delivery times are 30, 35, 40, 25 and 50 minutes and the training mean is 36, the absolute errors are 6, 1, 4, 11 and 14, so the baseline MAE is 36 divided by 5, which is 7.2 minutes. If your model predicts 32, 33, 41, 28 and 44, its errors are 2, 2, 1, 3 and 6, an MAE of 2.8 minutes, clearly better. For classification, the majority baseline predicts the most common class: if 92 percent of deliveries are on time, "always on time" scores 92 percent accuracy while catching zero late orders. For forecasting, use yesterday's value or the same day last week.

Rule-based baselines: Often the team already uses a rule: "flag orders over 8 km as likely late" or "call customers who have not ordered in 30 days". That rule is an important baseline too, because it is what the model must replace. If a complex model only beats the rule by a hair, the rule may be the better choice: it is free, explainable and easy to change.

Simple models first: After baselines, try a simple, explainable model like linear or logistic regression or a small decision tree. They train fast, show which features matter, and often get most of the possible gain. Then try a stronger model such as gradient-boosted trees, which are usually the best performers on tabular business data. Neural networks rarely beat boosted trees on ordinary tables, though they shine on images, audio and text. Prefer the simplest model whose performance is good enough, because every bit of complexity must be maintained.

Pipelines and honest preprocessing: Preprocessing steps such as filling missing values, scaling and encoding learn something from data: a mean, a standard deviation, a category list. If you fit them on the whole dataset before splitting, information from validation rows leaks into training and scores look better than reality. The fix is a pipeline: in scikit-learn, a Pipeline chains the imputer, scaler, encoder and model, so that fitting the pipeline on training data fits every step on training data only, and applying it to new data reuses those learned values unchanged. Pipelines also make deployment easier, since the exact same steps run in production.

Validation done right: Use a held-out test set that you touch only at the very end. For model choices, use k-fold cross-validation on the training data (deep-cse-6-1 lesson 12). For data over time, never shuffle randomly: train on earlier periods and validate on later ones, for example train on January to June and validate on July, then roll forward. If the same customer appears many times, keep all their rows in the same fold, called group k-fold, or the model can memorise customers instead of learning patterns.

The cost matrix, worked: Different mistakes cost different amounts. In fraud detection, suppose a missed fraud costs 5,000 taka on average and a false alarm, a blocked genuine payment that needs a call, costs 100 taka. Out of 100 frauds, model A misses 20 and raises 500 false alarms: cost is 20 times 5,000 plus 500 times 100, which is 100,000 plus 50,000, that is 150,000 taka. Model B misses 40 and raises 100 false alarms: 200,000 plus 10,000, that is 210,000 taka. Having no model costs 100 times 5,000, which is 500,000 taka. Model A is best even though it raises more false alarms. The same reasoning picks the decision threshold: move it and recompute cost to find the cheapest point. Ask the finance or operations team for the cost figures rather than guessing; even rough numbers agreed with them beat a metric nobody connects to money, and they make your recommendation far easier to accept.

Handling rare classes: When positives are rare, like 8 percent late orders or 1 percent fraud, a model can score well by ignoring them. Three practical tools help. First, class weights tell the model that a mistake on the rare class costs more, most libraries accept a setting for this. Second, resampling, either repeating rare examples or dropping some common ones, but only inside the training folds, never before splitting. Third, and often simplest, keep the model as it is and move the decision threshold, using the cost matrix above to find the best point. Whatever you choose, judge it with precision and recall on untouched validation data, which keeps its real class balance.

Is it good enough to ship?: A model is ready when it beats the baseline by a margin that matters in money or time, when its errors are acceptable in every important segment, not just on average, when the team can run and monitor it, and when the people using its output understand what it does. A model that is 2 percent better than a rule but needs a new server, a new team and nobody can explain, is often not worth shipping. Write this decision down with the numbers, so that next year's team knows why.

Iterate on data, not just models: When results disappoint, the best fix is usually not a new algorithm. Look at the errors (lesson 21): are labels wrong, such as deliveries marked late because riders forgot to tap "delivered"? Are important signals missing, such as rain or rider load? Is one segment, like a new city, behaving differently? Cleaning labels, adding a good feature, or collecting more examples of a rare case usually beats hours of hyperparameter tuning. Track each experiment: data version, features, model, settings and score, so you know what actually helped. A simple spreadsheet works fine at first.

Hyperparameter tuning, in proportion: Tuning settings like tree depth or learning rate does help, typically by a modest amount once the setup is sensible. Use cross-validation with random search or a library that searches efficiently, set a time budget, and remember that tuning many settings on a small validation set can overfit the validation set itself. The final, untouched test set protects you from fooling yourself.

Real-life example 1, predicting delivery time: A food delivery company frames "show customers a realistic arrival time" as regression of minutes from order to doorstep, predicted at order placement. The baseline, the average for that restaurant in the last month, has an MAE of 9 minutes. A linear model with distance, hour, rain and restaurant preparation time reaches 6.5. Gradient-boosted trees with rider load features reach 5. A time-based split on later weeks confirms the gain, and the team ships boosted trees with the linear model kept as a fallback.

Real-life example 2, an NGO dropout warning: An education NGO wants to flag students at risk of dropping out so that teachers can visit families. Framed as classification at the start of each term: will this student miss more than 30 days this term? Dropouts are about 8 percent. The baseline rule, flag students who missed more than 10 days last term, catches 45 percent of dropouts. A logistic regression with attendance trend, distance to school, sibling dropout and exam results catches 68 percent at the same number of flags. Because teachers can visit only 15 percent of students, the threshold is set to flag exactly that many, and the simple model is chosen because teachers can see why a student was flagged.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include skipping baselines, reporting accuracy on imbalanced data, fitting preprocessing on all data, random splits for time data, ignoring repeated customers across folds, choosing a model by a metric that does not match business cost, tuning endlessly instead of fixing data, and touching the test set repeatedly. Exams ask you to frame a scenario as regression, classification or forecasting, propose baselines, compute a baseline MAE, explain pipelines and data leakage in preprocessing, choose a validation scheme for time data, and compare models with a cost matrix.

Recap: Frame the problem with a clear type, target, prediction moment and metric. Build baselines and beat them honestly. Start simple, add complexity only when it clearly helps, and keep preprocessing inside pipelines fitted on training data. Validate with the right split, judge models by real costs, and spend most effort on data and features. Next lesson looks inside trained models: interpreting them, forecasting with them, and checking them after launch.
key_points: Framing decides the problem type, the target, the prediction moment and the metric before any model is chosen.
Baselines such as the mean, the majority class or yesterday's value set the bar every model must beat.
Start with a simple, explainable model; move to complex ones only if they clearly help.
Put preprocessing in a pipeline fitted on training data only, so validation stays honest.
Cross-validation, or time-based splits for time data, estimates performance on new data.
A cost matrix turns errors into money so the best model and threshold match business goals.
Most gains come from iterating on data, labels and features, not from swapping algorithms.
lessons.tip: Before training any model, write down the score of the dumbest sensible baseline. If your model cannot clearly beat it on validation data, you do not have a model yet, whatever the accuracy number says.
lessons.task: Pick a prediction problem from daily life, such as how long your commute will take. Frame it: is it regression, classification or forecasting? Define the target, the moment of prediction and the features available then. Propose two baselines and the metric you would use, and explain which mistake would cost more.

quiz.q: 92 percent of deliveries are on time. A model predicting late deliveries reports 92 percent accuracy. What is the most likely truth?
options: It may just predict "on time" for everything, matching the majority baseline
The data has no late deliveries
quiz.explain: Always compare with the majority-class baseline; recall and precision for the late class tell the real story.

quiz.q: Test delivery times are 30, 35, 40, 25 and 50 minutes. Predicting the training mean of 36 every time gives what MAE?
quiz.explain: Absolute errors 6, 1, 4, 11 and 14 sum to 36; 36 / 5 = 7.2 minutes.

quiz.q: Why must a scaler or imputer be fitted on training data only?
options: Fitting on all data lets information from validation rows leak into training and inflates scores
Scalers do not work on test data
quiz.explain: Means, standard deviations and fill values must come from training data, then be applied unchanged to new data.

quiz.q: A missed fraud costs 5,000 taka and a false alarm 100. Model A misses 20 of 100 frauds with 500 false alarms; model B misses 40 with 100 false alarms. Which is cheaper?
options: B, because it has fewer false alarms

quiz.q: Which split is right for forecasting next month's daily orders?
options: Train on earlier dates, validate on later dates
quiz.explain: Time-based splits mimic real use: you always predict the future from the past.

lessons.title: Modeling in Practice II: Interpreting, Forecasting and Checking
lessons.content:
Think about a weather forecaster on television. People do not only want to hear "70 percent chance of rain". They want to know why: a low-pressure system in the Bay of Bengal. They want the 70 percent to mean something: on days given 70 percent, it should rain about 7 times out of 10. And they want the forecaster to notice when the forecasts start going wrong, for example when monsoon patterns shift. A useful model at work needs the same three things: explanations people trust, numbers that mean what they say, and checking that never stops. This lesson covers interpreting models, forecasting over time, and checking models before and after launch.

Why interpretation matters: A model that predicts well but cannot be explained is hard to trust, hard to debug and sometimes illegal to use, for example in lending decisions in many countries. Interpretation helps you catch leakage (a suspiciously powerful feature), find bugs, convince managers, and give useful reasons to the people affected, like telling a customer why their delivery is estimated at 45 minutes.

Reading linear coefficients, worked: In a linear model each coefficient says how much the prediction changes when that feature rises by one unit, holding the others fixed. Suppose a delivery model is: minutes = 12 + 3.5 times distance in km + 6 times rain, where rain is 1 if raining and 0 otherwise. Each extra km adds 3.5 minutes, and rain adds 6 minutes. A 4 km order in rain gets 12 + 14 + 6 = 32 minutes. Two cautions: coefficients depend on units, so compare features only after scaling, and if two features are strongly correlated, like distance and number of roads crossed, their coefficients can become unstable and misleading. For logistic regression, a coefficient changes the log-odds; exponentiating it gives an odds ratio.

Feature importance from trees: Tree-based models report built-in importance, usually based on how much each feature reduced impurity across all splits. It is quick but biased: it favours features with many distinct values, like IDs or exact timestamps, and it is computed on training data. Use it as a rough first look, not a final answer.

Permutation importance, worked: A more honest method works on validation data. Measure the model's score, then randomly shuffle one feature's column, breaking its link to the target, and measure again. The worse the score gets, the more the model relied on that feature. Suppose validation MAE is 5.0 minutes. Shuffling distance raises it to 8.2, so distance's importance is 3.2. Shuffling rain raises it to 5.9, importance 0.9. Shuffling a feature for the length of the customer's name leaves MAE at 5.0, importance 0, so it can be removed. One caution: when two features carry the same information, shuffling one may barely hurt because the model leans on the other, so both can look unimportant.

Partial dependence and SHAP: Importance says how much a feature matters, not how. A partial dependence plot shows the average prediction as one feature varies while others keep their real values: for example, predicted delivery time rising slowly up to 5 km, then sharply beyond, where riders leave main roads. SHAP values, based on Shapley values from game theory, split each single prediction into contributions from each feature: this order's predicted 45 minutes is the average 30, plus 8 for distance, plus 5 for rain, plus 2 for peak hour. SHAP is widely used for explaining individual decisions, though it explains the model, not the real world, so a feature's large SHAP value does not prove it causes the outcome (lesson 18).

Error analysis by segment: An average score hides a lot. Break errors down by meaningful groups: city, zone, customer type, phone type, hour, order size. Suppose overall MAE is 5 minutes, but in a newly launched city it is 11 and for orders over 20 items it is 9. Those segments tell you where to dig: perhaps the new city lacks history for zone features, and big orders need packing time the model does not know. Also read the worst individual errors one by one; they often reveal label bugs, like a delivery marked complete two days late because a rider's phone was off.

Calibration, worked: When a classifier outputs probabilities, we want them to mean what they say. Group predictions into bins and compare. If 200 orders were each given about a 30 percent chance of being late and 90 actually were, the real rate is 90 divided by 200, which is 45 percent; the model underestimates risk in that range. A reliability diagram plots predicted against actual rates; a well-calibrated model lies near the diagonal. Calibration matters whenever probabilities feed decisions, such as expected cost, staffing or prices. Methods like Platt scaling and isotonic regression, fitted on validation data, can fix a poorly calibrated model without changing its ranking.

Forecasting basics: Forecasting predicts future values of a time series, like daily orders, electricity demand or rice prices. Time series have trend, a long-run rise or fall; seasonality, repeating patterns like weekly cycles or Eid peaks; and noise. You met moving averages in lesson 13. Always start with simple baselines, because they are surprisingly hard to beat.

Forecasting baselines: The naive forecast predicts tomorrow equals today. The seasonal naive forecast predicts each day equals the same day last week, which captures weekly patterns such as busy Fridays. The moving-average forecast predicts the average of the last k days. If the last 7 days' orders were 400, 420, 390, 410, 500, 620 and 560, the 7-day moving average forecast is 3,300 divided by 7, about 471. More advanced methods, such as exponential smoothing, ARIMA, or gradient-boosted trees with lag and calendar features, must beat these baselines on honest validation to earn their place.

Validating forecasts: Never shuffle time. Use a rolling origin: train on data up to a date, forecast the next week, record the error, move the cut-off forward a week, and repeat. This simulates real use. Make sure features only use information available at the forecast time; using "same day's weather" is fine only if you will have a weather forecast then, and real forecasts are less accurate than recorded weather.

MAE and MAPE, worked: Suppose actual orders on three days are 100, 120 and 80, and the forecasts were 110, 110 and 100. Absolute errors are 10, 10 and 20, so MAE is 40 divided by 3, about 13.3 orders. Percentage errors are 10 divided by 100, which is 10 percent, 10 divided by 120, about 8.3 percent, and 20 divided by 80, which is 25 percent; MAPE, their average, is about 14.4 percent. MAPE is easy to explain but breaks when actual values are near zero, since dividing by a tiny number explodes, and it punishes over-forecasts and under-forecasts differently. For products with many zero-sale days, use MAE or a scaled error instead.

Forecast ranges: A single number hides uncertainty, just like a single estimate in lesson 16. Planners need ranges: "between 430 and 530 orders tomorrow, most likely about 480". A simple way is to collect the errors your method made during rolling validation and take, say, their 10th and 90th percentiles; adding those to the forecast gives an 80 percent range built from real past performance. Ranges should widen the further ahead you forecast, since next month is harder to know than tomorrow. Staffing and stock decisions then use the upper or lower end depending on which mistake is costlier: running out of rice before Eid is usually worse than holding a few extra bags.

Forecasting in Bangladesh: Calendar effects are huge. Eid moves about 11 days earlier each year, so a model using "same week last year" will be misaligned; build holiday features from a calendar. Ramadan shifts meal times and shopping peaks. Hartals, floods and cyclone warnings cause sudden drops. Good forecasters keep an events table and treat such days specially, rather than letting them distort the regular pattern.

Model cards: A model card is a short document describing a model: its purpose and intended use, the training data and time period, the features, evaluation results overall and by important segments, known limitations, fairness checks, and who owns it. The idea was proposed by Margaret Mitchell and colleagues in 2019. Writing one forces clarity and helps future teams avoid misusing the model, for example applying a Dhaka-trained model to Sylhet without checking.

Monitoring and drift: The world changes after launch. Data drift means the inputs change: new zones, a new app version that logs differently, more orders from a new customer group. Concept drift means the relationship changes: after a new bridge opens, distance no longer predicts time the same way. Monitor input distributions, prediction distributions and, when labels arrive, real performance, with alerts when they move beyond set limits. Plan regular retraining, and keep the previous model ready so you can roll back. The engineering of this is often called MLOps; the data pipelines that feed it are covered in Data Engineering (deep-cse-7-11).

Real-life example 1, explaining a credit score: A digital lender in Bangladesh uses a gradient-boosted model to approve small loans based on mobile wallet history. For each rejection, SHAP values provide the top reasons, such as "irregular monthly inflows" or "short account history", which are turned into plain messages. Permutation importance on validation data shows a feature for phone brand ranks high; the team removes it after deciding it acts as a proxy for income in an unfair way, and accuracy drops only slightly.

Real-life example 2, forecasting Eid demand: A clothing retailer forecasts daily sales for the four weeks before Eid. Seasonal naive based on last year fails because Eid fell 11 days later then. The team builds features for "days until Eid" and "salary week", and validates with rolling origins over the last three Eids. The model beats the baselines by 25 percent in MAE. After launch, a monitor flags that online sales are growing faster than forecast, prompting a retrain mid-season.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include comparing raw coefficients across features with different units, trusting built-in tree importance alone, reading SHAP as causation, reporting only an average score, ignoring calibration when probabilities drive decisions, shuffling time series, skipping naive baselines, using MAPE with near-zero values, and launching without monitoring. Exams ask you to interpret a linear model, compute a prediction from coefficients, explain permutation importance and calibration, compute MAE and MAPE, describe naive, seasonal naive and moving-average forecasts, explain data and concept drift, and list the contents of a model card.

Recap: Interpret models with coefficients, permutation importance, partial dependence and SHAP, remembering they explain the model and not the world. Break errors down by segment and check that probabilities are calibrated. Forecast with seasonal and calendar awareness, starting from naive baselines and validating with rolling time splits and suitable metrics. Document with model cards and monitor for drift after launch. Next, we look at unsupervised tools analysts use every day.
key_points: Linear model coefficients show how much the prediction changes per unit of a feature, holding others fixed.
Permutation importance measures how much the validation score worsens when a feature's values are shuffled.
Partial dependence plots and SHAP values explain how features push individual and average predictions.
Error analysis by segment finds where a model fails even when the average looks good.
A calibrated model's probabilities match reality: of orders given 30 percent, about 30 percent are late.
Forecasting starts with naive, seasonal naive and moving-average baselines and uses time-based validation with MAE or MAPE.
After launch, model cards document the model and monitoring catches data drift and falling performance.
lessons.tip: After every model, slice its errors by at least three segments, such as city, customer type and time of day. An average score hides the group where the model fails, and that group is usually the one someone will complain about.
lessons.task: Write down the number of hours you slept each night for the last two weeks, or invent 14 values. Forecast the next 3 nights with three methods: last value, the same day last week, and the 7-day moving average. When the real values arrive, compute the MAE of each method and say which won.

quiz.q: A delivery-time model is: minutes = 12 + 3.5 x km + 6 x rain (rain is 1 or 0). What does it predict for a 4 km order in rain?
Validation MAE is 5.0. Shuffling distance raises it to 8.2; shuffling rain raises it to 5.9; shuffling a customer-name-length feature leaves it at 5.0. What do you conclude?
options: Name length is the most important feature
Distance matters most, rain somewhat, and name length adds nothing
All three features are equally important
quiz.explain: Permutation importance is the increase in error: 3.2 for distance, 0.9 for rain and 0 for name length.

quiz.q: Of 200 orders the model gave a 30 percent chance of being late, 90 were actually late. What does this show?
options: The sample is too small to say anything
The model underestimates risk for this group; the real rate is 45 percent
quiz.explain: 90 / 200 = 0.45, well above the predicted 0.30, so the probabilities are too low here.

quiz.q: Actual daily orders are 100, 120 and 80; the forecasts were 110, 110 and 100. What are MAE and MAPE?
options: MAE about 13.3 orders, MAPE about 14.4 percent
quiz.explain: Errors 10, 10, 20 give MAE 40 / 3, about 13.3. Percentage errors 10, 8.3 and 25 average about 14.4 percent.

quiz.q: A model's average error is fine, but its error in a newly launched city is twice as high. What is the best next step?
options: Ignore it, the average is fine
Investigate the city's data and features, and consider separate handling or more data
quiz.explain: Segment error analysis reveals where the model does not fit, often due to missing features or too little data.

lessons.title: Unsupervised Tools for Analysts: Segments, Anomalies and Baskets
lessons.content:
Imagine you work at a big library and someone dumps thousands of new books on the floor with no labels, no sections, no catalogue. Nobody tells you the right answer. You start anyway: you notice some books are thick and full of formulas, some are thin with pictures, some are in Bangla poetry style. You form piles of similar books, notice a few strange ones that fit nowhere, and see that people who borrow cookbooks often borrow gardening books too. That is unsupervised learning in daily analyst work: finding groups, oddities and patterns of things that go together, without a label telling you what is right.

What unsupervised learning is: In supervised learning (lessons 20 and 21) each row has a known answer to learn from. Unsupervised methods have no such answer; they find structure in the features alone. Deep-cse-6-1 covered the algorithms, k-means, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN and PCA. Here we focus on three jobs analysts do constantly: customer segmentation, anomaly detection and market basket analysis, plus how to check results when there is no label.

Why analysts need it: Businesses want to treat different customers differently, catch fraud or broken systems early, and know which products to place or promote together. These are rarely labelled problems: nobody hands you a list saying "this customer is a bargain hunter" or "this transaction is fraud". Unsupervised tools give a first map, which people then name, check and act on.

Segmentation with RFM, worked: Start from the RFM features of lesson 19: recency, frequency and monetary value per customer. A simple, robust method is scoring: split each feature into five equal-sized groups, quintiles, and give scores 1 to 5, where 5 is best (most recent, most frequent, highest spend). A customer who ordered 3 days ago, 20 times this year, spending 30,000 taka might score 5-5-5; one who last ordered 200 days ago, twice, spending 900 taka might score 1-1-1. Rules then form segments: 5-5-5 "champions", high frequency but low recency "slipping loyal", low on everything "lost". This needs no algorithm and is easy to explain.

k-means on RFM: For a data-driven version, run k-means on the RFM features. Prepare them first: take logs of frequency and monetary, which are right-skewed (lesson 19), then scale all three so each has mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Without scaling, spend in thousands of taka would dominate distances and recency in days would barely count. Then run k-means for several values of k, each with several random starts, since k-means can land in different solutions depending on where it begins.

Choosing k: The elbow method plots total within-cluster distance against k and looks for the point where adding clusters stops helping much. The silhouette score, from minus 1 to 1, measures how much closer each point is to its own cluster than to the next one; higher is better. But the deciding question is practical: can the business act on these segments? Four clearly different, stable segments that marketing can target beat nine that blur together. Check stability by re-running on a different month's data or a random half: if segments change a lot, they are not real structure.

Naming and profiling segments: Clusters come out as numbers 0, 1, 2, 3. Make them useful by profiling: for each cluster, compute the average and median recency, frequency and spend, plus other columns not used in clustering, like favourite category, city, payment method and app usage. Then name them in plain words: "weekly family shoppers", "Eid-only big spenders", "new and curious", "drifting away". Names make segments memorable, but check they match the numbers, not wishful thinking.

Other clustering choices: k-means assumes round, similar-sized clusters and forces every point into some cluster. When that does not fit, hierarchical clustering builds a tree of merges that you can cut at any level, handy for showing managers how small groups combine into big ones. DBSCAN finds clusters of any shape and labels sparse points as noise, which suits location data like delivery addresses. For a few thousand customers any of these runs in seconds, so try two and see whether they tell the same story.

Segments over time: Segments are not fixed. Re-score customers every month and track movement: how many champions slipped to "drifting away", how many new customers became regular. A simple table of last month's segment against this month's, a transition table, shows the flows. A rising flow from loyal to drifting is an early warning that something, perhaps prices or delivery quality, is going wrong, often weeks before total sales drop.

PCA for plotting: When you cluster on many features, you cannot draw ten dimensions. Principal component analysis finds new axes, combinations of the original features, ordered by how much variation they capture. Plotting customers on the first two components, coloured by cluster, shows whether clusters are well separated or overlap. Report how much variance the first two components explain; if it is only 30 percent, the plot is a rough sketch. PCA axes are mixtures, so read their loadings, the weights of the original features, to interpret them, for example "component 1 is mostly overall activity".

Anomaly detection, why: Anomalies are points very unlike the rest: a sudden spike in refunds, a card used in two cities ten minutes apart, a sensor reading of minus 40 degrees in Dhaka. Some are errors to clean (lesson 11), some are fraud, and some are important real events. Catching them early saves money and reputation.

Z-scores, worked: The simplest detector measures how many standard deviations a value is from the mean. If daily refunds average 50 with standard deviation 8, and today has 82, the z-score is (82 minus 50) divided by 8, which is 4. Under a normal shape, values beyond 3 are rare, so today deserves a look. Z-scores assume a roughly symmetric distribution and are themselves pulled by extreme values, which can mask outliers, as lesson 11 showed.

IQR fences and seasonal baselines: The IQR rule flags values below Q1 minus 1.5 times IQR or above Q3 plus 1.5 times IQR, and is robust to extremes. For time series, compare to the same weekday and season, not the overall average: 620 orders on a Friday before Eid is normal, while 620 on a quiet Tuesday might signal a bot or a pricing bug. A practical method is to compute each day's expected value with a seasonal baseline from lesson 21 and flag days whose error is unusually large.

Isolation forest and multi-feature anomalies: Some anomalies only show when several features are combined: an order amount that is normal, at an hour that is normal, but from a brand-new account, to a new address, using a new card, is suspicious together. Isolation forest, proposed in 2008, builds many random trees that split data at random points; unusual points get isolated in fewer splits, so a short average path length means a likely anomaly. It handles many features and large data well. Its output is a score, so set a threshold based on how many cases the review team can actually check each day.

Market basket analysis, worked: Market basket analysis finds items bought together. Three measures matter. Suppose there are 1,000 baskets; 200 contain bread, 150 contain eggs and 80 contain both. Support of bread and eggs together is 80 divided by 1,000, which is 0.08: 8 percent of baskets have both. Confidence of the rule bread to eggs is 80 divided by 200, which is 0.40: 40 percent of bread buyers also buy eggs. Lift is confidence divided by eggs' overall support, 0.40 divided by 0.15, about 2.67: bread buyers are about 2.7 times as likely as an average shopper to buy eggs. Lift above 1 means items appear together more than chance; below 1, less. Algorithms like Apriori and FP-Growth find frequent itemsets efficiently in huge data; deep-cse-7-6 covers them.

Using basket rules wisely: High confidence alone can mislead: "anything to rice" has high confidence simply because almost everyone buys rice, so its lift is near 1. Filter rules by minimum support, so they apply to enough customers, and by lift. Remember that co-purchase is not causation: placing eggs near bread may not raise sales if people already buy both. Test placements and bundle offers with an A/B test (lesson 17) before rolling them out.

Validating unsupervised work: Without labels, checking is harder but still possible. Show segments to people who know the customers and ask whether they ring true. Check stability over time and samples. Test usefulness: do targeted campaigns per segment beat a single campaign in an experiment? For anomalies, have reviewers label a sample of flagged and unflagged cases to estimate precision and how many real problems were missed. Over time, these labels let you move to a supervised model, which can then be measured with the precision and recall of lesson 20.

Real-life example 1, segmenting mobile wallet users: A mobile financial service segments users by monthly transaction count, average amount, share of cash-out versus merchant payments, and days active. k-means with k = 5 gives groups the team names "salary receivers", "village remittance families", "shop payers", "occasional users" and "power merchants". Profiles reveal the remittance families mostly cash out within a day of receiving money, so the company tests lower cash-out fees with merchant partners near rural agents to encourage digital spending.

Real-life example 2, catching fraud spikes in an e-commerce sale: During a flash sale, the anomaly monitor uses z-scores on hourly orders per product and an isolation forest on order features. At 2 am, it flags a burst of orders for one phone model from new accounts sharing a few delivery addresses. Reviewers confirm resellers abusing a one-per-customer limit, cancel the orders and add an address check. The same monitor also flags a payment gateway outage when successful payments drop to near zero, catching it within minutes instead of hours.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include clustering unscaled features, trusting one k-means run, choosing k only by a score, naming segments without checking profiles, reading a PCA plot without its explained variance, using z-scores on skewed data, ignoring seasonality in anomaly detection, trusting confidence without lift, and assuming co-purchase means causation. Exams ask you to compute RFM scores, explain k-means preparation and choosing k, describe PCA's purpose, compute z-scores and IQR fences, compute support, confidence and lift, and explain how to validate unsupervised results.

Recap: Unsupervised tools find structure without labels. Segment customers with RFM scores or scaled k-means, choose k by both numbers and usefulness, then profile, name and check segments. Use PCA to visualise many features. Detect anomalies with z-scores, IQR, seasonal baselines and isolation forests. Find items that go together with support, confidence and lift, and test actions before scaling them. Next, we turn all these findings into stories that people understand and act on.
key_points: Unsupervised methods find structure without labels: segments, unusual points and items that go together.
RFM scores plus k-means turn customer history into segments that need names, profiles and checks.
Choose k with the elbow plot, silhouette score and, above all, whether the segments are actionable and stable.
PCA squeezes many features into two or three for plotting, keeping as much variation as possible.
Anomaly detection uses z-scores, IQR fences or isolation forests to flag points unlike the rest.
Market basket analysis uses support, confidence and lift; lift above 1 means items appear together more than chance.
Unsupervised results must be validated with domain experts and follow-up data, since there is no label to check against.
lessons.tip: A segment is only useful if someone will treat it differently. Before clustering, ask the marketing or operations team what different actions they could take; then name and check segments with those actions in mind.
lessons.task: Ask 10 friends or family members three questions: how many times they ordered food online last month, how much they spent, and how many days since their last order. Score each person 1 to 3 on each RFM part, group them into three or four segments by hand, give each a name, and suggest one action per segment.

quiz.q: Out of 1,000 baskets, 200 contain bread, 150 contain eggs and 80 contain both. What is the confidence of the rule bread to eggs?
quiz.explain: Confidence = baskets with both / baskets with bread = 80 / 200 = 0.40.

quiz.q: In the same data, what is the lift of bread to eggs?
quiz.explain: Lift = confidence / support of eggs = 0.40 / 0.15, about 2.67, so they appear together far more than chance.

quiz.q: Daily refunds average 50 with standard deviation 8. Today has 82. What is the z-score?
quiz.explain: z = (82 - 50) / 8 = 4, a very unusual day worth investigating.

quiz.q: Why scale features before running k-means on RFM data?
options: Otherwise the feature with the largest numbers, like spend in taka, dominates the distances
quiz.explain: k-means uses distances, so a feature measured in thousands swamps one measured in single digits.

quiz.q: What does PCA mainly help an analyst do?
options: Plot many-feature data in two dimensions while keeping most variation
quiz.explain: PCA finds new axes along which data varies most, so the first two can be plotted to see structure.

lessons.title: Communicating Results and Data Storytelling
lessons.content:
Imagine a doctor who runs every test perfectly, finds that a patient has a vitamin deficiency, and then hands over a 40-page lab printout with no explanation. The patient goes home confused and changes nothing. All that careful work produced no benefit. Now imagine a doctor who says: "Your tiredness is from low vitamin D. Take this tablet daily and spend 20 minutes in the sun. We will check again in three months." Same science, completely different result. Data science is the same. Analysis creates value only when the right person understands it and acts. This lesson is about that last, often neglected step.

What communication in data science is: It is turning analysis into understanding and decisions. That includes written summaries, charts, slides, dashboards, conversations and documentation. It also includes listening: understanding what the audience needs before you start, and handling their questions afterwards. Lesson 03 began with a clear question; this lesson ends the loop by delivering a clear answer.

Why it matters so much: Decision makers are busy, have many other inputs, and often lack statistical training. A brilliant finding buried on slide 23 or written in jargon will be ignored. Surveys of data teams repeatedly report that a large share of analytics work never influences any decision. Clear communication is often the difference between analysis that changes a business and analysis that sits in a folder.

Know your audience: Different people want different things. Senior executives want the decision and its impact, in one or two minutes. Managers want to know what to do, who does it, by when and with what resources. Fellow analysts want methods, assumptions and code so they can check and build on your work. Frontline staff, like riders or shop managers, want practical guidance in their own words. Before preparing anything, ask: who will read this, what do they already know, and what decision will they make?

Answer first, the pyramid principle: Barbara Minto's pyramid principle, developed at McKinsey, says to start with the main point, then group supporting arguments beneath it, then details beneath those. In practice: put the conclusion in the first sentence of an email, the first slide of a deck, the top of a report. "Late deliveries can be cut by about a third by adding evening riders in two zones" comes before any description of data. Readers who trust you stop there; those who want proof read on.

From finding to recommendation: A finding is a fact: "late deliveries are highest in Mirpur and Uttara between 6 and 9 pm". An insight explains why: "riders there handle almost twice as many orders per hour as elsewhere". A recommendation says what to do: "Operations should add 15 riders in Mirpur and Uttara from 6 to 9 pm, which we expect to cut late orders in those zones by about a third, costing about 3 lakh taka a month". Good recommendations are specific about who, what, where, when, expected impact and cost, and they suggest how to check if it worked, ideally with a test (lesson 17).

One chart, one message: Each chart should make one point, chosen before the chart is drawn. Use the principles of lesson 14: the right chart type, clear labels, honest axes, and highlight colour only on what matters. Give it an action title that states the finding, like "Mirpur and Uttara cause 60 percent of late deliveries", rather than a label like "Late deliveries by zone". A reader should get the message from the title alone, then use the chart to confirm it.

Stating uncertainty plainly: Every estimate has uncertainty (lessons 16 and 17), and hiding it is dishonest, but drowning people in statistics is unhelpful. Give the best estimate plus a plain range: "most likely around 12 percent, probably between 4 and 20 percent". Say what would change your conclusion: "if delivery volumes keep rising, we will need more riders than this". Use words consistently: decide what "likely" means and stick with it. Avoid fake precision: "Sales will rise 12.37 percent" sounds confident and is almost certainly not that exact.

Writing clearly: Use short sentences and everyday words. Replace "utilisation of rider capacity exhibited elevated levels" with "riders were too busy". Put one idea in each sentence and one topic in each paragraph. Define any technical term the first time, or leave it out. Use active voice that names who did what: "the Mirpur team cut waiting time", not "waiting time was reduced". Read your summary aloud; if you stumble, your reader will too.

Numbers people can feel: Round numbers to what matters: "about 18 percent", not "17.94 percent". Turn rates into counts people can picture: "18 percent late" becomes "nearly 1 in 5 orders, about 900 a day". Compare with something familiar: "the extra riders cost less than one day of lost orders each month". Keep units consistent across the report, taka or lakh taka, not both. Each of these small choices makes a number land instead of slide past.

Executive summary, worked: A strong executive summary fits on half a page. Here is one for a delivery problem. "Answer: We can reduce late deliveries by about a third by adding evening riders in two zones. Evidence: Late deliveries rose from 12 to 18 percent over three months; 60 percent of them are in Mirpur and Uttara between 6 and 9 pm, where each rider handles about 4.5 orders per hour against 2.5 elsewhere. Uncertainty: Our estimate of the improvement ranges from about a quarter to about two-fifths, depending on demand growth. Recommendation: Operations should add 15 riders in these zones in the evening for a two-month trial, at about 3 lakh taka a month. Next step: Run the trial in Mirpur first with Uttara as comparison, and review results after four weeks." Five parts, every sentence useful, and nothing about how the data was cleaned.

Storytelling structure: A story keeps attention. A simple shape is situation, complication, resolution. Situation: "Customers are ordering more than ever." Complication: "But late deliveries have climbed to 18 percent and complaints are up." Resolution: "Two zones cause most of the problem, and evening riders can fix it." Use one concrete example, such as a real (anonymised) customer's 70-minute wait for ice cream that arrived melted, to make the numbers human. Do not invent drama; let the data provide the tension.

Slides, notebooks, dashboards and documents: Choose the format by purpose. Slides suit live presentations for decisions; keep them visual with few words, and put details in an appendix. Notebooks suit analysts: code, output and explanation together, though they are hard for non-technical readers. Dashboards suit ongoing monitoring of known metrics, not one-off findings (lesson 15). Written documents or memos suit careful decisions, because people can read at their own pace; some companies, like Amazon, famously prefer written narrative memos to slides for important meetings. Many projects need two: a short memo or deck for decision makers and a technical appendix or notebook for reviewers.

Reproducible reports: A report whose numbers no one can regenerate is fragile. Keep the code that produces every number and chart, ideally running from raw data to final figures with one command. Tools like Jupyter, Quarto or R Markdown mix code and text so reports refresh automatically when data updates. Record the data version and date range, and note any manual steps. When a manager asks "why did this number change from last month?", you can answer in minutes instead of days. Lesson 25 builds a full reproducible workflow.

Handling questions and pushback: People will challenge your findings, and that is healthy. Prepare for likely questions: "Did you account for Eid?", "Is this just one bad month?", "What about the new rider app?". Keep backup slides with the answers. When you do not know, say so and promise to check. When someone's experience contradicts the data, take it seriously: frontline staff often notice things data misses, like a road closure, and the conversation can reveal a data error or a new feature. Separate facts from interpretation, and be willing to change your view if the evidence supports it.

Answering "so what?": When someone asks "so what?", they are asking why they should care. Connect every finding to money, time, customers, risk or a decision. "Average delivery time rose by 4 minutes" becomes "the 4-minute rise pushed 6 percent more orders past the promised time, and those customers are about twice as likely to stop ordering". If you cannot answer "so what?" for a finding, leave it out or move it to an appendix. A useful habit is to write the "so what" sentence directly under every chart in your draft; if writing it feels forced, the chart probably does not belong in the main story.

Real-life example 1, a hospital waiting-time report: An analyst at a district hospital studies outpatient waiting times. Instead of 30 charts, the report to the hospital director opens with: "Patients wait longest, about 3 hours, on Sunday mornings, because two of five doctors are usually in ward rounds then. Moving ward rounds to the afternoon would likely cut Sunday waiting to under 2 hours." One chart shows waiting by day and hour with Sunday morning highlighted. The director approves a one-month trial, and the follow-up report compares waiting before and after with a similar hospital as reference.

Real-life example 2, an NGO funding pitch: A nutrition NGO wants a donor to fund expansion. The analyst's deck has six slides: the answer (the programme reduced child stunting in pilot unions), the evidence with a difference-in-differences comparison against similar unions (lesson 18) and a range for the effect, the cost per child, the plan for expansion with a monitoring design, and an appendix with methods. One photograph of a community health worker weighing a child, used with consent, sits beside the main chart. The donor's analyst checks the appendix, finds it sound, and funding is approved.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include presenting the analysis process instead of the answer, too many charts, chart titles that describe instead of state, jargon like "statistically significant at alpha 0.05" for a non-technical audience, hiding uncertainty or overwhelming people with it, findings without recommendations, recommendations without owners, and reports nobody can reproduce. Exams ask you to write an executive summary, explain the pyramid principle, turn a finding into a recommendation, rewrite a chart title as an action title, choose a format for an audience, and explain how to communicate uncertainty.

Recap: Analysis is only valuable when it is understood and acted on. Know your audience, put the answer first, and support it with a few charts that each make one point. Turn findings into specific recommendations, state uncertainty in plain ranges, choose the right format, keep reports reproducible, and welcome questions. Next, we look at the responsibilities that come with data: ethics, privacy and fairness.
key_points: Analysis only creates value when someone understands it and acts on it.
Know your audience: executives want decisions, managers want actions, analysts want methods.
Lead with the answer (the pyramid principle), then give supporting evidence.
One chart, one message, with a title that states the finding.
Turn findings into recommendations that say who should do what, with expected impact.
State uncertainty in plain words and ranges, without hiding it or drowning in it.
Choose slides, notebooks, dashboards or written reports by purpose, and keep reports reproducible.
lessons.tip: Before making any slide or chart, write your main message as one sentence a busy manager could repeat to their boss. If you cannot write that sentence, you are not ready to present.
lessons.task: Take any finding from your own life or an earlier lesson's task, for example how your sleep changed over two weeks. Write a five-sentence executive summary: the answer first, the key evidence with one number, the uncertainty, the recommendation, and the next step. Then design one chart whose title states the message.

quiz.q: According to the pyramid principle, how should a findings memo begin?
options: With a detailed description of the data cleaning
With the main conclusion or recommendation
With a history of the project
With all the charts in order of creation
quiz.explain: Busy readers need the answer first; supporting evidence follows for those who want detail.

quiz.q: Which chart title is best?
options: "Mirpur and Uttara cause 60 percent of late deliveries"
quiz.explain: An action title states the message, so the reader knows what to see before reading the axes.

quiz.q: How should you report a predicted sales rise of 12 percent with a 95 percent interval of 4 to 20 percent to a manager?
options: "Most likely around 12 percent, and probably somewhere between 4 and 20 percent"
quiz.explain: Give the best estimate plus a plain range; it is honest and still actionable.

quiz.q: Which is a recommendation rather than just a finding?
options: "Operations should add 15 riders in Mirpur from 6 to 9 pm, which we expect to cut late orders there by about a third"
"Late deliveries are higher in the evening"
quiz.explain: A recommendation names who does what, where and when, with expected impact.

quiz.q: A manager says "So what?" after your chart. What does that usually mean?
options: You have not connected the finding to a decision or consequence they care about
quiz.explain: "So what?" asks for the implication: what changes, how much it matters, and what to do.

lessons.title: Ethics, Privacy and Responsible Data Science
lessons.content:
Imagine you tell your closest friend a secret: you are worried about a health problem. A week later, a medicine company sends you advertisements about exactly that problem, and a relative asks about it at a wedding. You would feel betrayed, even if nobody said your name out loud. Data about people carries the same trust. Every row in a customer table, a hospital record or a survey is a real person who did not agree to be harmed. This lesson is about using data in ways that the people in it would accept: respecting consent and privacy, being fair, and being honest about results.

What responsible data science is: It is doing data work that is legal, fair, honest and respectful of the people behind the data. It covers what you collect, how you store and share it, how your models treat different groups, and how you report findings. It is not a separate final step; it runs through every stage from the question in lesson 03 to the report in lesson 23. Deep-cse-6-6 covers the wider professional ethics and cyber law; here we focus on issues specific to data analysis.

Why it matters: Harms are real. Leaked data enables fraud and harassment. Biased models can deny loans, jobs or medical care unfairly to whole groups. Misleading analysis can waste public money or harm patients. Organisations that lose trust lose customers and face fines. And as a data scientist, your name is on the work; integrity is part of the job.

Consent and purpose: People should know what data is collected and why, and agree where required. Purpose limitation means data collected for one purpose, such as delivering orders, should not quietly be used for an unrelated one, such as selling profiles to lenders, without a lawful basis and usually fresh consent. Consent should be clear, not buried in a 40-page policy, and as easy to withdraw as to give.

Personal and sensitive data: Personal data is any information about an identifiable person: name, phone number, national ID, address, device ID, location history, even a photo. Some categories are especially sensitive because misuse can cause serious harm: health, religion, ethnicity, political opinions, sexual orientation, biometric data and financial details. These need stronger protection and stronger reasons to use. Data minimisation means collecting only what you need, keeping it only as long as needed, and restricting who can see it.

Anonymisation is harder than it looks: Removing names is not enough. In a famous study, Latanya Sweeney estimated that ZIP code, full birth date and sex alone uniquely identify about 87 percent of Americans, and in the 1990s she re-identified the medical records of the governor of Massachusetts from supposedly anonymous hospital data by linking it with a public voter list. Fields like these are called quasi-identifiers: harmless alone, identifying together. Location traces, rare diseases and unusual purchase histories can identify people too.

k-anonymity, worked: One defence is k-anonymity, introduced by Pierangela Samarati and Latanya Sweeney: every combination of quasi-identifiers must be shared by at least k people. Suppose a survey table has area, exact age and sex. A 37-year-old woman in a small village may be the only one, so she is identifiable. Generalise: replace exact age with bands like 30 to 39, and village with union. Now check: if every combination of union, age band and sex appears at least 5 times, the table is 5-anonymous. Rows still unique after generalising can be suppressed. k-anonymity has limits: if all 5 people in a group share the same diagnosis, the diagnosis is revealed anyway, which led to refinements such as l-diversity.

Differential privacy: A stronger, mathematical approach is differential privacy, introduced by Cynthia Dwork and colleagues in 2006. The idea: add carefully measured random noise to results so that the output looks almost the same whether or not any single person's data is included. Then nobody can learn much about an individual from the published numbers. A privacy parameter, epsilon, sets the trade-off: smaller epsilon means more privacy and more noise. The United States Census Bureau used differential privacy for its 2020 census results, and large tech companies use it for some usage statistics.
