It works best for counts and averages over many people, not for tiny groups.

Security basics for analysts: Store data in approved, access-controlled places, not on personal laptops or shared drives. Use pseudonymous IDs instead of phone numbers in analysis tables. Never paste customer data into public tools. Delete local copies when done. Share aggregated results, not raw rows, and check that small cells, such as a count of 2 in a table, cannot reveal individuals. Deep-cse-6-2 covers the technical side of security; analysts' daily habits matter just as much.

Where bias comes from: Bias can enter at every step. Historical data reflects past discrimination: if fewer women were hired before, a model trained on past hiring learns that pattern; Amazon reportedly scrapped an experimental recruiting tool in 2018 for this reason. Sampling bias leaves out groups, such as people without smartphones in an app-based survey. Labels can be biased, such as "risky" defined by past officers' judgements. Features can act as proxies: area or phone brand can stand in for income or ethnicity. Feedback loops amplify bias: sending more inspectors to areas flagged as risky finds more problems there, which makes the model flag them even more.

A fairness check, worked: Compare outcomes across groups. Suppose a loan model approves 600 of 1,000 applicants from group A, a rate of 0.60, and 300 of 750 from group B, a rate of 0.40. The ratio is 0.40 divided by 0.60, about 0.67. A common warning line, from the four-fifths rule used in US employment guidance, is a ratio below 0.8. This does not prove unfairness, since groups may differ in ways that matter, but it demands investigation. Also compare error rates: among people who would truly repay, what share does the model approve in each group? Different fairness definitions can conflict mathematically, so choose deliberately with stakeholders and document the choice.

Transparency and accountability: People affected by data-driven decisions deserve to know that a model was involved, what kinds of data it used, and the main reasons for their result, in words they understand. Inside the organisation, every model and dataset should have a named owner who answers for it. Keep logs of which model version made each important decision, so that mistakes can be traced and corrected. When something goes wrong, such as a model wrongly blocking many genuine customers, fix it quickly, tell those affected, and record what was learned. Openness about failures builds more trust than pretending they never happen.

Reducing bias: Collect more representative data, remove or reconsider proxy features, check performance by group (lesson 21), adjust thresholds per group only where legally and ethically appropriate, and keep a human review for high-stakes decisions. Most importantly, involve people affected and domain experts in deciding what fair means for this decision.

Honest analysis and p-hacking: Ethics also means honesty with results. p-hacking means trying many analyses, subgroups or metrics and reporting only those that look significant. If you test 20 subgroups at 0.05 with no real effects, you expect about one false positive by chance, and the chance of at least one is about 64 percent. Other forms include stopping data collection when p dips below 0.05 (lesson 17), dropping inconvenient outliers without a rule, and changing the outcome after seeing data. Remedies: write the analysis plan before seeing results, a practice called pre-registration in science, report every test you ran, correct for multiple comparisons, and share code so others can check.

Laws and regulations: Many countries regulate personal data. The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, GDPR, in force since May 2018, is a widely copied example: it requires a lawful basis for processing, purpose limitation and minimisation, gives people rights to access, correct and delete their data, requires breach notification, and allows large fines. It applies to organisations anywhere that process data of people in the EU. Other countries have their own laws, and they change, so check the current rules for where you work and for whose data you handle. Laws are a minimum; ethical practice often asks more. When unsure, ask your organisation's legal or privacy officer before using the data.

A responsible data checklist: Before starting, ask: Do we have the right to use this data for this purpose? Do we need every field? Can we use aggregated or pseudonymised data? Who could be harmed if it leaked or if the model is wrong? Have we checked outcomes across relevant groups? Is there a human appeal for important decisions? Are we reporting all analyses honestly? Who is accountable? Writing answers in a short document, such as part of a model card (lesson 21), turns good intentions into practice.

Real-life example 1, mobile money and credit: A digital lender wants to use mobile wallet history to offer small loans to people without bank records, which can widen access to credit. The team limits features to transaction patterns, excludes contact lists and SMS content, explains reasons for rejections, checks approval and error rates across regions and genders, and gives applicants a way to appeal. When the check shows lower approval for rural women with similar repayment records, they find a feature tied to phone type acting as a proxy, remove it and recheck.

Real-life example 2, publishing health survey results: A health research team wants to publish union-level results from a survey on a sensitive disease. Some unions have only 3 or 4 cases, and the villages are small enough that neighbours might guess who they are. The team publishes at upazila level instead, suppresses cells below 10, and releases the detailed data only to approved researchers under a data use agreement. The public still learns where the disease is concentrated, without exposing individuals.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include assuming removing names makes data anonymous, collecting everything just in case, reusing data for new purposes without checking consent, ignoring proxies, checking only overall accuracy, p-hacking and selective reporting, publishing tables with tiny cells, and treating legal compliance as the whole of ethics. Exams ask you to explain consent, purpose limitation and minimisation, describe re-identification risk with an example, check k-anonymity on a small table, explain differential privacy in words, list sources of bias, compute a group approval ratio, explain p-hacking, and outline key GDPR rights.

Recap: Data is about people. Collect only what you need with clear consent and purpose, protect it, and remember that removing names is not anonymisation; k-anonymity and differential privacy help. Look for bias in data, labels, features and feedback loops, and check outcomes across groups. Report honestly, without p-hacking. Follow the law and go beyond it with a simple checklist. Last lesson brings everything together in a reproducible workflow and a full capstone project.
key_points: Responsible data science respects consent, collects only what is needed and uses data only for stated purposes.
Removing names is not anonymisation; combinations like area, birth date and sex can re-identify people.
k-anonymity requires every combination of identifying attributes to be shared by at least k people.
Differential privacy adds carefully measured noise so results reveal almost nothing about any one person.
Bias enters through data, labels, features and feedback loops; check outcomes across groups.
p-hacking and selective reporting mislead; pre-register plans and report all analyses honestly.
Laws such as the EU's GDPR set rights and duties; good practice goes beyond legal minimums.
lessons.tip: Before any project, imagine the people in your data reading a newspaper story about what you did with it. If they would feel betrayed, change the plan before you write a line of code.
lessons.task: Pick an app you use daily. List five kinds of data it probably collects about you. For each, write one helpful use and one harmful use. Then write three rules you would want the company to follow, using ideas from this lesson such as purpose limitation, minimisation and fairness checks.

quiz.q: A dataset has names removed but keeps area, full birth date and sex. Why is it still risky?
options: It is not risky once names are gone
The combination can uniquely identify many people when linked with other data
quiz.explain: Latanya Sweeney showed that ZIP code, birth date and sex alone uniquely identify a large majority of Americans.

quiz.q: Group A has 600 of 1,000 loans approved and group B has 300 of 750. What is B's approval rate divided by A's?
quiz.explain: A: 0.60, B: 0.40; 0.40 / 0.60 is about 0.67, below the common four-fifths (0.8) warning line.

quiz.q: What does k-anonymity with k = 5 require?
options: Every combination of quasi-identifiers appears for at least 5 people
quiz.explain: If each combination of area, age band and sex is shared by at least 5 people, no one can be singled out by them alone.

quiz.q: An analyst tests 20 customer subgroups and reports only the one with p below 0.05. What is the problem?
options: p-values cannot be computed for subgroups
Nothing, it is a valid finding
With 20 tests, about one false positive is expected by chance, so the result is likely noise
quiz.explain: Reporting only the "winner" from many tests is p-hacking; report all tests or correct for multiple comparisons.

quiz.q: Which practice follows data minimisation?
options: Collecting every possible field in case it is useful later
Collecting only the fields needed for the stated purpose and deleting them when no longer needed
Sharing data with all partners by default
quiz.explain: Minimisation means collect only what you need, keep it only as long as needed.

lessons.title: Reproducible Workflow and Capstone Project
lessons.content:
Imagine baking a cake that everyone loves. A month later, your cousin asks for the recipe. If you remember only "some flour, some sugar, baked until it looked done", the cake can never be made again, not even by you. If you wrote exact amounts, the oven temperature, the order of steps and the brand of baking powder, anyone can bake it again. Data analysis is the same. A result that nobody can recreate cannot be trusted, checked or improved. This final lesson shows how to organise a project so it can be rerun, then walks through a full capstone project that uses everything in this course.

What reproducibility is: An analysis is reproducible when someone else, with the same raw data and code, can rerun it and get the same results. It is not about getting a good result once; it is about recording the full path from raw data to every number and chart. Reproducibility protects against silent mistakes, lets reviewers check your work, makes updates with new data easy, and lets a teammate take over when you are on leave.

Why projects become irreproducible: Common causes are cleaning data by hand in a spreadsheet with no record, running notebook cells out of order, files named final, final2 and final_really_final, code that depends on a file on someone's desktop, library versions that change, and random steps without a fixed seed. Each one turns "what we found" into "what we found that one day on that one laptop".

Project folder structure: A simple, common layout keeps things clear. A data folder with raw, interim and processed subfolders; a notebooks folder for exploration; a src folder for reusable code; a reports folder with figures; plus a README file explaining the question, how to set up and how to run. Raw data is never edited by hand; cleaning code reads raw and writes processed. Templates like Cookiecutter Data Science provide such a structure ready-made. The exact names matter less than consistency across your team.

Version control with git: Git records every change to code with a message, so you can see what changed, when and why, and go back if something breaks. Commit small, meaningful steps: "add zone late-rate feature" rather than "updates". Use branches for experiments. Do not commit large data files or secrets like database passwords; use a .gitignore file to exclude them. Deep-cse-4-4 covers git in software engineering; data projects need the same discipline.

Data versioning and environments: Data changes too: new rows arrive, a source table is corrected. Record which data version, date range and query produced each result. Tools like DVC track data files alongside git; simpler teams save dated snapshots and log their source. Code also depends on library versions: a new pandas release can change a default and shift results. Record the environment in a requirements.txt or conda environment file with exact versions, and set random seeds for anything random, like train-test splits, so reruns match.

From notebooks to pipelines: Notebooks are excellent for exploring, but long notebooks run out of order become fragile. Once a step is settled, move it into a script or function in src with a clear input and output: load raw, clean, build features, train, evaluate, make figures. A simple pipeline runs these in order with one command, using a Makefile, a small Python script, or workflow tools such as Airflow or Prefect for scheduled production pipelines. Data Engineering (deep-cse-7-11) covers building such pipelines at scale, and Advanced Database Systems and Big Data (deep-cse-7-2) covers storing and processing very large data.

Testing data and code: Add simple checks that fail loudly: row counts within expected ranges, no duplicate order IDs, no negative prices, dates within the expected period, every zone in the lookup table. These assertions, run every time the pipeline runs, catch broken source data before it reaches a report. Small unit tests for tricky functions, like a holiday flag builder, prevent silent errors when code changes.

Documentation and handover: A short README answers four questions: what question does this project answer, where does the data come from, how do I set up the environment, and which command reproduces the results. Add a data dictionary listing each column with its meaning, unit and source, and a decision log noting choices like "orders with missing delivery time excluded, 1.5 percent, checked by zone". When a teammate can rerun the project and understand every choice without calling you, the handover is done.

Capstone, the problem: BazarKoro is an invented online grocery service in Dhaka. Customers order rice, vegetables, fish and household items, delivered within a promised one-hour window. Complaints about late deliveries have risen and app ratings are falling. The head of operations asks the data team: "Why are deliveries late, and what should we change first?" We will apply the full workflow.

Capstone, question and metric: Working with operations (lesson 03), the team defines late as more than 10 minutes after the promised time, the primary metric as the share of late orders per week, and guardrails as cost per delivery and order cancellations. The decision at stake is where to spend next quarter's operations budget. Success: cut late orders from 22 percent to under 15 percent within three months without raising cost per delivery by more than 5 percent.

Capstone, data and SQL: The data lives in the company database (lesson 06). The team writes SQL that joins orders, deliveries, riders, stores and zones for the last 90 days, selecting order time, promised time, delivered time, store, zone, distance, number of items, payment method and rider ID. Weather data comes from a public feed by hour. The query is saved in the project's src folder and the pull is dated, so the extract can be recreated exactly.

Capstone, cleaning: Cleaning code (lessons 10 and 11) finds about 3 percent duplicate rows from app retries and removes them by order ID, converts all times to Dhaka time, flags 1.5 percent of deliveries with delivered time missing because riders forgot to tap, and excludes those from the late rate after checking they are not concentrated in one zone. A few negative durations from clock errors are set to missing. Every rule is in code, with counts logged before and after.

Capstone, EDA: Exploration (lessons 12 to 14) of about 30,000 orders a month finds 6,600 late, 22 percent. Grouping by hour reveals the key pattern: 4,200 of 12,000 evening orders between 6 and 9 pm were late, 35 percent, against 2,400 of the other 18,000, about 13 percent. Mapping by zone shows two dense zones carrying most evening lateness. Riders per open order in those zones drop sharply in the evening. Rain roughly doubles lateness at peak hour. The team makes three charts with action titles, including "Evening orders are late almost three times as often as the rest of the day".

Capstone, test: Operations proposes two changes: adding evening riders and batching nearby orders. Rather than guessing, the team designs an experiment (lesson 17). Because riders and customers in one zone interact, they randomise by zone-evening: on randomly chosen evenings in matched zones, the new dispatch rules run. After four weeks with a pre-planned sample, late orders in treated zone-evenings fall by about a quarter compared with control, with an interval that excludes zero, while cost per delivery rises within the guardrail.

Capstone, model: To target riders better, the team builds a model (lessons 19 to 21) predicting each hour's late risk per zone, with features like day, hour, Ramadan and pre-Eid flags, forecast rain, recent orders per rider and the zone's smoothed late rate. A seasonal naive baseline is beaten clearly on a time-based validation. Permutation importance confirms orders per rider and rain as top drivers. The model is documented in a model card and monitored for drift.

Capstone, recommendation and ethics: The executive summary (lesson 23) leads with the answer: "Adding evening riders with smarter batching in two zones should cut late deliveries from 22 to about 15 percent at a 4 percent cost increase; we recommend rolling it out and using the hourly risk model to schedule riders." Ethics checks (lesson 24) confirm that rider-level data is used only for scheduling, not to punish individual riders, that analysis tables use pseudonymous IDs, and that the risk model does not reduce service to lower-income zones; the team checks late rates by zone after rollout.

Capstone, lessons from the journey: Not everything went smoothly. The first SQL pull double-counted orders with two payment attempts, caught only because a row-count check failed. An early chart suggested cash on delivery caused lateness, but grouping by zone showed cash orders were simply more common in the busy zones, a confounder (lesson 18). The first model looked excellent until the team noticed a feature computed from the whole day's orders, leakage that would not exist at prediction time. Each catch came from a habit taught in this course, which is exactly why the habits matter.

Course recap: You have walked the full data science workflow. Ask clear questions with useful metrics. Understand data types and tidy tables, collect data carefully, and query it with SQL. Use Python and pandas to clean, reshape and explore. Visualise honestly. Estimate with uncertainty, test with care, and think hard about causation. Engineer good features, start modeling from baselines, interpret and check models, and use unsupervised tools for segments, anomalies and baskets. Communicate answers first, act ethically, and keep everything reproducible.

What next: To go deeper, revisit Machine Learning (deep-cse-6-1) and Probability and Statistics (deep-cse-2-6), learn databases (deep-cse-4-2) and data mining (deep-cse-7-6), and explore data pipelines and big data tools. Practise on public data: Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics publications, open data portals, or Kaggle datasets. Most of all, learn the domain you work in, whether health, finance, agriculture or retail; the best data scientists know which questions matter. Build a small portfolio of two or three complete projects, each with a clear question, clean code and a short written report, to show employers what you can do.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Mistakes include editing raw data by hand, running notebooks out of order, no version control, unpinned library versions, no random seeds, secrets committed to git, and capstones that skip the question or the recommendation. Exams ask you to define reproducibility, sketch a project structure, explain why git, data versioning and environment files matter, convert a notebook workflow into a pipeline, and outline a full data science project for a scenario from question to recommendation.

Recap: Reproducible projects use a clear folder structure, untouched raw data, git, data and environment versions, seeds and pipelines with checks. The BazarKoro capstone shows the whole journey: a clear question and metric, an SQL pull, careful cleaning, revealing EDA, a randomised test, a validated model, a specific recommendation and ethics checks. With these habits, your analysis can be trusted, repeated and improved, which is what turns data into good decisions.
key_points: A reproducible project can be rerun from raw data to final results by anyone, giving the same answers.
A clear folder structure separates raw data, processed data, code, notebooks and reports.
Git tracks code changes; data versioning and environment files pin data and library versions.
Pipelines turn notebook steps into scripts that run in order, with raw data never edited by hand.
The full workflow runs question, data, cleaning, EDA, statistics or modeling, communication and ethics.
A capstone shows the whole workflow on one realistic problem with a clear recommendation.
Next steps include deeper machine learning, data engineering, databases and domain knowledge.
lessons.tip: Treat your future self as a stranger. Write every step so that someone who has never seen the project, including you six months from now, can rerun it from raw data to final report with a few commands.
lessons.task: Plan your own mini data science project on a topic you care about, such as bus waiting times, cricket scores or household spending. Write the folder structure, the question and metric, where the data comes from, three cleaning checks, two EDA charts with action titles, one test or model with its baseline, one ethical risk, and the one-sentence answer you hope to give.

quiz.q: What does it mean for an analysis to be reproducible?
options: It produced a good result once
Someone else can rerun it from the raw data and get the same results
quiz.explain: Reproducibility means the path from raw data to results is fully recorded and rerunnable.

quiz.q: In a good project structure, how should the raw data folder be treated?
options: Edit it directly to fix errors
Never edit it by hand; cleaning code writes to a separate processed folder
quiz.explain: Keeping raw data untouched lets anyone rerun the cleaning and check every decision.

quiz.q: Why record library versions in an environment file such as requirements.txt?
options: So the same code gives the same results on another computer or later in time
To make the code run faster
It is required for git to work
quiz.explain: Library updates can change defaults and results; pinned versions keep runs consistent.

quiz.q: In BazarKoro's data, 4,200 of 12,000 evening orders and 2,400 of 18,000 other orders were late. What are the two late rates?
Which step should come first in a data science project?
options: Defining the question, decision and success metric with stakeholders
quiz.explain: Everything else depends on a clear question and how success will be measured (lesson 03).
